title: A.R.S. 33-1000: How Competing Mechanics Liens Rank in Arizona
shortSummary: Arizona A.R.S. 33-1000 puts every mechanics lien on your home on equal footing, no matter who recorded first. If the property is foreclosed and the sale does not cover all the liens, the claimants split the proceeds pro rata rather than by filing order. Recording early does not buy a spot at the front of the line.
bodyHtml:
When more than one subcontractor or supplier liens the same home, you might expect whoever recorded first to get paid first. Arizona does the opposite for mechanics liens. Section 33-1000 puts them all on equal footing and splits the money proportionally when there is not enough to go around.

What the statute says

Every mechanics and materialman lien on your home holds the same rank as the others:

on an equal footing without reference to the date of recording the notice and claim of lien.

So the framer who recorded a mechanics lien in month two and the painter who recorded in month eight stand in the same position against your property. There is no first-come advantage among the trades. A sub who races to the recorder gains nothing over one who files on the last allowable day.

Equal footing settles rank, not validity. Each claimant still has to clear its own hurdles: the twenty day preliminary notice, the deadline to record the lien, and the six-month window to sue. A lien that misses one of those drops out of the group. Section 33-1000 only sorts the claims still standing.

What happens if a foreclosure sale falls short

If the home is foreclosed and the sale does not raise enough to pay every lien in full, the claimants share what there is in proportion to what they are owed:

the proceeds of the sale...shall be prorated over the respective liens that have equal footing with the foreclosing lien.

For example, say three subcontractors are owed thirty thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand dollars. That is sixty thousand in claims. The sale produces only thirty thousand for the mechanics liens. Each sub collects half of what it claimed: fifteen thousand, ten thousand, and five thousand. Every claimant takes the same percentage cut, and no one moves ahead by having recorded earlier.

Read the statute's phrase "equal footing with the foreclosing lien" closely. The proration runs across the mechanics liens as a class. It does not sweep in every other interest recorded against your title.

Why this matters to you as the owner

This rule ranks the lien claimants against each other. Where a mechanics lien sits against your mortgage and other recorded interests is a separate question, covered by lien priority and relation-back under 33-992. For you, a race to record changes neither your total exposure nor who is entitled to foreclose. Your exposure is the sum of the unpaid claims, in whatever order they land. Because every unpaid trade has the same standing, the only reliable protection is making sure each one is actually paid and has signed off as the job moves along.

How this connects to the rest of the lien process

Section 33-1000 is the internal ranking rule of Arizona's lien system, and it works alongside the six-month deadline a claimant has to foreclose. Sorting out priority is always worse than avoiding liens in the first place, which is what lien waivers at each draw are for. If liens are already stacked on your title, start with what a mechanics lien is and how releases work on a new home. The equal-footing and proration rule is in A.R.S. 33-1000.

title: A.R.S. 33-1003: Using a Payment Bond to Block Liens on Your Arizona Home
shortSummary: Arizona A.R.S. 33-1003 lets an owner require the contractor to furnish a payment bond. Once the bond and the contract are recorded with the county recorder, subcontractors and suppliers can no longer lien the home. They must claim against the bond instead, leaving only the direct contractor able to record a lien.
bodyHtml:
Most Arizona homeowners deal with mechanics liens after the fact. Section 33-1003 gives you a way to head them off before they can happen. By requiring your contractor to post a payment bond and recording it, you can put your home out of reach of subcontractor and supplier liens before the first shovel hits the dirt.

What the statute allows

You, the owner, can require the general contractor you sign with to furnish a payment bond. That bond stands in for the lien rights that subcontractors and suppliers would otherwise have under the right to a lien. The bond has to be written by a licensed surety company, not an individual, and its amount and form follow Arizona's public-project bond rules in Title 34.

The protection turns on recording. Once you record the bond together with a copy of the construction contract at the county recorder, the statute is blunt about the effect:

no lien shall thereafter be allowed or recorded...except by the person who contracts, in writing, directly with the owner.

What that means in practice

After the bond is recorded, subcontractors and suppliers can no longer put a mechanics lien on your home. If one of them goes unpaid, they make a claim against the bond instead of clouding your title. The only party that keeps a lien right against the property is your direct contractor, the one you signed the contract with.

That flips the usual risk. Normally you can pay your builder in full and still get liened by an unpaid sub. With a recorded payment bond, that exposure moves off your house and onto the surety company that wrote the bond.

Imagine two identical builds where the tile supplier goes unpaid. On the bonded job, the supplier's claim runs to the surety, the owner's title stays clear, and the construction loan converts on schedule. On the unbonded job next door, that same supplier records a lien against the house, and the owner has to clear it before the lender will fund. Same unpaid bill, opposite outcomes, decided by whether the bond and the contract were recorded first.

When it is worth doing

On a nine hundred thousand dollar custom build, you want your title spotless through a construction-to-permanent loan. You write the bond requirement into your contract with the general, the general's surety issues the bond, and you record it with the contract before work starts. Now if the drywall subcontractor is not paid, they pursue the bond, and your home stays clean. The trade-off is cost. The general prices the bond premium into your contract, so you weigh that premium against the value of taking lien risk off your property.

How this connects to the rest of your lien protection

The payment bond is the prevention route. It sits next to the tools that protect you when there is no bond: the rule that your payments are held in trust for the trades, the lien waivers you collect at each draw, and, if a lien is filed and later paid, the release rules. To see the risk this bond is designed to remove, read can a subcontractor put a lien on my house if I already paid the builder. The bond mechanism itself lives in A.R.S. 33-1003.

title: A.R.S. 33-1004: Bonding a Recorded Mechanics Lien Off Your Arizona Home
shortSummary: Arizona A.R.S. 33-1004 lets you clear a recorded mechanics lien off your home by recording a surety bond worth 150 percent of the lien claim. The property is released from the lien and the claimant pursues the bond instead. It is how an owner frees a clouded title while a payment dispute is still unresolved.
bodyHtml:
A recorded mechanics lien can freeze a sale or a loan closing while you are still fighting over whether the money is even owed. Section 33-1004 gives you an escape hatch. You can move the lien off your property and onto a surety bond, so your title clears and the dispute carries on against the bond instead of your home.

What the statute allows

An owner, or anyone with a legal or equitable interest in the land, along with a contractor, subcontractor, or mortgagee, can discharge a recorded lien by recording a surety bond. The release of the property is immediate and does not wait on the claimant:

the property shall be discharged of such lien whether or not a copy of the bond is served on the claimant.

So the moment the bond is recorded, your real estate is free of that lien, even before the claimant is told it happened.

The 150 percent bond

The bond is not dollar for dollar with the lien. Arizona sets it higher:

in an amount equal to one hundred fifty percent of the demand set forth in and secured by the notice and claim of lien.

That extra fifty percent cushions the claimant for the interest, costs, and fees they could win on top of the base claim. Like the up-front payment bond, this one has to be written by a surety company authorized to do business in Arizona, never an individual.

How 33-1004 differs from the other lien tools

This is the after-the-fact version of the up-front payment bond in 33-1003. Section 33-1003 keeps most liens from ever attaching, while 33-1004 removes one that is already on record. It is also different from a release after payment under 33-1006. A release happens once the lien is actually paid or resolved. A 33-1004 bond clears your title while the fight is still live and the debt is still disputed.

What it means for your build

Suppose a stucco subcontractor records a fifty thousand dollar mechanics lien on your finished home, and you are two weeks from closing your permanent loan. You believe the sub was already paid through your builder, but you cannot wait out a lawsuit. A surety issues a bond of seventy-five thousand dollars, which is 150 percent of the fifty thousand claim, and you record it. Your title clears, your loan closes on time, and the subcontractor now has to prove the debt against the bond rather than against your house.

How this connects to the rest of your lien protection

Section 33-1004 is the release valve for when prevention did not hold. The payment bond, the trust-fund rule, and your lien waivers all failed to keep a lien from landing. Keep the six-month foreclosure deadline in mind too, since a claimant who never sues to foreclose can leave a lien to expire. To act on a lien already clouding your title, walk through how to remove a mechanics lien from your Arizona home. The bond-discharge procedure is set out in A.R.S. 33-1004.

The bond's form, the surety's authorization, and the exact amount all have to be right for the discharge to hold. This page explains the rule in general terms. A construction attorney or your title company is who works those details out on a live claim.

title: A.R.S. 33-1005: Construction Payments Held in Trust in Arizona
shortSummary: Arizona A.R.S. 33-1005 says the money an owner-occupant pays a contractor for labor, materials, and services is held in trust for the subcontractors and suppliers who earned it. The contractor cannot keep it for other uses and must pay the people who did the work when payment comes due.
bodyHtml:
When you write a check to your builder, Arizona law does not treat that money as simply theirs to spend. It is trust money, earmarked for the subcontractors and suppliers who put labor and materials into your home. That rule sits behind much of the protection you have if a builder gets paid but the trades do not.

What the statute requires

When an owner-occupant pays a contractor for labor, professional services, materials, machinery, fixtures, or tools, that payment is not an ordinary business receipt. The statute makes it a trust:

deemed for all purposes to be paid in trust and shall be held by the contractor for the benefit of the person or persons furnishing such labor, professional services, materials, machinery, fixtures or tools.

In plain terms, the contractor holds your money for the subs and suppliers. The builder cannot spend it on other jobs or other debts, and has to pay the right people when their payment comes due. The rule runs to owner-occupant payments, using the same owner-occupant definition as the owner-occupied dwelling exemption.

Why this protects you as the owner

This is the flip side of the lien system. A subcontractor who never got paid can still record a mechanics lien on your home even after you paid the builder in full. Section 33-1005 explains why that is the builder's fault, not yours: your money was never the builder's to keep, it was a trust fund for that sub. A builder who takes your draw and stiffs the trades has misapplied trust funds. For a licensed contractor, that is a far more serious problem than a simple billing dispute, and it can become grounds for ROC discipline.

This is why builders and title companies insist on a lien waiver at each draw. The waiver is your proof that the trust money actually reached the sub or supplier who signed it.

What it means for your build

Take the framing draw, for instance: sixty thousand dollars. You pay it to your builder, and under 33-1005 that sixty thousand is trust money for the framing crew and the lumber yard. If the builder instead spends it to cover a shortfall on another project and your framers go unpaid, the builder has diverted trust funds. Your framers can still lien your home, and the builder now faces a misapplied-funds problem on top of the contract fight. Your defense is the paper trail: the draw, the signed waiver, and proof the trades were paid before you released the next payment.

How this connects to the rest of the lien process

The trust-fund rule works hand in hand with the lien waivers you gather at each draw and the release of a satisfied lien once payment clears. If a sub liens you despite your payments, start with can a subcontractor put a lien on my house if I already paid the builder. The trust duty itself is set out in A.R.S. 33-1005.

title: A.R.S. 33-1006: Releasing a Paid-Off Mechanics Lien in Arizona
shortSummary: Arizona A.R.S. 33-1006 gives a lien claimant twenty days to record a release once a mechanics lien is paid off. If they miss that window, they owe you one thousand dollars plus any actual damages the unreleased lien causes. This is the law that clears a satisfied lien off your new home's title.
bodyHtml:
A paid mechanics lien does not fall off your home's title on its own. Someone has to record a release. Arizona law puts that job on the lien claimant, sets a hard deadline, and adds a penalty if they drag their feet. That matters most when a sub or supplier has already been paid in full and still has a lien sitting against your new house.

What the statute requires

Once a mechanics lien is satisfied, meaning it has been paid or otherwise resolved, the claimant has a short window to clear it:

When any lien established by the provisions of this article has been satisfied, the lienholder shall, within twenty days after satisfaction, issue a release of the lien.

Twenty days is the whole clock. The same duty applies when an owner-occupant sends a written request about a lien that should never have attached to their home. That ties directly to the owner-occupied dwelling exemption. The release also has to meet Arizona's standard recording-document format under A.R.S. 11-480, or the county recorder can reject it.

The penalty for sitting on a release

A claimant who ignores the twenty-day deadline owes you money:

Failure to grant such a release shall subject the lienholder or person to liability in the amount of one thousand dollars and also to liability for actual damages.

So a claimant who was paid and still refuses to release owes a flat one thousand dollars plus whatever the lingering lien actually costs you. On a new home, that damage number can climb fast. An open lien can block a closing, freeze a construction-to-permanent loan conversion, or force a rate-lock extension.

What it means for your build

Suppose your framing subcontractor recorded a mechanics lien during the build, and you clear it with a forty thousand dollar payment. Once that payment lands and the lien is satisfied, the sub has twenty days to record the release. Now put yourself fifteen days from closing on your permanent loan. Do the subtraction. The sub's twenty-day window runs five days past your closing date, so a claimant who takes every day the statute allows is still inside the law while the lien sits on your title the morning you sign. If the sub lets the release slide past day twenty, the statute makes them liable for the flat thousand dollars. On top of that comes your actual damage, such as an extension fee on your rate lock.

Do not rely on the deadline alone. Get a signed release or lien waiver at the moment of each payment. Then confirm the release is actually recorded at the county recorder, not just handed to you.

How this connects to the rest of the lien process

Section 33-1006 is the exit door of Arizona's mechanics lien system. It closes out the chain that starts with the right to a lien and recording the lien. It works alongside the lien waivers you collect at each draw, which keep liens from surviving payment in the first place. If a lien is already clouding your title, walk through how to remove a mechanics lien from your Arizona home. The exact wording, including the twenty-day clock and the recording standard it points to, is in A.R.S. 33-1006.

title: A.R.S. 33-1101: The Arizona Homestead Exemption Explained
shortSummary: A.R.S. 33-1101 is Arizona's homestead exemption. It automatically shields $400,000 of equity in the home you live in from most creditors, protecting it from attachment, execution, and forced sale. Any Arizona resident 18 or older gets one homestead, and the dollar figure rises every year with inflation.
bodyHtml:
Arizona automatically shields a large chunk of the equity in your main home from most creditors. Under A.R.S. 33-1101, that homestead exemption protects $400,000 of value in the place you live, and the figure climbs every year with inflation. If a creditor wins a money judgment against you, they generally cannot seize that protected equity or force a sale of your home to reach it.

How much equity is protected

The exemption covers $400,000 of value in your primary residence, and it protects that equity from three specific creditor moves: attachment, execution, and forced sale. Here is who the law gives it to:

Any person who is at least eighteen years of age, married or single, and who resides within this state may hold as a homestead exempt from attachment, execution and forced sale.

Read the word "equity" carefully. The homestead protects your stake in the home, which is the market value minus what you still owe on it, not the full sale price. If your house is worth $700,000 with a $350,000 loan, your equity is $350,000, and all of it sits under the current $400,000 shield. Build equity past the exemption amount and only the slice above the line is exposed to an ordinary judgment creditor.

Who qualifies and what property counts

Any Arizona resident at least 18 years old, married or single, gets one homestead on the home they live in. The property can take almost any common form: a house on land you own, a condominium or cooperative, or a mobile home, park model, motor home, travel trailer, fifth wheel, houseboat, or manufactured home, along with the land it sits on. You have to actually reside there. The one hard limit is quantity:

Only one homestead exemption may be held by a married couple or a single person under this section.

That last line trips people up. A married couple does not stack two exemptions for $800,000. They share one. And you cannot spread the homestead across a primary home and a vacation place. It attaches to the single residence where you live.

The protected amount rises every year

The $400,000 base is not frozen. It steps up each January for the cost of living:

...shall be adjusted annually beginning on January 1, 2024 and thereafter on January 1 of each successive year by the increase in the cost of living...

The adjustment tracks the Consumer Price Index, measured August over August, and rounds up to the nearest $100. Arizona voters set the $400,000 base through Proposition 209 in 2022, raising it from the old $250,000. Because of the yearly bump, the amount actually protected in the current year runs somewhat higher than $400,000. The statute page prints the $400,000 base rather than each year's computed figure, so confirm the exact current-year number before you rely on a precise amount.

What it means for your build

Say you finish a custom home in Cave Creek worth $900,000 with a $500,000 construction-to-permanent loan, leaving $400,000 of equity. If an unrelated creditor, such as the winner of a business lawsuit, gets a judgment against you, the homestead shields that $400,000 of equity, so they generally cannot force a sale to collect. The exemption is automatic, so you do not file anything to claim it on your main home. What it does not do is stop a creditor you agreed to pay, like your mortgage lender, or a construction lien, which is exactly where A.R.S. 33-1103 draws the lines.

How this connects to lien law

The homestead is a shield against general judgment creditors, and it sits beside the construction-lien protections in this module. It is not the same as the owner-occupied dwelling lien exemption in A.R.S. 33-1002, which blocks certain subcontractor liens rather than shielding equity. A valid mechanics lien under A.R.S. 33-981 is one of the debts the homestead does not stop. The exceptions and the creditor-sale procedure live in sections 33-1103 and 33-1105. You can read the exemption amount, the eligible persons, and the annual-adjustment rule at View A.R.S. 33-1101 on azleg.gov.

Because the homestead only guards equity up to the yearly figure, the number that matters to you is your equity, not your home's price. For instance, hold that same Cave Creek home at $900,000 and pay the construction loan down to $350,000. Equity is then $550,000, so the homestead covers $400,000 of it and leaves $150,000 above the line, where an ordinary judgment creditor can reach it.

title: A.R.S. 33-1103: Four Debts the Arizona Homestead Cannot Stop
shortSummary: A.R.S. 33-1103 lists the debts that beat the Arizona homestead exemption. Your homestead protects home equity from a forced sale, but not against a consensual lien like a mortgage, a mechanics lien for labor or materials, child support or spousal maintenance arrearages, or a recorded judgment reaching equity above the exemption.
bodyHtml:
The Arizona homestead exemption has holes in it. A.R.S. 33-1103 says your homestead protects your equity from a forced sale, then lists four kinds of debt that punch straight through that protection. The two that matter most to anyone building a home are your own mortgage and a construction lien for unpaid labor or materials. Neither one is stopped by the homestead.

What the exemption covers, and its limit

The homestead makes the protected equity in your primary residence off-limits to an involuntary sale, but only against creditors who are not on the exceptions list. The dollar amount and eligibility come from A.R.S. 33-1101, which currently shields $400,000 of equity and rises each year with inflation. This section is where the law names the debts that ignore that shield entirely, or that can reach the equity sitting above it.

The four debts that beat a homestead

Four categories of lien or debt survive the homestead and can still reach your home:

A consensual lien, including a mortgage or deed of trust, or contract of conveyance... A lien for labor or materials claimed pursuant to section 33-981... A lien for child support arrearages or spousal maintenance arrearages... A recorded civil judgment or other nonconsensual lien [where] the debtor's equity in the real property exceeds the homestead exemption.

In plain terms, here is what each one means:

  • A consensual lien. This is any debt you agreed to secure with the home, most often a mortgage or deed of trust. You signed it, so the homestead never blocked it, and your lender can still foreclose if you default.
  • A mechanics lien under 33-981. A valid lien for unpaid construction labor or materials can force a sale despite the homestead. This is why an unpaid subcontractor is a real threat even on a home with equity.
  • Child support or spousal maintenance arrearages. Past-due family support that has been reduced to a judgment, secured by a statutory lien under A.R.S. 25-516, or given a court-ordered security interest can reach the home.
  • A recorded civil judgment or other nonconsensual lien. A general creditor who wins a money judgment can reach only the equity above the exemption, not the protected slice below it.

What this means when you build

For example, say your Scottsdale custom home is worth $1.2 million with a $600,000 mortgage, leaving $600,000 of equity. A business creditor wins a $250,000 judgment against you. Because the homestead protects the first $400,000 of equity, that creditor can only reach the $200,000 sitting above the line, and could force a sale to collect from that portion. Your mortgage lender is a different story: as a consensual lienholder it can foreclose regardless of the homestead if you stop paying. And a roofing sub holding a valid $18,000 mechanics lien under 33-981 is on the exceptions list too, so the homestead will not shield your equity from that lien.

How this fits homestead and lien law

The exemption amount and who qualifies are in A.R.S. 33-1101. This exceptions list is the reason a mechanics lien is dangerous even when you have equity, and why the owner-occupied dwelling exemption in A.R.S. 33-1002, which can block subs who never signed a contract with you, is worth having as a front-line defense. A creditor on this list still has to use the judgment-creditor sale procedure in A.R.S. 33-1105 to actually reach your equity. If a lien is already on your home, see how to remove a mechanics lien from your Arizona home. The full exceptions text is at View A.R.S. 33-1103 on azleg.gov.

The lesson from 33-1103 is that the homestead is built to stop strangers with money judgments, not debts you signed for or construction bills you left unpaid. On a build, that puts the weight back on keeping your loan current and paying or bonding off valid liens, because those are precisely the debts the law wrote the homestead to let through.

title: A.R.S. 33-995: Your Contractor Must Defend a Sub's Lien
shortSummary: A.R.S. 33-995 puts the burden of a subcontractor or supplier lien back on your general contractor. When someone other than your contractor records a lien and sues, the contractor must defend that action. You can withhold the amount sued for, or recover it back if you already paid the contractor in full.
bodyHtml:
If a subcontractor or supplier you never hired records a lien on your home and files suit, Arizona law does not leave you to fight it alone. A.R.S. 33-995 makes your general contractor defend that lawsuit, because the contractor is the party who took your money and was supposed to pay the people below them. It also gives you a direct way to make the contractor, not you, absorb the cost.

Who has to defend the lien lawsuit

Your general contractor does, whenever the lien comes from someone who is not itself a contractor. That means the subcontractors, material suppliers, and equipment lessors working under your builder. The statute states the duty plainly:

When a lien is recorded or notice given by any person other than a contractor, the contractor shall defend any action brought thereon.

A mechanics lien filed by a sub or supplier is really a symptom of a payment your general contractor collected but did not pass down. So the law hands the defense of that lawsuit to the contractor you did hire, not to you. You are not required to fund the fight or hire your own lawyer to answer a claim that your builder created.

How you make the contractor pay, not yourself

You get two money tools, depending on whether you still owe your builder anything. While the sub's foreclosure suit is pending, you can hold back the amount being claimed:

During pendency of such action the owner may withhold the amount sued for, and if judgment is given upon the lien, he may deduct from any amount due or to become due from him to the contractor the amount of the judgment and costs.

If money is still left on the contract, you withhold the sum the sub is suing for, and if the sub wins, you deduct that judgment plus court costs from the contractor's remaining balance. If you already paid the contractor in full, you can instead recover back from the contractor whatever you were forced to pay to clear the lien, since the contractor was the party originally liable. The section also lets a court award the winning side its reasonable expenses, including attorney fees, so a builder who forces a pointless fight risks paying for it.

What this looks like on a real build

For example, say you are building in Fountain Hills and your general contractor bills a $22,000 draw that covers the plumbing. You pay it. The contractor never pays the plumbing sub, and the sub records a $22,000 lien and sues to foreclose. Under 33-995, your contractor must step in and defend that suit. If you still have $40,000 left on the contract, you withhold the $22,000 the sub is claiming, and if the sub wins, you subtract the judgment and costs from the builder's remaining balance. If the job was already paid off, you turn around and collect the $22,000 back from the contractor. Either way, the unpaid-sub problem lands where it belongs.

Where this sits among your lien defenses

This section works next to your other homeowner protections. The proactive version, where you formally hold back money to cover potential liens, is A.R.S. 33-994. If you are a true owner-occupant, a sub with no direct written contract may have no valid lien at all under A.R.S. 33-1002. The lien right itself starts under A.R.S. 33-981, and it can only become a forced sale through the court process in A.R.S. 33-997. For the practical playbook when a sub liens your home after you paid the builder, see can a subcontractor put a lien on my house if I already paid the builder.

Full text and source

The duty to defend and the owner's deduction and recovery rights are spelled out at View A.R.S. 33-995 on azleg.gov.

The protection in 33-995 only bites when there is contract money left to deduct from, or a solvent contractor to collect back from. That is why the real safeguard is releasing funds on a draw schedule and holding retention until each sub signs a lien waiver, so a defended lien never outruns the money you still control.

title: A.R.S. 33-997: A Lien Cannot Sell Your Home Without a Court Order
shortSummary: A.R.S. 33-997 stops a mechanics lien from forcing a sale of your Arizona property on its own. No sale to satisfy the lien can happen until the claimant sues, wins a court judgment of foreclosure, and obtains a separate order of sale. A recorded lien alone gives no power to sell your home.
bodyHtml:
A mechanics lien on your Arizona home cannot force a sale by itself. A.R.S. 33-997 blocks any sale to satisfy a lien until the claimant has gone to court, won a judgment of foreclosure, and obtained a separate order directing the sale. Recording a lien clouds your title, but it is a long way from taking your house, and this section is the reason.

What the statute actually requires

Two court decisions have to exist before your property can be sold over a lien: a judgment of foreclosure and an order of sale. The section says it in a single sentence:

No sale of property to satisfy a lien granted under the provisions of this article shall be made except upon judgment of foreclosure and order of sale.

A recorded lien is a claim, not a power to sell. To turn it into a sale, the claimant must file a foreclosure lawsuit, prove the debt is real, prove the lien is valid, show they hit every deadline, and win. Only then can a court order the property sold. Each of those steps is a separate place the lien can fall apart.

What has to happen before any sale

The claimant has to clear the whole lien process, and most liens never finish it. The chain looks like this: serve the twenty day preliminary notice early, record the lien within the deadline under A.R.S. 33-993, then file suit to foreclose within six months under A.R.S. 33-998. Miss any one of those and there is no valid lien left to foreclose, so 33-997 never comes into play. If your home is an owner-occupied dwelling, the exemption in A.R.S. 33-1002 can wipe out a sub's lien before the process even starts.

What a lien sale looks like in practice

Suppose a grading sub records a $30,000 lien on your Rio Verde lot and does everything right: it sued within six months and won a foreclosure judgment for $30,000 plus costs. Even now the sub cannot list or sell your land. It has to obtain a court order of sale, and the sale is then carried out like other court-ordered sales of real property, usually a public sheriff's sale, with the proceeds paying the judgment first. If the property sells for more than the debt and costs, the surplus comes back to you. In practice, almost no residential lien reaches this point, because owners pay, bond the lien off under A.R.S. 33-1004, or beat the claim long before a judge signs an order of sale.

How this fits the lien timeline

This section is the last gate, the point where a paper claim could finally reach your equity, and it is guarded by a judge on both sides. The right to lien comes from A.R.S. 33-981, your builder has to defend a sub's lien suit under A.R.S. 33-995, and if a lien is already clouding your title, walk through how to remove a mechanics lien from your Arizona home. You can read the full one-line rule at View A.R.S. 33-997 on azleg.gov.

Because a lien sale needs a judge to sign both a foreclosure judgment and an order of sale, the moment that actually decides whether you keep the home is the foreclosure lawsuit, not the recording of the lien. If a claimant files suit, treat the court case, not the lien paper on your title, as the deadline you cannot ignore.

title: A.R.S. 9-467: What an Arizona City Building Permit Does, and Its Limits
shortSummary: A.R.S. 9-467 sets the ground rules for city building permits in Arizona. A city that issues your permit must send a copy to the county assessor and the state, cannot deny the permit over which utility serves your lot, and cannot make a later owner permit a prior owner's finished work first.
bodyHtml:
A building permit is the city's sign-off that your plans meet code and your project can go ahead. A.R.S. 9-467 frames how a city handles that permit. It also fences off several things a city cannot do with one. The section covers where your permit copies go, your right to pick a capable utility provider, and what happens when a prior owner's work shows up on a lot you buy.

Where your permit information goes

The first job of the statute is administrative, and it explains how your new home lands on the tax roll.

Any municipality requiring the issuance of a building permit shall transmit one copy of the permit to the county assessor and one copy to the director of the department of revenue.

When your city issues a permit for a new custom home, it forwards a copy to the county assessor and to the Arizona Department of Revenue. That is the paper trail that puts your new construction into the property-tax system. It is also why a big build shows up in the assessor's records not long after the permit issues. That record feeds the reassessment that raises your property taxes once the home is finished.

The utility-provider protection

A newer part of this section keeps utility choice out of the city's permit power.

A building permit applicant's ability to use a utility provider that is capable and authorized to provide utility service is not subject to further regulation by a municipality.

The statute calls utility regulation a matter of statewide concern, then bars a city from denying your permit based on the utility provider you plan to use. Utility service here means water, wastewater, natural gas including propane, or electric service. In practice, a city cannot reject your permit because you plan to run propane or natural gas instead of going all-electric. It also cannot reject it over which authorized water or power provider serves your parcel. On the metro fringe, a lot may be served by one specific water company or propane supplier. This section keeps that choice with you rather than the permit counter.

The limit on a prior owner's work

The section also protects a buyer from inheriting someone else's permit problem.

A municipality shall not require a subsequent owner to obtain a permit for the construction or addition done by the prior owner before issuing a permit for a building addition ...

Consider a buyer who closes on a Cave Creek lot where the prior owner enclosed a patio without a permit, and who now wants to add a casita. The city reviews the casita application on its own merits. It cannot force that buyer to permit the old patio work first, as a condition of issuing the permit for the new casita. The one carve-out is for genuine public health and safety provisions, so a real hazard can still be flagged. Outside of that, you are not on the hook to legalize a prior owner's project before you can move forward with your own.

What this means for you

9-467 mostly works in your favor, but the tax-roll piece is the part to plan for. Pulling the permit is what triggers your new home's entry into the assessor's system, so budget for the property-tax jump that follows a new build. On the utility side, this statute is your backstop if your design depends on gas or a particular provider. It gives you something to cite when a city tries to steer you elsewhere at permit time. And if you are buying a home with unpermitted prior additions, you can still permit your own new work without first curing the old.

For the mechanics of pulling and tracking a permit, our building-codes pages lay out what each city wants: see Scottsdale residential building permit requirements and Phoenix residential building permit requirements.

How this connects to the rest of the law

The permit under 9-467 is what lets you build to the code your city adopted under A.R.S. 9-802. It is separate from the sprinkler limit in A.R.S. 9-807. Counties issue their building permits under A.R.S. 11-861. Before the city issues the permit, your contractor has to show a valid license under A.R.S. 32-1169. The city may also charge development impact fees on the new home. The office that issues and inspects the permit is your authority having jurisdiction (AHJ). For the applied steps, see how to look up a building permit in Arizona and how long it takes to get a building permit in Arizona.

Full text and source

Read the current section, including the fee and definition subsections, on the legislature's site: View A.R.S. 9-467 on azleg.gov. The same text is on codes.findlaw.com.

The utility-choice language is recent. If a city pushes back on a gas or propane design at permit intake, cite this section by number and ask for any denial in writing.

title: A.R.S. 9-802: How an Arizona City Adopts a Building Code by Reference
shortSummary: A.R.S. 9-802 is the shortcut cities use to put a building code in force. Instead of reprinting a model code like the International Residential Code, a city passes one ordinance that adopts the code by reference, files at least three copies with the clerk, and the whole code becomes local law.
bodyHtml:
The building code that governs your Arizona custom home usually is not written by your city at all. Your city adopts it. A.R.S. 9-802 is the procedure behind that. It lets a town take a model code someone else wrote, like the International Residential Code, and make it local law. One ordinance does the job, with no retyping of hundreds of pages. Knowing how that works tells you where your code actually comes from and how to read it.

What adoption by reference means

A city does not have to reprint an entire model code inside its own municipal code. This section lets it point to the code instead.

A municipality may enact the provisions of a code or public record theretofore in existence without setting forth the provisions, but the adopting ordinance shall be published in full.

In plain terms, the city writes a short ordinance that says, in effect, we adopt this named code, this edition, with these local changes. The named code, the International Residential Code for one- and two-family homes for example, is the document you and your builder actually design to. The ordinance is the legal hook that pulls it into force inside city limits. The city can amend a code it adopted this way, using the same process. That is how local changes get layered on top of the base model code.

The filing and public-copy rule

Because the full code is not reprinted, the statute makes the city keep copies the public can read.

At least three paper copies or one paper copy and one electronic copy ... of the code or public record shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the municipality and kept available for public use and inspection.

That filing requirement is your access point. The exact edition and the local amendments that apply to your build are on file with the city clerk and the building department, not hidden. The ordinance itself has to be published in full, even though the code it adopts does not. So the adopting law is public even when the several-hundred-page code sits at the clerk's office rather than inside the ordinance text.

What this means for you

When someone says Scottsdale uses the 2018 International Residential Code, or Phoenix amended the energy code, 9-802 is the mechanism behind that sentence. Each Valley city runs its own adopting ordinance, which is why the base code can match across town lines while the local amendments differ. Before you finalize plans, get two things from the city: the exact code edition adopted, and the list of local amendments. A local change to a setback, a wall-bracing rule, or an energy requirement can move your design.

For example, Phoenix, Scottsdale, and Cave Creek each adopt the International Residential Code by reference, then add their own amendments. Our building-codes pages capture what each adopted: see Phoenix adopted building codes, Scottsdale adopted building codes, and Cave Creek adopted building codes. The edition and amendments there all trace back to an ordinance passed under this statute.

How this connects to the rest of the law

9-802 is the general adoption-by-reference tool, and building codes are one of its biggest uses. Once a city adopts a code this way, other statutes limit what that code can contain. A.R.S. 9-807 blocks a mandatory home-sprinkler provision. A.R.S. 9-467 governs the permit you pull to build under the adopted code. Counties use a parallel adoption power in A.R.S. 11-861. The code your city adopts is usually the International Residential Code, enforced by your authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) during plan review. For the city-by-city answer, see what building codes apply in Phoenix and what building codes apply in Scottsdale.

Full text and source

Read the current section on the legislature's site: View A.R.S. 9-802 on azleg.gov. FindLaw carries the same text at codes.findlaw.com.

The model code advances on a three-year cycle. The adopting ordinance does not. A city can sit years behind the newest published book, so ask which edition it has actually adopted before you design to the current one.

title: A.R.S. 9-807: Arizona Cities Cannot Force Fire Sprinklers on Your New Home
shortSummary: A.R.S. 9-807 bars an Arizona city from forcing you to install fire sprinklers in a new single-family home or a building with two or fewer units. The choice is yours. One exception survives: a sprinkler ordinance a city adopted before December 31, 2009 still stands, which is why Fountain Hills keeps its rule.
bodyHtml:
Most Arizona cities cannot make you put fire sprinklers in a new custom home. A.R.S. 9-807 is the reason. It takes the sprinkler decision away from city hall on any single-family house or small duplex and hands it to the owner, with one narrow exception for old ordinances that predate the rule. Here is what the statute blocks, what it still allows, and why one Valley town is different from its neighbors.

What the statute blocks

A.R.S. 9-807 speaks to cities and towns, not to you. It says a municipality cannot pass a code or rule that forces the sprinkler question one way or the other on a small home.

A municipality shall not adopt a code or ordinance ... that prohibits a person or entity from choosing to install or equip or not install or equip fire sprinklers in a single family detached residence or any residential building that contains not more than two dwelling units.

The protection covers the two housing types most custom-home clients build: a detached single-family house, and a building with no more than two units, such as a duplex or a main house with an attached second unit. The city also cannot charge a fine, a penalty, or tack on another requirement because of how you answer. Sprinklers stay an option you can add for safety or insurance reasons. They are not a line the city gets to force onto your plans.

The one exception: pre-2009 ordinances

The ban is not retroactive. A city that already required home sprinklers before the state stepped in gets to keep that rule.

This section does not apply to any code or ordinance that requires fire sprinklers in a residence and that was adopted before December 31, 2009.

That single date decides everything. A sprinkler mandate a town put on the books on or after December 31, 2009 is void under this section. One adopted before that date is grandfathered and still enforced. The statute sets no fire-flow, lot-size, or water-pressure trigger that would let a city bring back a mandate through a side door. If the local ordinance is newer than the cutoff, the city cannot require sprinklers on your house, and that is the end of it.

What this means for you

Whether your new home needs sprinklers comes down to one question: did your city grandfather a pre-2009 rule? Across most of the Jematell service area the answer is no. Scottsdale, Phoenix, Cave Creek, and Carefree cannot force sprinklers on a new single-family house, so that system is your call.

Fountain Hills is the standout. The town adopted its residential sprinkler requirement in April 2008, before the December 31, 2009 line, so 9-807 lets it keep the mandate. Build inside Fountain Hills town limits and your house needs an engineered sprinkler system covering every level plus the garage, which can add roughly 2 to 5 dollars per square foot to the job. Suppose a client prices one 4,000 square foot plan on two lots a few miles apart. On the Fountain Hills lot, the sprinkler system adds somewhere between $8,000 and $20,000 at that rate. On the Scottsdale lot, the same plan carries no sprinkler line at all, because Scottsdale has no grandfathered ordinance to enforce. Our page on Fountain Hills fire sprinkler requirements walks through the cost and the coverage.

One more practical point from the statute: a city has to accept the sprinkler permit application in print or electronic form, and it has to print the choice language from the statute on that application, so the option is spelled out where you sign.

How this connects to the rest of the law

9-807 is the sprinkler-specific limit on a city's broader power to write building rules. A city gets that power by adopting model codes under A.R.S. 9-802, and 9-807 carves the sprinkler mandate out of what those adopted codes can force on a small home. The county twin of this protection sits in A.R.S. 11-861 for unincorporated land. The town that enforces or waives the rule is your authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), and its fire rules ride on the International Fire Code. For the applied version, see do I need fire sprinklers in a new home in Fountain Hills and what building codes apply in Fountain Hills.

Full text and source

Read the current section, including the permit-format language, on the legislature's site: View A.R.S. 9-807 on azleg.gov. FindLaw mirrors the same text at codes.findlaw.com.

Because the whole rule turns on that 2009 cutoff, confirm your specific town carries no grandfathered sprinkler ordinance before you decide to leave the system off your plans.

title: Apache Junction Fence, Wall, and Retaining Wall Permit: The 6-Foot and 4-Foot Triggers
shortSummary: Apache Junction requires a building permit for a fence or wall over 6 feet and for a retaining wall over 4 feet measured from the bottom of the footing. Shorter walls are exempt if they meet zoning. A taller wall, or a retaining wall holding a surcharge, needs engineered plans.
bodyHtml:
Whether a wall or fence in Apache Junction needs a building permit comes down to two heights. A fence or wall over 6 feet, and a retaining wall over 4 feet, both need a permit through the Division of Building Safety and Inspection. Build shorter than that and you skip the permit, as long as the wall meets zoning. What catches people is how the city measures those heights. A fence is measured 3 feet out from its face, and a retaining wall is measured from the bottom of the buried footing.

When a wall or fence needs a permit

You need an Apache Junction building permit once a fence or wall passes 6 feet, or a retaining wall passes 4 feet of gross height including the footer. Below those lines, the city exempts the work in its Work Exempt from Permits handout:

Fences or block walls not over six (6) feet (91.44 cm) in height measured at three (3) feet from the exterior side.

Retaining walls which are not over four feet (4') (1,219 mm) in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, provided the retaining wall is not supporting a surcharge, is not impounding Class I, II, or III-A liquids, and is not located on a public easement.

So a plain fence or block wall at 6 feet or under is exempt, and a retaining wall at 4 feet or under is exempt only when it carries no extra load, holds no flammable liquid, and sits off any public easement. Cross those limits and the wall needs a permit reviewed against Apache Junction's adopted 2018 International Residential Code.

The measurements that trip people up

Two measuring rules decide whether you clear the exemption. A fence or wall is measured at 3 feet from its exterior side, so a wall built at the top of a slope reads taller from the low side. The city is blunt about it: a wall set at the top of an embankment does not meet the fence exemption. A retaining wall is measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, so the buried footer counts against the 4 feet.

Two smaller details matter. Intermittent posts or pillars may rise above 6 feet, but no higher than 7 feet. And a fence in a federally patented easement, next to a public right-of-way, or across a natural drainage way needs zoning review even under 6 feet.

When you need an engineer

Once a wall passes the exemption, the plans have to be engineered. Apache Junction's adopted 2018 IRC carries no prescriptive table for a free-standing wall over 6 feet or a retaining wall over 4 feet. Those walls get designed and stamped by an Arizona registered professional.

The reason is structural. A taller privacy wall catches more wind. A retaining wall holds back soil that grows heavier every time a monsoon storm soaks it. Apache Junction's expansive soil swells when it takes on that water and shrinks when it dries, which is what shoves a footing out of level and cracks the wall sitting on it. The engineer sizes that footing and the steel for the load.

A retaining wall also loses the exemption at any height in three cases. One is a surcharge, meaning added load pressing on the soil behind the wall from a driveway, a slope, or a structure. The second is impounding a Class I, II, or III-A liquid. The third is sitting on a public easement. Hit any of the three and you pull a permit with engineered plans, even for a 2-foot wall.

The walls you can build without a permit

A fence or block wall at 6 feet or under, and a retaining wall at 4 feet or under with no surcharge, stay permit-free. They do not skip zoning, though. Where a wall can sit, how tall it can be in each yard, and which materials are allowed all come from your zoning district, covered in Apache Junction residential zoning and setbacks. Keep the wall off any easement and out of a drainage path, since a solid wall can dam water onto a neighbor. A short front-yard garden wall is the classic no-permit case, as long as it meets those zoning rules.

A real Apache Junction example

For example, say a homeowner on an RS-GR lot wants a 6-foot block privacy wall plus a 3-foot retaining wall to level a building pad. Measured 3 feet out, the privacy wall lands right at 6 feet. The retaining wall is under 4 feet with nothing loading it. Both clear the exemption, so no building permit. If a natural wash crosses the back of the lot, the fence there still gets a quick zoning review.

Now change one thing. Raise the privacy wall to 7 feet, or the retaining wall to 5 feet, or pour a patio slab behind the retaining wall so it carries a surcharge. Any one of those turns the job into a permit with plans stamped by an Arizona registered engineer. The setbacks get checked either way.

How this connects to your other Apache Junction steps

Where a wall can go ties into your parcel's zoning and setbacks, which draw the buildable lines on the lot. When a taller wall needs a permit, it moves through the same city permit process as the house and gets checked during the Apache Junction inspection sequence, against the 2018 codes the city adopted. If the wall encloses a pool, it is reviewed with the pool as covered in the Apache Junction pool and spa permit. For related permit questions, see whether a shed or detached structure needs a permit and how long it takes to get a building permit in Arizona.

Source

The 6-foot fence and 4-foot retaining-wall triggers and the exemptions are published by the City of Apache Junction Division of Building Safety and Inspection and its Work Exempt from Permits handout on the Applications, Forms & Typical Details page. The walls are engineered to the 2018 IRC that Apache Junction adopts, tracked in the ICC code adoptions for Arizona.

Take your wall height and your lot's slope to the Division of Building Safety and Inspection before you order block. Exemption heights move when the city adopts a newer code edition, and the slope question is the one a plan reviewer will raise first.

title: Apache Junction Manufactured Home and Park Model Permit: The HUD, State, and City Split
shortSummary: Setting a manufactured home or park model in Apache Junction takes a city installation permit. Federal HUD standards and the Arizona Department of Housing govern how the home is built and anchored, while the city permits and inspects the foundation, utilities, and site before it issues a Certificate of Installation.
bodyHtml:
A manufactured home or park model cannot be set in Apache Junction until the city issues an installation permit. Three levels of government each own a piece of the job. Federal HUD rules govern how the home is built. The Arizona Department of Housing sets how it is installed and anchored. The city permits and inspects the foundation, the utilities, and the site. These homes make up a large share of Apache Junction's housing, and the city adds its own standards on top of the state and federal ones. The split matters most on two questions: whether your lot needs a permanent foundation or only skirting, and whether the home is new enough to be titled here at all.

Who handles what: HUD, the state, and the city

Three layers stack on one home. HUD sets the federal build standard. The home leaves the factory with a red HUD label showing it was built to 24 CFR 3280. A home earns that label only if it was built on or after June 15, 1976. An older unit is a mobile home. The city will not let a mobile home be installed unless it holds a state certificate showing it was brought up to code. The Arizona Department of Housing, through its Office of Manufactured Housing, sets the install rules. The city code points straight to the state rules:

M H installation shall comply with the requirements of Arizona Revised Statutes, Title 41, Chapter 37, Article 3 § 41-4001 thru 4010 and Arizona Administrative Code, Title 4, Chapter 34, § R4-34-101 thru 805.

The City of Apache Junction is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for the local permit. Its Division of Building Safety and Inspection issues the permit. It reviews the foundation and site, runs the inspections, and issues the Certificate of Installation that clears the home for use.

The permit path

You cannot install a manufactured home or park model without a city permit. The same holds for its electrical, plumbing, and mechanical connections. You apply through the city's permit intake. The set permit runs with separate trade permits for the hookups. Two limits catch buyers early. On a vacant lot in the modular districts (RS-7M, RS-10M, RS-20M, RS-54M, and RS-GR), the home must be titled no more than two years before the permit year. So you cannot drop a decade-old used home on a bare lot. The home also needs the HUD label. A park model is treated as an RV set. It follows the maker's install instructions and must be secured against tipping over.

Foundation, anchoring, and skirting

Where the home sits decides how it is held down. Apache Junction splits a private lot from a park. On a single-family lot in the larger districts, the home goes on a permanent foundation:

set upon a permanent foundation, as specified by the manufacturer and approved by the Arizona Department of Housing, Manufactured Housing Division, and that the space at the perimeter, between the home and the ground, be enclosed by concrete, concrete masonry units, brick or stone, with required access.

A permanent foundation carries the home's loads down to the soil through its footing. It is a poured base, not a strap-and-anchor tie-down. In a licensed home or RV park, the rule is lighter. The home is skirted in a uniform way and needs no permanent foundation. The city sets size minimums that change by location. On the larger lots, a home has two sections, each at least 12 feet by 36 feet, with a masonry perimeter, a 3:12 roof pitch, and a driveway at least 12 feet wide.

Utility hookups and the final inspection

The home has to be tied to power, water, and sewer through permitted work. If the temporary connections shipped with the unit are not used, the city requires hard connections made to the adopted codes. Any ABS drain pipe run above ground has to be rated or shielded against the sun. Apache Junction sits in Pinal County. A lot off the city sewer runs its waste through a Pinal County septic permit, a separate county track. The set ends at the final inspection. The skirting or foundation, the stairs and landings, and the site drainage all have to be done first. Only then does the city issue the Certificate of Installation.

A real Apache Junction example

For example, say you place a new double-wide on a vacant RS-20M lot, two sections each 14 by 40 feet. Because it is on a private lot, it needs a permanent foundation approved by the Arizona Department of Housing. The perimeter is enclosed in masonry. It gets a 3:12 shingle roof, a 12-foot driveway, and a carport or garage at least 10 by 20 feet. The home must be titled within two years and carry the post-1976 HUD label. You pull the city set permit plus the electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits. The Certificate of Installation issues after the final inspection, once the foundation, egress, and drainage pass. That same home in a manufactured home park would need only uniform skirting, at least 400 square feet of floor area, 48 square feet of storage, and a 9-by-19-foot parking pad. Get the setbacks right on the site plan either way.

How this connects to your other Apache Junction steps

Which district your lot is in, and the modular (M) sub-districts that allow these homes, come from Apache Junction residential zoning and setbacks. The set permit moves through the same city permit intake as a site-built house. It is checked during the Apache Junction inspection sequence. Any attached addition is built to the 2018 codes the city adopted. For how these homes compare to other build types, see modular versus stick-built versus custom homes in Arizona and the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.

Source

The city installation permit, the foundation and skirting standards, and the state and HUD references are published by the City of Apache Junction Division of Building Safety and Inspection and in the city's MH, PM, RV Construction Standards on the Applications, Forms & Typical Details page. The state install standards the city cites live in A.R.S. Title 41, Chapter 37.

Site minimums swing hard between a private lot and a licensed park, and the zoning district on your deed decides which set you are held to. Have the Division of Building Safety and Inspection confirm the standards for your exact parcel before you put a deposit on a home.

title: Apache Junction Pool and Spa Permit: When It's Required and the Barrier Rules
shortSummary: A swimming pool or spa in Apache Junction needs a city pool and spa permit, and the water cannot be filled until the safety barrier passes inspection. The barrier follows Arizona's statewide floor: a five-foot fence with a self-closing, self-latching gate that opens away from the water.
bodyHtml:
Almost every backyard pool and spa in Apache Junction needs a permit. The city's exempt list has room for exactly one kind: a prefabricated above-ground pool under 18 inches deep and under 5,000 gallons. Anything you would actually swim in clears that line. So you file for a pool and spa permit with the Division of Building Safety and Inspection through the MyGovernmentOnline portal, and the barrier around the finished pool has to pass inspection before you can add water. The city reviews against the 2018 International Swimming Pool and Spa Code layered on Arizona's statewide barrier law, A.R.S. 36-1681.

When you need a pool or spa permit

The city lists residential swimming pools and spas among the permits its Division of Building Safety and Inspection reviews, in-ground or above-ground alike. Apache Junction is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) inside city limits, so the city runs the review and the inspection, not Pinal County.

The one carve-out is a small prefab pool. The city's exempt-work list is narrow:

Prefabricated swimming pools accessory to detached one- and two-family dwellings, which can contain no more than eighteen inches (18") of water, do not exceed five thousand (5,000) gallons (18,925 L), and are installed entirely above ground.

So a prefab pool that stays under 18 inches of water, holds less than 5,000 gallons, and sits entirely above ground skips the permit. Anything deeper, larger, or dug into the ground, which describes nearly every real backyard pool or spa, needs the permit. That 18-inch line is the same depth that triggers the state barrier law, so a pool worth swimming in is a pool that needs a fence.

The barrier rules: five feet and a self-latching gate

The barrier has to be at least five feet (60 inches) tall on the side facing away from the pool, with a gate a small child cannot work. Apache Junction enforces the 2018 International Swimming Pool and Spa Code, which carries the detailed geometry, on top of the statewide floor in A.R.S. 36-1681. The state law sets the core height:

The pool shall be entirely enclosed by at least a five foot wall, fence or other barrier as measured on the exterior side of the wall, fence or barrier.

The gate rules are where most barriers fail, so plan them first. A gate must be self-closing and self-latching. It has to swing outward, away from the pool. The latch release sits at least 54 inches above the ground, out of a toddler's reach.

Where a wall of the house forms part of the barrier and a door opens to the pool, you protect that door instead of fencing it off. Three options work: self-latching hardware, a door alarm, or a motorized safety cover meeting the ASTM standard. The rule bites at any home where a child under six lives or is expected to live. The pool code adds spacing limits on pickets and bottom gaps that your fence detail has to meet, and those code editions are listed in Apache Junction adopted building codes.

Spas and hot tubs count too

A spa or hot tub falls under the same permit and the same barrier logic once it holds 18 inches of water. The alternative to a fence is an approved safety cover that latches shut and meets the ASTM F1346 standard, which lets a spa on a deck stay code-compliant without its own enclosure. For the full picture on covers versus fencing, see does a hot tub or spa need a pool barrier in Arizona.

What you submit and how it gets inspected

The pool and spa application asks for a scaled site plan showing the property lines, the pool, and the barrier and gates, with the setbacks from each property line called out, plus the plumbing, equipment, and electrical bonding details. You file it through MyGovernmentOnline. The inspection that matters most comes at the end. The final inspection on the pool has to pass before the pool can be filled and used, so the barrier is not a detail you finish later.

For example, say you build a new home in an RS-7 neighborhood in Apache Junction and add a 14 by 28 foot in-ground pool holding about 15,000 gallons. Because it is dug in and far over the 18-inch and 5,000-gallon lines, it needs the city pool and spa permit. You fence it with a five-foot barrier, hang a self-closing gate that swings away from the water with the latch 54 inches up, and put self-latching hardware on the patio door that opens to the deck. At the final inspection the city checks that barrier, and only then can you add water. A prefab kiddie pool under 18 inches deep on the same lot would need no permit at all.

How this ties to A.R.S. 36-1681 and the rest of your build

Apache Junction's barrier rules carry out the statewide floor in A.R.S. 36-1681, Arizona's pool barrier law, which sets the five-foot fence, the self-latching gate, and the 18-inch depth trigger for any home where a young child lives. The city adds the working detail through the 2018 pool code. Your pool permit runs alongside the city building permit for the house, and the barrier is one of the stages in the Apache Junction inspection sequence that ends with a certificate of occupancy. For the money side, see the cost to add a pool to a new home in Arizona and what permits you need to build a pool with a new home.

Source

The pool and spa permit and the online intake are published by the City of Apache Junction Division of Building Safety and Inspection, and the prefab-pool exemption is in the city's Work Exempt from Permits handout on the Applications, Forms & Typical Details page. The five-foot barrier and gate rules are set in state law at A.R.S. 36-1681.

Barrier specs get amended whenever the city moves to a newer pool code edition. Walk your fence line and your gate swing past the Division of Building Safety and Inspection, and past your pool contractor, while the yard is still a drawing.

title: Fountain Hills Masonry Block Wall Permit: The 30-Inch Trigger and the Town's Wall Details
shortSummary: In Fountain Hills, a masonry block wall over 30 inches tall needs a Town building permit. The Town publishes pre-approved 4-inch and 8-inch wall details you can build to, both up to 6 feet. Retaining walls have their own trigger: a permit once they pass 2 feet or hold back a surcharge.
bodyHtml:
In Fountain Hills, most yard walls need a Town building permit before you pour a footing. The Town amended the model code so that only a fence not over 30 inches high is exempt, which means a normal 6-foot block privacy wall is in. To make that permit easy, the Town publishes two pre-approved standard details, a 4-inch wall and an 8-inch wall, that you can build to without separate engineering. The trade is worth understanding. That 30-inch trigger pulls nearly every real wall into the permit system, and the standard details are what keep it from also costing you an engineer.

When a wall needs a permit

A freestanding wall or fence needs a permit once it stands more than 30 inches tall. Fountain Hills sets this in its amended 2024 building code (Ordinance 25-06), which lists the few walls that do not need a permit:

b. Fences not over 30 inches high. c. Retaining walls that are not over 2 feet in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, unless supporting a surcharge.

That 30-inch line is much lower than the fence exemption in the base International codes, which is set in feet. In Fountain Hills, a knee-high garden wall may be exempt, but almost any real privacy or screen wall clears 30 inches and needs a permit. The same logic covers retaining walls, with an even lower bar, which the next sections break down.

The Town's 4-inch and 8-inch wall details

The Town gives you two ready-made wall designs so you do not have to hire an engineer for a standard wall. Both build to a maximum height of 6 feet and share the same material specs: concrete at 2,500 psi, Grade 40 reinforcing steel, ASTM C-90 block, Type S mortar, and grout at 2,000 psi. The Town also requires the finished wall to be painted or stuccoed on all sides, and the footing to sit on undisturbed, well-drained soil.

  • The 4-inch detail (FH4MW). This is a thin panel-block wall built from 4-by-8-by-16 blocks. It leans on pilasters, thicker columns spaced 13 feet apart, each with a single #5 bar in a grouted cell that is not spliced. Horizontal joint reinforcement runs every 16 inches. It suits a lighter privacy or screen wall on flat ground.
  • The 8-inch detail (FH8MW). This is a heavier wall built from 8-inch block, with a #4 vertical bar every 48 inches in a solid-grouted cell and joint reinforcement every 16 inches. It carries a continuous #4 bar in the footing and includes a footing-step detail for sloped ground, so it handles longer runs and grade changes better than the 4-inch wall.

Both details are marked "city approved standard," and both carry the same condition in plain type: you still have to submit a plot outline, pull a permit, and call for inspection. Building to the standard detail is what lets you skip custom engineering, not the permit itself.

Retaining walls and surcharge

A retaining wall, one that holds back soil, follows a lower and stricter trigger than a fence. It is exempt only when it stands 2 feet or less, measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, and only when nothing pushes extra load against it. Any retaining wall taller than 2 feet needs a permit. So does any retaining wall of any height that supports a surcharge, which is added lateral load from something above or behind it, like a slope, a driveway, a patio, or a pool.

For example, a 2-foot garden-bed border that only holds its own dirt can be exempt. But a 3-foot wall holding up a raised patio is over 2 feet, so it needs a permit. And a short wall that retains soil under a driveway carries a surcharge, so it needs a permit and engineered plans no matter how low it is. This is the same surcharge idea that shows up when a pool is dug close to a house footing, covered in the Fountain Hills pool and spa barrier permit. Because walls also sit inside your yard setbacks and can block corner sight lines, check the wall against Fountain Hills residential zoning and setbacks before you place it.

What you submit and inspect

For a standard wall, your submittal is short: a site plan or plot outline showing where the wall goes, its height and length, and which standard detail you are building to. If the wall is taller than 6 feet, retains over 2 feet, or carries a surcharge, you add engineered plans stamped by an Arizona professional engineer. The permit is pulled by a licensed contractor or under an owner-builder exemption, because A.R.S. 32-1169 requires the applicant to file a signed statement of proper licensing.

After the permit issues, the wall is inspected before it is covered, chiefly at the footing and reinforcement stage before grout and block hide the steel. The Town of Fountain Hills runs these checks the same way it inspects a house, described in Fountain Hills building inspections. What you file for the house itself is in Fountain Hills residential building permit requirements, and the fee basis is in Fountain Hills building permit and impact fees.

Source

The 30-inch and 2-foot triggers come from the Town's amended 2024 building code, adopted by Ordinance 25-06 and listed on Adopted Codes, effective September 1, 2025. The 4-inch and 8-inch standard wall details, with their footing, rebar, and material specs, are published on the Town's Building Permit Forms & Checklists page. The licensing statement behind the permit is A.R.S. 32-1169.

Ordinance 25-06 took effect September 1, 2025, and the Town reissues its standard details from time to time. Pull the current FH4MW or FH8MW sheet off the Town's forms page rather than reusing a copy from an older job, and check the trigger heights with the Building Safety Division while you are there.
