title: Fountain Hills Pool and Spa Barrier Permit: The 60-Inch Rule and the Terraced Hillside Detail
shortSummary: A pool or spa in Fountain Hills needs its own Town permit, and the water must be enclosed by a barrier at least 60 inches tall on the side facing away from the pool. The Town follows the 2024 International Swimming Pool and Spa Code, with a special terraced barrier detail for hillside lots.
bodyHtml:
Fountain Hills is built on slopes, and that is what separates its pool barrier rules from a flat-lot town's. A barrier is measured on the side facing away from the pool. On a terraced yard, the same fence reads one height from the pool deck and a different one from the yard below it. The Town publishes a Terraced Pool Barrier Detail for exactly that problem. Everything else runs off the 2024 International Swimming Pool and Spa Code (ISPSC), adopted by Ordinance 25-06 for permit applications filed on or after September 1, 2025, plus the Town's own amendments to the barrier section. The pool takes its own Town permit, separate from the house permit, and cannot be filled until the barrier passes inspection.

What the barrier has to be

The barrier has to stand at least 60 inches tall, measured on the side that faces away from the pool. The Town's Pool Checklist states the core rule, which is its amended ISPSC Section 305.2.1:

The top of the barrier shall be not less than 60 inches above grade where measured on the side of the barrier that faces away from the pool or spa. Such height shall exist around the entire perimeter of the barrier and for a distance of 3 feet measured horizontally from the outside of the required barrier.

The Town's Pool Barrier Detail caps the height at 72 inches and sets the rest of the geometry:

  • Bottom clearance. The gap between the ground and the bottom of the barrier can be at most 2 inches over loose surfaces like grass or gravel, and at most 4 inches over a solid surface like concrete.
  • Openings. No opening in the barrier can let a 4-inch sphere pass. Where horizontal rails sit less than 54 inches apart, the rails go on the pool side and the gaps between vertical pickets drop to 1 3/4 inches, so the rails cannot be used as a ladder.
  • Climbable objects. Anything a child could climb, like a planter or a low wall, must sit at least 36 inches back from the outside of the barrier.
  • Gates. A gate has to open outward, away from the pool, and be self-closing and self-latching. The latch release sits at least 54 inches above the ground. If it is lower, the gate needs a no-reach zone with no opening over 1/2 inch within 18 inches of the latch.

Where a wall of the house forms part of the barrier and a door or window opens to the pool, you pick one of three protections: a water-hazard alarm listed to UL 2017 on that opening, a safety cover listed to ASTM F1346, or self-closing and self-latching hardware on the door.

The terraced barrier detail for hillside lots

On a flat lot, a 5-foot fence is simple to measure. On a Fountain Hills hillside lot it is not, because the yard is often terraced with retaining walls and the ground is higher on one side of a wall than the other. Height is measured on the side facing away from the pool, so a step in grade changes how tall the barrier reads from the lower terrace. That is the gap the Town's Terraced Pool Barrier Detail closes.

The detail shows a pool on an upper pad with a retaining wall stepping down to a lower yard. It combines the retaining wall with a fence on top so the barrier still presents at least 60 inches on the downhill side. Two notes on the detail matter most: the fence bottom rail is anchored to the top of the retaining wall, so there is no gap or foothold where the two meet, and a narrow-picket wrought-iron section keeps openings at 1 3/4 inches or less while staying about 50 percent open for the view.

For example, take a lot where the pool sits on a pad held up by a 3-foot retaining wall. A 3-foot fence on top of that wall reads as roughly 6 feet from the lower terrace, which clears the 60-inch minimum. The terraced detail shows the fence anchored to the wall top with no climbable step, and the gate latch still at least 54 inches up. Drawing it to the Town detail up front keeps the barrier from failing its final inspection, which is the check standing between you and a full pool.

What you submit for the pool permit

The Pool Checklist lists what your plan set has to show. A body of water counts as a pool once it is more than 18 inches deep or more than 8 feet across, so most spas are in too. Plan on these items:

  • A scaled site plan with property lines, the pool, and the barrier and gates called out, showing the direction each gate swings.
  • The barrier method between the house and the pool, including any door or window that opens to the pool deck.
  • A plumbing and equipment set with pump, filter, heater, drains, and grates, all meeting the anti-entrapment rule of the federal Virginia Graeme Baker Act.
  • An electrical one-line drawing, panel and load information, and bonding and grounding details.
  • Pool and yard lighting cut sheets showing bulbs at 3000 Kelvin or less, because Fountain Hills is a Dark Sky community and limits outdoor light color and glare.

One line on the checklist trips people up. You have to show the distance from the house foundation and any columns to the pool. The Town uses it to check whether the excavation comes close enough to press load against the house footing, a condition called a surcharge. If it does, the pool engineering has to account for it. The permit itself is billed on the Town's fee schedule, covered in Fountain Hills building permit and impact fees.

How this ties to state law and the rest of your build

The Town rule sits on top of a state law. A.R.S. 36-1681 is Arizona's statewide pool-barrier floor, and it already requires a five-foot barrier, self-closing and self-latching gates, and the same 18-inch water-depth trigger. Fountain Hills adopts that floor and adds the detailed geometry above through its amended ISPSC, so the Town version is the one your plans are drawn to. The Town is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) that reviews the plan and inspects the finished barrier.

Fold this into the build like any other permit. What you file for the house is in Fountain Hills residential building permit requirements, the code editions behind it are in Fountain Hills adopted building codes, and the barrier is checked during the stages in Fountain Hills building inspections. Pool equipment screen walls and the surcharge setback tie back to Fountain Hills residential zoning and setbacks. For the money side, see the cost to add a pool to a new home in Arizona.

Source

The barrier rules, the terraced detail, and the submittal list are published by the Town of Fountain Hills on the Building Permit Forms & Checklists page, which hosts the Pool Checklist, the Pool Barrier Detail, and the Terraced Pool Barrier Detail. The 60-inch height comes from the Town's amended ISPSC Section 305, adopted by Ordinance 25-06 and listed on the Town's Adopted Codes page, effective September 1, 2025. The statewide floor is A.R.S. 36-1681.

The Town revises its detail sheets, and the code edition behind them already moved once on September 1, 2025. Download the Pool Checklist and both barrier details fresh before your designer starts drawing, and have the pool contractor check the gate hardware against the current sheet rather than the last job's.

title: Fountain Hills Rooftop Solar PV Permit: The 2023 NEC Checklist and Fire-Access Rules
shortSummary: A rooftop solar PV system in Fountain Hills needs its own Town permit before install. You submit to the Town's Solar Photovoltaic and Energy Storage checklist, which is built on the 2023 National Electrical Code and the 2024 fire code. The plans cover wiring, rapid shutdown, roof fire-access pathways, and structural attachment.
bodyHtml:
A rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) system in Fountain Hills needs its own Town permit before a single panel goes up. The Town's plan review runs against its Solar Photovoltaic & Energy Storage Submittal Checklist. That checklist is written to the 2023 National Electrical Code (NEC) and the 2024 International Fire Code, both adopted by Ordinance 25-06. The review looks at three things: the electrical design, the fire-access layout on the roof, and how the array is anchored. Of those three, fire access is the one that costs you panels.

What you submit for a solar permit

Your plan set has to show the whole system on paper before it is built. The Town's checklist asks for these pieces:

  • A site plan showing the house, other structures, and where the panels sit.
  • A system description and equipment cut sheets for every major part: panels, inverters, any charge controllers, and batteries.
  • A single-line (one-line) diagram running from the PV array through the inverter to the main service panel, plus a three-line diagram with wire sizes, conduit, overcurrent protection, disconnects, grounding, and bonding when required.
  • Panel and wiring specs with the numbers the reviewer checks against the code: wire and conduit sized per NEC 690.8(A), overcurrent protection per NEC 690.9, and rapid shutdown per NEC 690.12.
  • Disconnect and hazard labels, including the rapid-shutdown label, marked per NEC 690.13 and 705.10.
  • Grounding for the array, including the grounding electrode. That is a ground rod, or a UFER (a bar tied into the foundation concrete). PV equipment is grounded per NEC 690.43.

Rapid shutdown is worth calling out. NEC 690.12 makes a rooftop array able to drop its rooftop wiring to a safe voltage fast, so a firefighter is not standing near live DC conductors. It is a code requirement here, not an upgrade.

The fire-access rules that reshape a layout

The rule that surprises homeowners is not electrical, it is fire access. Fountain Hills follows the 2024 fire code, which keeps clear paths and setbacks on the roof so crews can move during a fire. The checklist sets the ridge setbacks by how much roof the array covers:

For photovoltaic arrays occupying 33 percent or less of the plan view total roof area, a setback of not less than 18 inches wide is required on both sides of a horizontal ridge. For photovoltaic arrays occupying more than 33 percent of the plan view total roof area, a setback of not less than 36 inches wide is required on both sides of a horizontal ridge.

On top of the ridge setback, the code wants at least two 36-inch-wide pathways from the lowest roof edge up to the ridge, on separate roof planes, with one on the street or driveway side. For example, a homeowner who wants to blanket the south roof will cover more than 33 percent of it, so the array loses a 36-inch strip on both sides of the ridge plus the eave-to-ridge pathways. That can drop several panels from the first layout, which is why the fire-access paths are drawn before the panel count is locked.

Structural attachment and battery storage

A roof-mounted array adds weight and wind load, so the Town wants proof the roof can take it. If the system is roof-mounted, the checklist asks for structural load calculations, certified by an engineer, plus attachment methods that meet the local wind-speed rating. This is the part that keeps panels from lifting in a monsoon microburst.

Battery, or energy storage system (ESS), plans follow their own rules from NEC Article 706 and IRC Section R330. Each ESS unit is capped at 20 kWh. The total depends on where it sits. A utility closet or basement allows up to 40 kWh. A garage, an accessory structure, an exterior wall, or the ground outdoors allows up to 80 kWh. Batteries cannot go in a sleeping room or a closet that opens into one, and an outdoor unit stays at least 3 feet from doors and windows. Rooms with a battery also need smoke and heat detection.

Permit, contractor, and review

The PV permit is pulled by a properly licensed contractor. Under A.R.S. 32-1170.01, it is unlawful to install a solar device in Arizona without qualifying as a solar contractor. Your installer needs the right license, or the right dual license, to do the work and sign the permit. The Town of Fountain Hills is the authority that reviews the plans and inspects the finished system before it can be energized.

Slot the solar permit into the rest of the project. The codes behind the review are in Fountain Hills adopted building codes, the house permit is in Fountain Hills residential building permit requirements, the inspection sequence is in Fountain Hills building inspections, and the fee basis is in Fountain Hills building permit and impact fees. On a new home, folding solar in during the build sits alongside the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.

Source

The submittal items, the NEC 2023 code references, and the fire-access pathways and ridge setbacks are published by the Town of Fountain Hills in its Solar Photovoltaic & Energy Storage checklist, posted on the Building Permit Forms & Checklists page. The 2023 NEC and 2024 fire code editions, adopted by Ordinance 25-06, are listed on Adopted Codes, effective September 1, 2025. The solar contractor requirement is A.R.S. 32-1170.01.

Fountain Hills moved to the 2023 NEC on September 1, 2025, and a plan set drawn to an older edition comes back marked up. Have your installer pull the current Solar Photovoltaic & Energy Storage checklist off the Town's forms page before anyone drafts the one-line diagram.

title: Maricopa County Grading and Drainage Permit: Drainage Clearance and Rio Verde Washes
shortSummary: A new home on unincorporated Maricopa County land needs a drainage clearance before the building permit issues, and a grading or paving job can need its own permit. A county grading matrix sets how detailed your grading and drainage plan must be, and a lot in a mapped floodplain also needs a floodplain permit.
bodyHtml:
How water moves across your lot is a permit question in unincorporated Maricopa County. Before the county issues your building permit, the project has to earn a drainage clearance. Moving dirt or laying pavement can take its own grading permit on top of that. On Rio Verde Foothills land, where desert washes cut across many parcels, this is often the review that decides where the house can sit. The Maricopa County Planning and Development Department runs it for land outside any city. Run the county's grading matrix before you hire anyone to draw plans, because it tells you whether a basic sheet will do or whether you are buying an engineered one.

The drainage clearance for your building permit

Your building permit does not issue until the county signs off on how your site handles storm water, a step called a drainage clearance. Drainage review is a standing county function, not an optional add-on:

Drainage Administration is one of the regulatory activities that the Planning and Development Department provides for the benefit of the residents of unincorporated Maricopa County.

How much engineering your plan needs is not guesswork. The county publishes a grading matrix that sizes the plan to the project:

The Grading Matrix tool is intended to give the property owner an estimate of the level of plan detail required to obtain a Drainage Clearance in connection with a construction permit.

A flat, simple lot away from any wash may need only a basic grading and drainage plan. A lot on a slope, near a wash, or in a flood-prone area can trigger an engineered plan stamped by a registered civil engineer. The matrix tells you which side you are on before you spend money on drawings. Either way, the clearance is tied to the building permit. A drainage problem stalls the whole house, not just the dirt work.

When grading or paving needs its own permit

Moving earth or laying pavement can take a separate permit. Both change how water runs and how the land holds habitat. The county states the reason and its authority:

Grading and paving activities can affect the natural habitat and drainage patterns and can cause other related impacts to the surroundings.

The Planning and Development Department may regulate this activity through a permit process.

A common rural trigger is a new driveway or private road. Every new private road in the unincorporated county needs a permit, dirt or paved, and paving one always does. A large enough earth-moving job also pulls in dust control rules. The county requires a dust control permit for any dust-generating operation that disturbs 0.1 acres, which is 4,356 square feet. On a big custom-home site, the pad, the driveway, and utility trenching cross that line fast.

What a wash or floodplain adds

A lot in a mapped floodplain needs a floodplain permit on top of the drainage clearance, with its own fees and review. The county is direct about it:

Projects that fall within a designated floodplain may require a floodplain permit with additional fees and reviews initiated by Planning & Development staff.

This is the Rio Verde wrinkle. The Foothills are cut through with desert washes, and stretches of that land sit inside FEMA-mapped flood zones. You can look up any parcel's flood status on the FEMA flood maps before you buy or design. A parcel in a floodplain is still buildable. It does mean three things come under engineered review: the house pad, the finished floor elevation, and the path storm flow takes around the home. The floodplain flag reaches other permits too. A solar array on a floodplain parcel, for example, drops out of the county's faster SolarAPP+ path.

What this means for you

Suppose you plan a home on a five-acre Rio Verde Foothills parcel with a desert wash across one corner. The grading matrix sets how detailed your plan has to be to earn the drainage clearance. Part of the lot sits in a mapped floodplain, so a floodplain permit comes with it, and that adds fees and staff review. Your engineer sets the house and pad out of the wash. The finished floor gets raised as required. The plan then has to show storm flow moving around the home without pushing water onto the neighbor. The new gravel driveway crossing the wash needs its own attention, and disturbing more than 4,356 square feet brings in the dust control permit.

Check the flood status and the wash lines during due diligence, before you buy. Either one can move the house or add an engineered plan. Run the grading matrix early, so you know which kind of drawing you are paying for. Budget the drainage clearance, a possible floodplain permit, and any grading or dust permit as their own line items, separate from the building permit fee. On rural land the house, the driveway, the septic field, and the wash setbacks all interact, so draw them on one site plan.

Drainage sits upstream of the rest of the unincorporated-county set. The building permit the clearance feeds into is in Maricopa County Residential Building Permit Requirements, the permit and drainage fees are in Maricopa County Building Permit and Impact Fees, and the yard rules the house layout follows are in Maricopa County Residential Zoning and Setbacks. For the rural picture, see what you need to build on rural land in Rio Verde and Rio Verde Foothills water rules.

Source

Maricopa County publishes the drainage review function, the grading matrix, and the floodplain permit rule on Drainage Review at maricopa.gov. The grading and paving permit basis is at Additional Permit Information, and the engineered-plan standard is at Residential Engineered Grading and Drainage. Look up a parcel's flood status at FEMA Flood Maps.

No two parcels drain the same way, which is why this review turns on your legal description rather than a standard checklist. Take that description to Maricopa County Planning and Development before you commission drawings.

Sources

  • Maricopa County Additional Permit Information (Grading and Paving)
  • Maricopa County Residential Engineered Grading and Drainage (DD-4002-01)
  • FEMA Flood Maps and flood zone information

title: Maricopa County Pool and Spa Barrier Permit: When It Is Required and the Rules
shortSummary: A swimming pool, spa, or any contained water over 18 inches deep or wider than 8 feet on unincorporated Maricopa County land needs a barrier permit issued before you install the barrier, plaster the pool, or fill it. The barrier must stand 60 inches tall with self-closing, self-latching gates.
bodyHtml:
On unincorporated Maricopa County land, the timing rule bites first. The barrier permit has to be issued before you install the barrier, before the plaster crew arrives, and before anyone puts water in the pool. The trigger is wide, too. Any contained water more than 18 inches deep, or wider than 8 feet, needs a barrier, which catches fishponds and garden water features along with pools and spas. The Maricopa County Planning and Development Department is the authority for land outside any city, so its rules, not a city's, govern a pool near Rio Verde Foothills or the Cave Creek fringe.

When a pool or spa needs a barrier permit

The rule reaches well past a full swimming pool. The county sets a size that pulls almost any backyard water feature in:

All fishponds, spas and other contained bodies of water, either above or below ground level, being greater than 18 inches in depth and/or wider than 8 feet at any two measured points, shall require a barrier.

So a spa or hot tub deeper than 18 inches counts, the same as a pool. A small fountain under 12 inches deep does not. The timing is strict, and it is the part rural builders miss:

Permits for outdoor swimming pool barriers must be ISSUED prior to installing the barrier, plastering the pool and/or filling the pool with water.

You apply through the county's online Permit Center, the same system that handles the home's building permit. The pool also has to sit in a legal spot on the lot:

Pools must not be located within the required front yard of the property. Pools must be set back at least 3 feet from all property lines.

On a rural parcel that 3-foot line is rarely the tight constraint, but the setback still has to show on your site plan alongside the house, the septic field, and the well.

What the barrier and gates must be

The barrier is a continuous 60-inch wall or fence with a gate built so a small child cannot get through. The county fixes the height and the gate hardware, because the gate is where most barriers fail:

Top of barrier shall be at 60" above finished grade on exterior side.

Access and pedestrian gates must be self-closing, self-latching and open AWAY from pool.

The gate latch has to sit high, out of a toddler's reach, at "Latch at 54" or greater." Where a wall of the house forms part of the enclosure and a door opens straight to the pool, the county allows an alarm on that door instead of a separate gate:

an alarm that sounds continuously for a minimum of 30 seconds at a level not less than 85 decibels within 7 seconds of the door and its screen, if present, being opened.

The barrier gets inspected before the pool is filled, so it is not a finish-line item you can add later.

How this ties to Arizona's statewide pool law

The county numbers match Arizona's statewide floor set in A.R.S. 36-1681, so a compliant county barrier also meets state law. The statute calls for a barrier at least five feet (60 inches) tall. Gates must be self-closing and self-latching and swing away from the pool, with the latch at least 54 inches up. Where a house wall forms part of the enclosure, the statute allows door or cover alternatives instead. The state rule applies at any home where a child under six lives or is expected to live. As the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for unincorporated land, the county enforces that floor through the pool permit and the final inspection. The full statute, its exceptions, and the cover option are broken down in A.R.S. 36-1681, Arizona's pool barrier law.

What this means for you

For example, say you add a 40-foot pool and an attached spa to a new home on a five-acre parcel near Rio Verde Foothills. Both sit behind the house, so they clear the front-yard rule, and you hold them at least 3 feet off every property line. Before the plaster crew arrives, the barrier permit has to be issued. You fence the pool with a 60-inch barrier. Its gate self-latches at 54 inches up and swings away from the water. The great-room patio door opens toward the pool, so that door gets an alarm instead: 85 decibels, sounding within 7 seconds of the door opening and running at least 30 seconds. The county checks all of it before you fill.

Budget the barrier as part of the pool, not an add-on. Pull the permit ahead of the plaster and fill dates, because those are the moments the rule locks in. Draw the pool, its 3-foot property-line offset, and the barrier on the same site plan as the house and the septic field. If a young child lives with you, decide early between the door alarm and a code-compliant safety cover on any house door opening to the pool deck.

The barrier permit runs in step with the rest of the unincorporated-county filings. The building permit alongside it is in Maricopa County Residential Building Permit Requirements, the yard rules the pool location follows are in Maricopa County Residential Zoning and Setbacks, and the final barrier check is part of the Maricopa County building inspections process. For the applied questions, see what permits you need to build a pool with a new home in Arizona and whether a hot tub or spa needs a pool barrier in Arizona.

Source

Maricopa County publishes the barrier trigger size, the permit timing, the pool setback, and the 60-inch and 54-inch specs on Residential Pool and Barrier Requirements at maricopa.gov. The statewide floor the county enforces is A.R.S. 36-1681 on azleg.gov.

A local rule can sit above the state floor but never below it, so read the county sheet as the controlling one. Get the current barrier and gate specs from Maricopa County Planning and Development before your pool contractor prices the fence.

Sources

  • Maricopa County Residential Pool and Barrier Requirements
  • A.R.S. 36-1681 (Pool enclosures; requirements; exceptions; enforcement)

title: Maricopa County Solar PV Permit: Rooftop, Ground-Mounted, and the SolarAPP+ Path
shortSummary: A rooftop solar array on unincorporated Maricopa County land needs a minor residential electrical permit, and a ground-mounted array needs a residential accessory permit, both filed online. Eligible rooftop systems can run through SolarAPP+, an automated code-compliance review, but that step does not issue the permit by itself.
bodyHtml:
Adding solar to a home on unincorporated Maricopa County land takes a county permit, and which permit depends on where the panels go. Rooftop and ground-mounted systems follow two different application types, both filed online through the county Permit Center. For eligible rooftop systems the county offers SolarAPP+, an automated tool that checks the design against code before you apply. The Maricopa County Planning and Development Department is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for land outside any city. So a solar array near Rio Verde Foothills is permitted by the county, not a utility or a city. One thing to fix in your head up front: a SolarAPP+ approval is not a permit.

Rooftop versus ground-mounted: two permit types

The mounting location decides the permit. The county splits residential photovoltaic (PV) work into two application types:

Roof-Mounted PV systems are classified as a minor residential electrical permit.

Ground-Mounted PV systems are classified as a residential accessory permit.

Both are filed online. A rooftop array is treated mainly as electrical work, since it ties into the home's panel and wiring. A ground-mounted array counts as an accessory structure. It puts a framed support on the lot, with its own footing and setback questions, the same way a shed does. On a rural parcel with room to spare, many owners pick ground-mount for easier cleaning and better tilt. That puts them on the accessory permit path, not the electrical one.

The county also moves fast on a clean submittal:

For complete submittals with attachments applications will be processed within the same business day.

Applications received after 11:00 am, may be processed on the next business day.

So a complete package filed in the morning can clear the same day. A package missing attachments does not.

What SolarAPP+ is, and what it is not

SolarAPP+ is an automated code check for eligible rooftop systems, not an instant permit. The county describes it plainly:

SolarAPP+ is a third-party software program that can be used to verify code compliance for residential photovoltaic (PV) projects.

The tool checks the design against the electrical and residential codes the county has adopted. If it passes, the tool returns an approval. It stands in for the manual plan review a reviewer would otherwise do. The important limit is that the SolarAPP+ approval is not the permit. The county spells this out:

This step does not issue a building permit. Proceed to the next step to apply for your building permit and required inspections.

So the path is two steps. Your contractor submits the design to SolarAPP+, and once it is approved, applies to the county with that result in hand:

Once you have SolarAPP+ approval, submit for the permit online.

SolarAPP+ is limited to rooftop systems that meet the county's list. The parcel must be in unincorporated Maricopa County. The system must sit on a legal, permitted main home. And the work must be done by a licensed solar contractor. The tool also excludes ballasted systems, manufactured homes, hillside and sensitive-land lots, and parcels in a flood hazard or floodplain area. That last exclusion matters near Rio Verde Foothills. A parcel in or beside a mapped wash or floodplain would not qualify. There you would use the standard online rooftop permit instead. Ground-mounted systems also fall outside SolarAPP+ and go through the accessory permit.

Why the licensed contractor requirement is there

SolarAPP+ and the standard path both expect a licensed solar contractor, which matches state law. Arizona sets a specific solar contractor qualification under A.R.S. 32-1170.01. The person who pulls the permit and stands behind it must show solar-specific skill, beyond a general electrical background. Using a properly licensed solar contractor also protects you. If the install goes wrong, it keeps your Registrar of Contractors recovery options open. Hire an unlicensed installer and that route closes. The state rules for solar contractors are covered in A.R.S. 32-1170.01, the solar contractor qualification.

What this means for you

For instance, take a 9 kW rooftop array going on a new home near Rio Verde Foothills. The parcel is not in a mapped flood hazard area, so it qualifies for SolarAPP+. Your licensed contractor runs the design through the tool and gets an approval. Then the contractor files the minor residential electrical permit online through the county Permit Center, with that approval attached. The complete submittal lands before 11 a.m., so the county processes it the same business day. A ground-mounted array on that same lot would be a residential accessory permit instead, filed online with no SolarAPP+ shortcut available.

Decide rooftop or ground-mount early. It changes the permit type and whether SolarAPP+ is even an option. Use a licensed solar contractor. The county expects it, and it protects you if there is a defect later. If your lot touches a wash or floodplain, plan on the standard rooftop permit. Want same-day processing? File a complete package, attachments and all, before 11 a.m. And check your parcel's SolarAPP+ eligibility with the county before you count on the faster path.

Solar is usually the last county permit on a new build, and it leans on the ones before it. The main home permit is in Maricopa County Residential Building Permit Requirements, the code editions the SolarAPP+ check runs against are in Maricopa County Adopted Building Codes, and the field checks come at the Maricopa County building inspections process. For the applied questions, see whether solar is worth it on a new construction home in Arizona and whether to prewire a new home for solar and automation.

Source

Maricopa County publishes the two permit classifications, the same-business-day processing, and the SolarAPP+ steps on Residential Solar Permits at maricopa.gov and Go Solar for Residential Service. The state solar contractor rule is A.R.S. 32-1170.01 on azleg.gov.

Eligibility is the piece that moves. The county can add or drop exclusions, and the tool tracks newer code editions. Have your contractor check the current criteria against your parcel with Planning and Development before quoting a timeline.

title: Paradise Valley Fence and Site Wall Permit: When a Wall Needs a Permit and How Tall It Can Be
shortSummary: In Paradise Valley, almost any fence or site wall needs a permit, including block walls, gates, planters, and retaining walls. Solid walls and view fences top out at six feet, measured from the outside grade. A three-foot fence can sit near the street, but a six-foot wall must set back forty feet.
bodyHtml:
A fence or site wall in Paradise Valley almost always needs a permit before you build it, and the Town caps most walls at six feet. The Fence/Site Walls permit is a separate filing from your house permit, and it exists because walls shape both privacy and sight lines on the Town's large lots. The rule worth memorizing is the trade between height and distance from the street. A solid six-foot wall has to sit forty feet back from the front property line. Drop the wall to three feet and you can come within ten.

When a fence or site wall needs a permit

The permit covers far more than a backyard fence. The Town's materials spell out the scope:

[Use this permit] for any fence, including block, chain, etc. Additionally, this permit should be used for gates, planters, gardens and retaining walls.

So a block privacy wall, a driveway gate, a raised planter, a garden wall, and a retaining wall each need this permit. You apply through the Town's online Citizen Portal. The submittal is short but specific: a site plan showing the wall on the lot, a dust control plan (or a Maricopa County air quality permit if the work disturbs more than a tenth of an acre), an agent authorization letter if someone files for you, and an HOA acknowledgement where a homeowners association governs the lot. The HOA item matters in Paradise Valley's gated communities, where the CC&Rs often fix wall style and color before the Town ever sees the plan.

How tall a wall or fence can be

Paradise Valley limits most walls and view fences to six feet, set in Article XXIV, Table 2404A of the Zoning Ordinance. Two measurement rules go with that cap. Height is measured from the finished grade on the outside of the wall, and you cannot pile fill against a wall just to make it taller. In a front yard, height is traded against how far the wall sits from the street:

  • A three-foot fence may sit as close as 10 feet from the front property line.
  • A six-foot combination view fence (solid base with an open metal top) needs a 20-foot setback.
  • A solid six-foot wall needs a 40-foot front setback.

The logic is sight lines. A tall solid wall close to the road blocks views and driveway visibility, so the Town pushes it back or keeps it low near the street. The Town of Paradise Valley is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), so its planners read these numbers against your setback lines before the permit issues.

Hillside and large-lot site walls

On Paradise Valley's sloped and estate lots, site walls do more work, and they draw extra review. A retaining wall that holds back a cut or fill is part of the grading picture, so on a hillside lot the Town's Hillside Building Committee looks at your walls along with land disturbance and drainage before earth moves. Long perimeter walls are common here because lots run an acre or more, which means more wall length to permit and more chances for a height or setback miss.

For example, say you build on a sloped one-acre lot and want a six-foot privacy wall along a front yard that drops toward the street. Two things follow. Because the grade falls, the wall's height is measured from the lower outside grade, so a wall that looks six feet from your yard can read taller from the street and fail. And because the wall retains soil, it goes through hillside review, not just a flat wall check. If that same wall also encloses a pool, it has to meet the five-foot pool barrier rules on top of the fence rules. Planning the wall around all three tests at once saves a redraw.

What this means for you

Assume any wall, fence, gate, or planter needs a permit, and file it through the Citizen Portal with your site plan. Draw walls to the six-foot cap, and remember height is measured from the outside grade, so a wall on a slope needs the low side checked. Keep solid walls back from the front line, 40 feet for a six-foot wall, or step down to a three-foot fence or a view fence if you want to build closer to the street. On a gated-community lot, clear the wall with your HOA first, because the Town asks for that acknowledgement. On a hillside lot, fold retaining walls into the grading and hillside review from the start. Confirm the current wall heights and front-setback numbers in Article XXIV with the Paradise Valley Planning Department before you finalize the site plan.

A wall in Paradise Valley is rarely reviewed on its own. The base yard and setback rules it reads against are in Paradise Valley Residential Zoning and Setbacks. Retaining walls on a slope tie into Paradise Valley Hillside Development Requirements. A wall that encloses a pool also has to pass the Paradise Valley pool and spa barrier rules. For the full build sequence, see the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.

Source

The Fence/Site Walls permit scope and submittal list are published by the Town of Paradise Valley: Permits and Handouts on paradisevalleyaz.gov. The six-foot cap, the outside-grade measurement, and the front-yard setback steps are set in the Zoning Ordinance, Article XXIV (Walls and Fences), linked from the Town Planning page. The dust control permit for larger disturbance is run by Maricopa County Air Quality.

title: Paradise Valley Grading and Drainage Permit: When Earthwork Needs a Permit and What the Plan Must Show
shortSummary: You need a grading permit in Paradise Valley whenever earthwork changes the slope or drainage of your lot. An Arizona registered civil engineer must draw the grading and drainage plan, the legal survey, and the stormwater plan. A house permit alone triggers a grading plan once you add 999 square feet of hard surface.
bodyHtml:
You need a grading permit in Paradise Valley any time you move enough dirt to change the lot's slope or the way water drains across it. This is a separate permit from the house permit and the hillside review, though on a sloped lot all three run together. The grading permit is where the Town checks that your cut, fill, and drainage keep water on your lot and off your neighbors. One threshold catches nearly every custom build here. Add 999 square feet of hard surface, or price the work above $500,000, and a grading and drainage plan attaches to the house permit whether or not you thought you were grading.

When grading needs a permit

The permit is tied to changing the land, not just to big excavation. The Town's own materials describe the trigger directly:

[A grading permit is] required when dirt or earth work is being completed (excavating or filling) and there are changes made to the current gradient of the land and drainage conditions.

So cutting a building pad, filling a low spot, or reshaping how water runs all call for the permit. A grading plan also gets pulled into the house permit at a size threshold. The Town requires a grading and drainage plan with a building permit:

where 999 sf or more of impervious area is added or if the value of the work is greater than $500,000.

A new custom home in Paradise Valley clears both marks easily. The house, driveway, and patios add well over 999 square feet of hard surface, and estate-scale valuations pass half a million dollars. So plan on the grading and drainage plan as part of the build, not an extra.

What the grading and drainage plan must show

Grading in Paradise Valley is an engineer's document, not a sketch. An Arizona registered civil engineer has to prepare the core sheets: a legal survey, the grading and drainage plan, and a Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP). Two outside approvals attach at set thresholds:

  • If your project disturbs one acre or more, you also file a Notice of Intent with the state. That earns coverage under Arizona's AZPDES Construction General Permit, the stormwater permit ADEQ runs, and the SWPPP is the plan behind that coverage.
  • If the work disturbs a tenth of an acre or more (4,356 square feet), you file a dust control plan, or a Maricopa County air quality permit for larger disturbance.

The drainage half of the plan is the part the Town checks hardest. Your engineer has to show where stormwater goes. A graded lot cannot push runoff onto the lot next door, or into a wash in a way that erodes it. On the Town's large lots, that often means shaping the pad and driveway to hold and route water on your own ground.

How hillside rules cap your grading

On a sloped lot, the grading permit is not the only limit. Paradise Valley's Hillside Development Regulations (Article XXII) cap how much of a lot you may disturb once the slope hits 10 percent. The steeper the ground, the smaller that share gets. The Town's Hillside Building Committee reviews grading, drainage, and retaining walls before any earth moves. So your grading plan has to fit inside the disturbance cap, not merely balance cut against fill.

For example, take a 1.2-acre lot on a 15 percent slope. Three thresholds stack up. Total disturbance tops one acre, so you file the ADEQ Notice of Intent and a SWPPP on top of the Town permit. It also tops a tenth of an acre, so a dust control plan comes with it. And the slope is over 10 percent, so Article XXII caps how much of the site you may touch at all. Your civil engineer then has to fit the pad, the driveway, and the drainage inside that cap while still routing water safely downhill. All three have to agree before the Town issues the permit.

What this means for you

Budget the grading and drainage plan as a real line item on almost every Paradise Valley build, drawn by an Arizona registered civil engineer. Pin down your total disturbance early. Crossing one acre adds the ADEQ stormwater permit, and crossing a tenth of an acre adds dust control. Get the drainage right the first time, because pushing water onto a neighbor is a common and expensive correction. On a sloped lot, hand your engineer the hillside disturbance cap up front, so the plan is drawn to fit it rather than reworked around it. The Town of Paradise Valley is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) here, and its Building and Engineering staff can confirm your lot's thresholds before you finalize anything.

Grading is the permit the rest of a Paradise Valley build waits on. The disturbance caps that limit it on a slope are in Paradise Valley Hillside Development Requirements. The house permit that the grading plan attaches to is in Paradise Valley Residential Building Permit Requirements, and the field checks are in Paradise Valley Building Inspections. For the lot-buying side, see how to buy land to build a house in Arizona, and for the full sequence, the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.

Source

The Town of Paradise Valley publishes the grading permit trigger, the building-permit grading threshold, and the required civil-engineered submittals on Permits and Handouts at paradisevalleyaz.gov. The one-acre stormwater rule is set by ADEQ's AZPDES Construction General Permit. The dust control permit is run by Maricopa County Air Quality.

Three agencies set the numbers on this page, and they revise them on separate schedules. Check the 999-square-foot and one-acre thresholds against each agency's current page before your engineer starts drawing.

title: Paradise Valley Pool and Spa Permit and Barrier Rules: When You Need One and What Passes
shortSummary: Paradise Valley requires a Pool/Spa permit before you build any pool, spa, or spool. You apply through the Town's Citizen Portal with a site plan, structural calculations, and an engineer's pool plan. Every pool must be enclosed by a barrier at least five feet tall, with self-latching gates, before it can be filled.
bodyHtml:
You need a Pool/Spa permit from the Town before you dig a pool, set a spa, or pour a spool on a Paradise Valley lot. Two items on the Town's submittal list surprise people: structural calculations, and a pool plan drawn by an engineer rather than laid out by the pool contractor. The Town checks the pool's structure, its drainage, and its safety barrier against those sheets. The barrier piece traces back to a statewide law that says a pool has to be fenced before it can hold water.

When a pool or spa permit is required

You need this permit for any pool or spa you build, in the ground or above it. The Town's own materials describe the permit's scope plainly:

[Use this permit] for project including a pool, spa or "spool," either in-ground and above-ground.

A spool is a small pool-spa combination, and it counts too. You apply through the Town's online Citizen Portal, the same Accela system used for the house permit. A complete pool submittal includes a site plan showing the pool on the lot, structural calculations, and a pool plan drawn by an engineer. If your pool and deck work disturbs a tenth of an acre (4,356 square feet) or more, you also file a dust control plan, or a Maricopa County air quality permit for larger disturbance. Like every Town filing, a pool application has to be in before the 3:30 p.m. counter cutoff to count that day.

What the safety barrier has to be

Your pool has to be enclosed by a barrier before it holds water. Paradise Valley enforces Arizona's pool barrier law, A.R.S. 36-1681, and keeps its own barrier handout so builders can check the details. The state rule sets the floor, and it is specific:

  • The barrier must be at least five feet tall, measured on the outside.
  • Gates must be self-closing and self-latching and must open outward, away from the water.
  • The latch release has to sit at least 54 inches above the ground, too high for a small child to reach.
  • The rule applies to any pool or contained water 18 inches or more deep at a home where a child under six lives or may live.

Where a wall of the house forms one side of the enclosure, the law lets you use a listed safety pool cover or self-latching hardware on the doors that open to the pool. Paradise Valley also checks the pool's drain safety through its entrapment protection and suction vacuum relief handouts, so the covers and drains are reviewed alongside the fence. The Town is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), so its inspector, not the state, signs off on your barrier.

How Paradise Valley's setting shapes the pool

Because Paradise Valley is built on large estate and hillside lots, a pool here is rarely a simple rectangle in a flat yard. Two Town wrinkles show up often. First, a site wall you already have may double as part of the pool barrier, but only if it meets the five-foot height and the gates pass, so the wall permit and the pool barrier get checked together. Second, the Town regulates where pool water drains, because runoff on a slope can wash onto a neighbor or a wash.

For example, take a new home on a one-acre lot near Mummy Mountain with a pool off the patio. The pool and decking disturb more than 4,356 square feet, so a dust control plan goes in with the permit. Your engineer's pool plan shows a five-foot perimeter barrier, and because your great-room doors open straight onto the pool deck, you add self-latching hardware on those doors as the code option. At inspection, the Town checks the barrier height, the gate latch at 54 inches, and the drain covers before you are cleared to fill the pool.

What this means for you

Pull the pool permit as its own filing, separate from the house permit, and get the engineer's pool plan and structural calculations ready before you apply. Plan the barrier into the yard from the first sketch, because a five-foot fence, a self-latching gate, or a listed safety cover is required, not an upgrade you can add later. If a house door opens to the pool, decide early whether you will use self-latching door hardware or a safety cover. Budget the dust control plan if your pool work tops a tenth of an acre. The barrier and drain covers are checked before the pool is filled, so treat that inspection as the gate to using the pool, the same way the final inspection gates moving into the house.

The pool permit leans on one state law and two Town filings. The statewide barrier law behind it is explained in A.R.S. 36-1681, Arizona's pool barrier law. The house permit that runs in parallel is in Paradise Valley Residential Building Permit Requirements, and the field checks are in Paradise Valley Building Inspections. For the wider question, see what permits you need to build a pool with a new home in Arizona and whether a hot tub or spa needs a pool barrier.

Source

The Pool/Spa permit scope, the required submittals, and the barrier and drain-safety handouts are published by the Town of Paradise Valley: Permits and Handouts on paradisevalleyaz.gov, with the permit types listed on the Town Building Department page. The five-foot barrier, the 54-inch latch, and the self-latching gate come from the state pool law, A.R.S. 36-1681.

The Town keeps separate handouts for the barrier, for entrapment protection, and for suction vacuum relief. Pull all three from the Building Department before your engineer draws the pool, rather than working from a set carried over from another job.

title: Pinal County Adopted Building Codes: Which I-Code Editions Apply to Your Rural Build
shortSummary: Unincorporated Pinal County builds to the 2018 International Residential Code and the rest of the 2018 International Code family, plus the 2017 National Electrical Code, adopted through the county's 2018 Building Code Ordinance and local amendments. These apply on county land outside any city, where the county is the building authority.
bodyHtml:
Pinal County checks a custom home on unincorporated land against the codes the county itself adopted. Not the state's, and not a nearby city's. The county builds to the 2018 family of International Codes, one edition behind the 2021 codes Scottsdale and Phoenix enforce. That one-edition gap moves real numbers: how much insulation the walls need, how the framing is fastened, how the house is wired. Find out what the county enforces before your designer starts drawing.

Which codes Pinal County enforces

Pinal County adopted the 2018 International Codes for almost everything, plus the 2017 electrical code. Here is the current list:

  • 2018 International Residential Code (IRC): one- and two-family homes and townhouses. This is the main code for a custom house.
  • 2018 International Building Code (IBC): larger and commercial structures.
  • 2018 International Mechanical Code (IMC): heating, cooling, and ventilation.
  • 2018 International Plumbing Code (IPC): water supply, drains, and fixtures.
  • 2018 International Fuel Gas Code (IFGC): gas piping and gas appliances.
  • 2018 International Fire Code (IFC): fire safety, access, and defensible space.
  • 2018 International Property Maintenance Code (IPMC): upkeep of existing buildings.
  • 2018 energy code: insulation, windows, and equipment efficiency.
  • 2017 National Electrical Code (NEC): all wiring and electrical work.

The county put these in force through its 2018 Building Code Ordinance and Amendments. That ordinance layers local changes on top of each model code. The International Residential Code (IRC) is the book a single-family builder lives in day to day.

Who these codes apply to

Pinal County Building Safety has authority over unincorporated land only, meaning the ground outside any city or town. Say your lot sits inside Casa Grande, Maricopa, Apache Junction, Eloy, or Florence. That city's building department is then the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), and its codes apply in place of the county's.

Much of Pinal County's growth sits on unincorporated land: large lots around San Tan Valley, acreage near Florence and Coolidge, rural parcels between the cities. If you are buying raw land, confirm whether the parcel is unincorporated county or inside a city boundary. That one fact decides whose plan reviewers, whose inspectors, and which code edition you answer to.

Why the 2018 edition matters

Arizona does not adopt building codes at the state level. The International Code Council describes it plainly:

Codes are adopted locally in Arizona and are predominantly the I-codes.

Every county and city picks its own edition and writes its own amendments. That is why a build in Pinal County and a build 20 miles away can follow different rules. Pinal sits on the 2018 codes. Several neighboring jurisdictions have moved to 2021. The gap is widest in the energy code, which tightened between the two editions. It shows up again in scattered framing, wiring, and safety rules. Your designer and contractor draw to the 2018 books, not a newer or generic version.

What this means for your build

On unincorporated county land, reviewers check your whole submittal against the 2018 IRC and the county amendments, so the edition is what your drawings have to answer to. How you file, what documents go in the package, and what plan review costs are covered under Pinal County residential building permit requirements.

Suppose you want a 2,800 square foot custom home on a one-acre parcel in San Tan Valley. The land is unincorporated, so Pinal County reviews the plans. Your engineer designs the structure to the 2018 IRC. Your electrician wires to the 2017 NEC. A county inspector signs off at each stage. Once the final passes, the county issues the certificate of occupancy that lets you move in. Move that same house inside the Casa Grande city limits and the city runs every one of those steps instead.

Where the code edition fits in the rest of your build

Adopted codes are the starting point. Most rural parcels have no city water or sewer, so you also clear well and septic requirements. To see how Pinal's 2018 codes line up against nearby cities and counties, compare them in Arizona building code editions by city. For the whole sequence, start with the steps to building a custom home in Arizona. Counties re-adopt on their own schedule. Check the edition on the county Building Safety page before you finalize a design.

Sources

  • Pinal County Building Safety
  • Pinal County 2018 Building Code Ordinance and Amendments
  • ICC Code Adoptions for Arizona

title: Pinal County Building Inspections for a New Home: The Sequence Through Final
shortSummary: Pinal County inspects a new home in stages, from footing to framing to final. You schedule each visit by permit number at 520-866-6299, and a call by 6 am gets same-day service. Every stage must pass before it is covered up, and the final inspection comes before your certificate of occupancy.
bodyHtml:
On unincorporated Pinal County land, a county inspector checks your new home several times during construction. The last visit is far from the only one that counts. Each stage has to pass before you cover that work up, so the inspection calendar sets the pace of the whole build. This page lays out the order Pinal County follows and how to book each visit.

How you schedule an inspection

You book an inspection by calling the county inspection line at 520-866-6299 and entering your building permit number. Keep that number where the superintendent can reach it the day the permit issues. Timing matters:

Inspections can be called in until 6 am and still receive a same-day inspection.

Call after that window and the visit slides to the next day. On a pour day that means a crew and a concrete truck standing idle. The county also asks you to keep the approved building plan, the site plan, and the inspection record card on the job site and reachable at every visit. Post the address so it reads from the street. An inspector who cannot find the address or the paperwork writes up a wasted trip.

The inspection sequence

Pinal County anchors a house build around three key inspections, with the 2018 codes it adopted driving what each one checks:

  • Footing. This one comes before any concrete is poured. The inspector looks at the foundation excavation, the depth and width of the footings, and the placement and size of the reinforcing steel. Then he checks that the house sits where your approved site plan shows it. That last check is how the county confirms your setbacks from each property line.
  • Framing. Once the shell and roof are up, the inspector confirms the truss engineering package is on site, the lath is complete, and the gas and plumbing top-out tests hold. Rough plumbing, mechanical, and electrical all have to be visible and testable at this point. Drywall covers every bit of it next.
  • Final. At the end, the final inspection has to pass and earn the Building Official's approval. The final inspection is not the same thing as your certificate of occupancy.

Final inspection versus the certificate of occupancy

This trips up a lot of first-time owners. Passing the final inspection means the work is built to code. The certificate of occupancy is a separate document the county issues afterward, and it is the one that legally lets you move in. You need both, in that order.

For example, take a 2,400 square foot custom home going up on a one-acre lot near Coolidge. The footings are dug Tuesday afternoon and the concrete is ordered for Wednesday morning. Someone has to call 520-866-6299 with the permit number before 6 am Wednesday, or the inspection lands Thursday and the pour waits a day. The inspector measures the footings and rebar and confirms the house sits where the site plan shows. Weeks later the framing inspection checks the truss packet on site and the top-out tests. Then the final passes, the Building Official signs off, and the certificate of occupancy follows.

Where inspections sit in the county process

Inspections fall in the middle of the build. They start only after you clear permit review and pull the permit, and each one measures your work against the county's adopted 2018 codes. The county is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for unincorporated land, so its inspectors sign off rather than a city's. For the full path from raw land to keys, start with the steps to building a custom home in Arizona. Check the stage list in the county's Residential Inspection Requirements bulletin before your superintendent starts calling in visits.

title: Pinal County Building Permit and Impact Fees: How a New Home Is Priced
shortSummary: A new home in unincorporated Pinal County carries two kinds of county money. The building permit and plan review fees are based on your home's construction valuation, read from a fee table tied to ICC valuation data. Separate development impact fees for parks, public safety, and streets are collected when the permit issues, and they vary by area.
bodyHtml:
A new home on unincorporated Pinal County land comes with two separate buckets of county fees. First, building permit and plan review fees pay the county to check your plans and inspect the work. Second, development impact fees help pay for the public services your new home will draw on. Here is how each one is figured and when you pay it.

How permit and plan review fees are set

Pinal County ties your building permit and plan review fees to your home's construction valuation, not a flat rate. A bigger, higher-end house costs more to permit than a small, simple one.

The county reads that valuation from Table I of its Building Permit Fee Schedule. Table I is built on the International Code Council's Building Valuation Data, February 2012 edition. In plain terms: the county multiplies a cost per square foot by your home's area to reach a construction valuation, and both fees come off that number. If the standard figure does not fit your project, the Building Official can accept an alternative valuation based on your actual construction cost.

That is the valuation method, and it is worth telling apart from the alternative. Some Arizona cities, Scottsdale among them, charge a straight rate per square foot instead. The Arizona building permit fees valuation versus per square foot reference explains why that difference can move your number.

Development impact fees

Impact fees are separate from permit fees, and they catch a lot of rural buyers by surprise. Pinal County charges them so new homes pay a share of the public facilities their demand helps create. The county's impact fees fund parks facilities, public safety, and streets. On timing, the county is specific:

Development Impact Fees are assessed and collected at the time of Building Permit Issuance.

The amount depends on where your lot sits. Pinal County sets impact fees by benefit area, and each area carries its own capital improvement plan and its own 2022 impact fee map. Two identical homes in different parts of the county can owe different impact fees. If you are unsure whether they apply to your parcel, the county takes an Impact Fee Information Request to check.

What this means for your budget

For example, take two 2,500 square foot custom homes with the same floor plan, one near San Tan Valley and one outside Coolidge. Both draw the same permit and plan review fee, because Table I reaches the same valuation from the same square footage and finish level. Their impact fees can still differ, because they fall in different benefit areas with different capital plans. The lesson is to price the two buckets separately: the permit fee follows the house, the impact fee follows the parcel.

Both are due before the county hands over the permit. The dollar figures live in the county's Building Permit Fee Schedule and its impact fee schedule. Both change, so pull the current versions before you lock a budget.

When county money comes due

Fees are collected at the end of plan review, when you pull the permit, and the county is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) taking them. The valuation that drives your permit fee traces back to the codes the county adopted. For the full path from raw land to move-in, start with the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.

title: Pinal County Pool and Spa Barrier Permit: When You Need One and the Barrier Rules
shortSummary: A backyard pool or spa in unincorporated Pinal County needs a county pool permit, and it cannot be filled until a barrier inspection passes. The barrier must stand at least 60 inches tall with self-closing, self-latching gates that swing away from the water. It follows the statewide floor set by state law.
bodyHtml:
On acreage in unincorporated Pinal County, the fence already around the property almost never counts as a pool barrier. The county is blunt about the two substitutes rural owners reach for: livestock "no climb" fencing is not an approved barrier, and a plain pool cover is not one either. A pool or spa out here takes its own county permit, and the barrier has to pass inspection before water goes in. Pinal County sets the specs in Information Bulletin 010, which sits on top of the statewide floor in A.R.S. 36-1681.

When you need a pool permit

You need a Pinal County pool and spa permit any time you build a pool or spa on unincorporated county land, and the barrier is part of the deal. The county is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for land outside any city, so its Building Safety Division reviews the plans and inspects the work. If your lot sits inside Casa Grande, Maricopa, Apache Junction, or another incorporated city, you apply to that city instead. The county draws a clear line on timing:

Final pool inspection must pass prior to filling the pool.

That means the barrier is not a detail you finish later. The inspector checks it, and only then can water go in.

What counts as a pool or spa

Pinal County treats a body of water as a pool once it is 18 inches or more deep at any point, wider than 8 feet, and meant for swimming. A spa or hot tub falls under the same bulletin. This matters because a shallow water feature below that depth is handled differently, while anything that meets the definition triggers the full barrier rules. Commercial pools are regulated by the state, not the county.

The barrier rules: height, gaps, and gates

The perimeter barrier must be at least 60 inches (five feet) tall, measured on the outside, and built so a small child cannot slip under it or climb it. Here are the core numbers the county checks:

The top must be at least 60 inches above finished grade measured on the outside of the barrier.

  • Bottom gap. With a fence like wrought iron or chain link, the gap between the bottom of the barrier and the ground can be no more than 2 inches. Over a solid surface such as a concrete deck, that gap can go to 4 inches.
  • No foothold. If the barrier design gives a foothold or ladder effect, like some wrought iron, the horizontal members have to be at least 45 inches apart so a child cannot climb them.
  • Chain link. Openings cannot pass a sphere 1-3/4 inches across, and the wire must be at least 11 gauge.
  • Gates. Pedestrian gates must be self-closing and self-latching and must swing away from the pool. The latch release normally sits 54 inches up. When the latch is lower than that, it has to be on the pool side, at least 3 inches below the gate top, with no opening larger than 2 inches within 18 inches of the release.

Doors and windows that open to the pool

When a wall of the house forms part of the barrier and has doors that open straight to the pool, the county gives you three ways to protect those doors. You can put self-closing, self-latching hardware on every door to the pool with the release at least 54 inches above the floor. You can install a UL-listed door alarm at least 54 inches up that sounds for 30 seconds when the door opens. Or you can add an interior intermediate barrier that need only be 48 inches tall, does not block the view of the pool, and has its own self-latching gate.

Spas and hot tubs

A spa or hot tub can skip the fence if it uses an approved safety cover and meets four tests: it is no wider than 8 feet at the widest point, the cover latches with a tool or device so children cannot open it, the cover holds a 100-pound static load, and it blocks a 4-inch sphere from reaching the water when closed. That 8-foot limit lines up with the county's own pool definition, so a spa any wider is treated as a pool and gets fenced like one. For the full picture on spas, see does a hot tub or spa need a pool barrier in Arizona.

What you submit and how it gets inspected

The Pool/Spa Permit Application asks for the parcel, the property owner, and a licensed pool contractor with a license class, plus the estimated pool value and the surface square footage. You also list the pool setbacks from each property line, any gas line and heater details, and whether a wash or water course crosses the lot. You pick up the issued permit at the Florence, Casa Grande, or Apache Junction office. Building Safety runs out of 85 North Florence Street in Florence at 520-509-3555.

Suppose a family on an acre near San Tan Valley adds a 15 by 30 foot pool. They pull the pool and spa permit, name their licensed pool contractor, and note that no wash crosses the lot. They fence the pool with a 60-inch wrought-iron barrier whose pattern gives no foothold, a self-closing gate that swings away from the water with the latch 54 inches up, and self-latching hardware on the patio door that opens to the deck. At the final pool inspection the county checks the barrier, and only after it passes can they fill the pool.

Where the county goes past the state minimum

A.R.S. 36-1681 gives you a five-foot barrier and a self-latching gate. That is the floor. Bulletin 010 is where the numbers a builder actually needs live: the 2-inch and 4-inch bottom gaps, the 45-inch spacing on climbable members, the 11-gauge chain link, the 30-second door alarm, the 48-inch interior barrier option. Build to the statute alone and you can still fail the inspection. The statute itself is broken down in Arizona's pool barrier law under A.R.S. 36-1681.

Your pool permit moves alongside the county building permit for the house, both get checked against the codes Pinal County adopted, and the barrier is one stage in the county inspection sequence. In a planned community, the HOA's recorded restrictions can dictate fence style on top of all of it. Read the current specs in Information Bulletin 010 with your pool contractor before the dig, and price the barrier into the pool bid rather than treating it as a later yard project.

title: Pinal County Residential Building Permit Requirements: What You File for a New Home
shortSummary: A new home on unincorporated Pinal County land needs a county building permit before any work starts. You apply through the Accela Citizen Access portal or in person, and submit a building permit application, a property owner authorization form, a site plan, and construction drawings for review against the county's 2018 codes.
bodyHtml:
A new custom home on unincorporated Pinal County land needs a county building permit before any work starts. You file with the county Building Safety Division and submit your plans for review against the 2018 codes the county adopted. No footing gets poured until that permit issues. This page walks through how you apply, what you file, and what happens next.

How you apply

Pinal County takes building permit applications two ways. You can file online through the county's Accela Citizen Access portal, or in person at the Community Development Department. Building Safety runs out of 85 North Florence Street in Florence. The phone numbers are 520-509-3555 and 888-431-1311. The county is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for unincorporated land only. This process applies when your lot sits outside every city boundary. Inside Casa Grande, Maricopa, Apache Junction, or another city, you apply to that city instead.

What you submit

The county reviews a set of documents before it issues a permit. For a new single-family home, plan to file:

  • A building permit application plus a property owner authorization form. The county now asks for that second form with every application.
  • A site plan showing the house, driveway, and other features on the lot. Dimension the distance to each property line so reviewers can check your setbacks.
  • Construction drawings, meaning floor plans, elevations, and structural details for the house.
  • Engineered drawings for specific elements. Structures like retaining walls above a set height need plans prepared by an Arizona registered engineer.

The county spells out the exact document set in its bulletin 004R, Residential Submittal Requirements. It also publishes sample drawings you can build from:

Some of these pages can be used in your actual submittal; for instance, write in the correct dimensions on the sample drawings and incorporate them into your own drawings.

Two more items are common on rural county land. Most parcels sit off city utilities, so your well and septic approvals move alongside the building permit. If the lot falls in a mapped floodplain, the county also asks for grading and drainage plans and an elevation certificate.

What the county checks your plans against

Your plans get reviewed against the editions Pinal County adopted, currently the 2018 International Residential Code and the rest of the 2018 family. Drawing to a newer or generic code earns a correction and costs you a review cycle, so confirm your designer is working from the 2018 books.

Plan review, fees, and getting the permit

For example, say you are building a 2,600 square foot home on a two-acre parcel near Florence. You file the application and the owner authorization form. With it goes a site plan showing the house set back from each line, stamped structural drawings, and your well and septic paperwork. Staff check the package against the 2018 IRC. They may send back a short correction list to fix and resubmit. Once the plans are approved and the fees are paid, the permit issues and you break ground. Plan review time turns on how complete your submittal is and how many correction rounds it takes. A clean, engineer-ready package is the fastest path through.

Fees are due before the permit issues. Pinal County takes checks, money orders, online payments, and credit cards. Cards add a 2.29 percent processing fee, and the county takes cash only up to 150 dollars. On a custom home that card surcharge is real money, so plan to pay by check. How the dollar amount is calculated, and the separate impact fees that come due the same day, are worked through in Pinal County building permit and impact fees.

What comes before and after the permit

The permit is the gate between design and construction. Before it, your plans have to match the county's adopted codes and clear well and septic review. After it, the county inspects the build in stages and issues a certificate of occupancy at the end. If you are still mapping the full journey, start with the steps to building a custom home in Arizona. Check the current document list on the county's Applications and Information Bulletins page before you file.

title: Pinal County Residential Zoning and Setbacks: Why Your Parcel's District Decides
shortSummary: In unincorporated Pinal County, your building setbacks and minimum lot size come from your parcel's zoning district under the county Development Services Code, and they change from one district to the next. Rural districts like General Rural require large lots and deep yards, while single-residence districts allow smaller lots. Verify your parcel's zoning before you design.
bodyHtml:
When you build on unincorporated Pinal County land, how far your house must sit from each property line is not one countywide number. It depends on your parcel's zoning district. The county sets different setbacks and minimum lot sizes for each district, so the first real step is finding out which district your land falls in and what it requires.

What sets your setbacks

The rules live in the county's Development Services Code, the zoning code administered by the Pinal County Planning Division. The county states the principle plainly:

The Ordinance requires certain setbacks from lot lines, the requirements depend on the zoning of a particular lot.

Each residential or rural district has its own minimum lot area, minimum lot width, front, side, and rear yard setbacks, and height limit. Change the district and you change every one of those numbers. That is why a neighbor a mile away can build closer to the line than you can, or has to sit farther back.

The residential and rural districts

Pinal County divides unincorporated land into a range of zoning districts. The rural ones, like GR (General Rural) and GR-10, are written for large-acreage parcels and keep homes well off the property lines and away from neighbors. Suburban Ranch (SR) sits between rural land and platted subdivisions. Single-residence districts, such as R-12, cover smaller lots with tighter setbacks.

The pattern runs one way: the more rural the district, the larger the minimum lot and the deeper the required yards. Knowing the district letter is still not the same as knowing your numbers. Each district fixes five things at once, and all five shape the box your house fits in: minimum lot area, minimum lot width, front yard, side and rear yards, and height. A narrow parcel can meet the minimum lot area and still leave you a thin building envelope once the side yards come off both edges. Read the standards table for your district rather than a rule of thumb.

How to find your parcel's zoning

Because the standards are parcel-specific, confirm your zoning before you spend money on a design. The county gives you a few ways to do it:

  • Use the county's Citizen Access portal to request a zoning verification. The same request also covers flood status, fence and wall rules, and other land-use limits on your lot.
  • Call the county's 311 Citizen Contact Center, or reach the Planning Division directly at 520-509-3555.

Once you know your district, you read that district's development standards in the Development Services Code, or ask Planning to confirm your exact front, side, and rear setbacks in writing.

Why this matters for your build

Suppose you own a five-acre parcel near Florence zoned GR, General Rural. It follows the rural large-lot standards, and the house has generous room off every line. A half-acre lot in a single-residence district a few miles away follows tighter setbacks and a smaller minimum lot, so the buildable area comes out a very different shape. Same county, same building codes, different box to build in.

Designing to the wrong district's setbacks is one of the most common ways to fail plan review and lose weeks. Pin down your district first, then draw the house to fit it.

Where your setbacks get checked again

Setbacks do not stop at the drawing. They get measured on site at the footing stage, where the inspector confirms the house sits where your site plan shows. That check happens before the concrete truck comes, which is the one mercy in it: a house staked a few feet off the approved location costs you a re-dig instead of a saw. Your plans also have to meet the county's adopted building codes, and the whole package moves through permit review with the county as the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ). If you are starting from raw land, walk the full path in the steps to building a custom home in Arizona.
