title: Pinal County Solar PV Permit: What Rooftop and Ground-Mount Systems Need
shortSummary: A rooftop or ground-mount solar array in unincorporated Pinal County needs a county photovoltaic permit and a plan review before install. You submit a site plan, one-line and three-line electrical diagrams, component cut sheets, and mounting details. The county checks structural load, roof access pathways, and fire setbacks against the 2018 codes and 2017 electrical code.
bodyHtml:
Solar on unincorporated Pinal County land takes a county photovoltaic permit and a plan review before anyone climbs on the roof. Rooftop and ground-mount both. Two things set the county's review apart. It works from the 2018 code family with the 2017 electrical code, an edition behind the metro cities. And a modular or mobile home carries a requirement no stick-built house does: a sealed letter from an Arizona registered engineer. The county lists the whole package in Information Bulletin 021.

When a solar permit is required

Any residential solar install on unincorporated land needs a county PV permit, roof or ground. Pinal County Building Safety is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) outside any city, so it runs both the plan review and the inspections. Inside Casa Grande, Maricopa, or another incorporated city, you apply to that city. Your HOA can weigh in on where the panels go, within the limits state law puts on it. That side is covered in can an HOA stop me from putting solar on my house in Arizona.

What you submit: the plan set

The county reviews a plan set with several parts before it issues the permit. For a residential PV system, plan to file:

  • A site plan that shows the roof-mounted or ground-mounted arrays and the major components on the lot.
  • Electrical diagrams, meaning a one-line and a three-line diagram. Each shows wire type and size, the number of conductors, conduit type and size, the modules and inverter, and the utility disconnect.
  • Major component information: the inverter, modules, array, and any batteries. Give model numbers, manufacturer cut sheets, and UL listings. Array data covers the number of modules in series, operating voltage and current, maximum system voltage, and short circuit current.
  • Mounting details. For a roof mount, note the weight of the array in pounds per square foot, the roof covering (comp, tile), and the roof framing, such as trusses at 24 inches on center. Show how the panels attach and how the roof penetrations are sealed. For a ground mount, detail the anchoring system.

Roof access, pathways, and fire setbacks

Rooftop arrays have to leave room for firefighters, so the county sets access pathways and clear space at the ridge. The bulletin is specific:

Provide no fewer than two access pathways, on separate roof planes; one pathway to be from the street side or driveway.

Those pathways run at least 36 inches wide, from the lowest roof edge up to the ridge. The clear space at the ridge depends on how much roof the panels cover. Take up a third of the roof area or less and you leave an 18-inch clear setback on both sides of the ridge. Cover more than a third and that setback grows to 36 inches on each side. The rules come from the International Fire Code (IFC), Section 1204 of the 2018 edition, which governs conductor marking, roof access, and spacing.

Structural and electrical review

The county confirms two things: that the roof can carry the panels, and that the wiring meets code. On the structural side, the array weight in pounds per square foot and the roof framing tell the reviewer whether the existing structure holds the load. Electrical notes cite the 2017 National Electrical Code. Equipment goes in under NEC Article 690 and carries the required warnings and signage. Arizona leaves code adoption to each local jurisdiction, and Pinal County sits on the 2018 I-codes with the 2017 electrical code.

One rule stands out for manufactured housing. A PV system on the roof of a modular or mobile home has to be structurally evaluated. The permit application must include a sealed certification letter from an Arizona registered engineer. That letter states the home can carry the loads under the county's adopted 2018 codes, and that the panel assembly and standoffs meet the manufacturer's specs. Budget for that letter before you sign an install contract, because it is engineering work no rooftop quote assumes.

What a clean Pinal submittal looks like

For example, take a homeowner near Florence adding a 7 kilowatt rooftop array to a tile roof framed with trusses at 24 inches on center. The plan set gives the array weight in pounds per square foot and both electrical diagrams. Cut sheets and UL listings cover the modules and inverter. The roof plan draws two 36-inch access pathways on separate roof planes, one of them reaching the driveway side. The panels cover under a third of the roof, so the plans leave an 18-inch clear setback along the ridge. Notes cite the 2017 NEC and 2018 IFC Section 1204. A reviewer checks the package, the permit issues, and an inspector signs off the mounting and wiring before the system goes live.

Fitting solar into the rest of the county process

If you are adding panels during a new build, the PV plans move alongside the county building permit for the house, and both get reviewed against the 2018 codes Pinal County adopted. The install is checked in the county inspection sequence like any other trade. Whether solar pencils out on a new home is a separate question, taken up in is solar worth it on a new construction home in Arizona. Have your installer pull the current submittal list from Information Bulletin 021 rather than reusing a plan set drawn for a city job.

title: Pinal County Wall and Fence Permit: Height Limits, Retaining Walls, and When You Need an Engineer
shortSummary: In unincorporated Pinal County, a wall or fence up to 7 feet and a retaining wall up to 4 feet can be built to the county's example drawings through the Wall/Fence permit. Go taller, or stack a wall on a retaining wall, and you need a building permit with plans stamped by an Arizona registered engineer.
bodyHtml:
A wall or fence on unincorporated Pinal County land runs through the county's Wall/Fence permit. Two height numbers decide how hard that is. A wall or fence up to 7 feet, and a retaining wall up to 4 feet, can follow the county's own example drawings. Go past either limit and you need a building permit with plans prepared by a licensed engineer. Pinal County spells this out in Information Bulletin 014.

Which permit the county wants

Pinal County reviews walls and fences through a Wall/Fence permit. The bulletin ships with an application and example drawings you can build from, which is why most yard walls out here never see an engineer. The county is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) for land outside any city, so its Building Safety Division handles the review. Inside Casa Grande, Apache Junction, or another incorporated city, that city runs the process instead. The building permit is only half of it. Where the wall may sit comes from zoning, a separate check covered below.

The height limits: 7 feet for walls, 4 feet for retaining walls

The county caps a plain wall or fence at 7 feet and a retaining wall at 4 feet before engineering kicks in. How you measure is the part people get wrong. A wall or fence is measured from the side with the lowest adjacent grade. A wall that reads 6 feet tall from your yard can measure over 7 from a neighbor's lower grade, and the neighbor's side is the one that counts. A retaining wall is measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, so the buried course counts against your 4 feet. The county also bars stacking. Put another wall or added load on top of a retaining wall and you fall outside the standard drawings. These two numbers are not local inventions. They match the permit-exemption thresholds in the 2018 International Residential Code the county adopts.

When you need an engineer

Once a wall passes those limits, the county steps up the requirements:

Walls, fences and retaining walls exceeding the limits outlined above will require a building permit and the plans prepared by an Arizona Registered Engineer.

So an 8-foot privacy wall, a 5-foot retaining wall, or a fence set on top of a retaining wall all need a building permit with engineered, stamped drawings. The reason is structural. A taller wall carries more wind load, and a retaining wall holding back more soil carries more soil pressure, which is a live problem where expansive soils swell and monsoon runoff loads one face of a wall in an afternoon. The county wants an engineer to size the footing and the reinforcement. Under the standard height, the example drawings did that sizing for you.

Drainage, washes, and zoning

Two more checks sit alongside the height rules. First, a solid wall can dam up water. The county recommends drainage openings at grade so sheet flow passes through instead of pooling behind the wall. If a regulated wash crosses your land, call the county Flood Control District at 520-866-6411 for its rules. Second, where the wall may sit, and how tall it may be along each yard, comes from your zoning rather than the building code. Confirm those setbacks and height limits with the county Planning Division at 520-866-6442. Watch for any easement on the parcel, since you generally cannot block one with a wall. The application asks for front-yard height separately from rear and side, because zoning usually allows more height in back.

A wall that stays out of the engineer's office

For example, take a homeowner on an acre near Coolidge who wants a 6-foot masonry privacy wall plus a 3-foot retaining wall to level a building pad. The privacy wall is under 7 feet. The retaining wall is under 4 feet with nothing stacked on it. So they build to the county's example drawings and file the Wall/Fence permit with no engineer involved. Raise that wall to 8 feet later, or the retaining wall to 5, or set a fence on top of the retaining wall, and the county wants a building permit with plans stamped by an Arizona registered engineer. They still call Planning at 520-866-6442 to check the wall against their district's setbacks, and Flood Control at 520-866-6411, because a wash runs across the back of the lot.

Zoning, permits, and inspections around a wall

Where a wall can go traces back to your parcel's zoning and setbacks, which draw the buildable lines on the lot. A taller wall that needs a building permit moves through the same county permit process as the house, and an engineered wall gets checked during county inspections. Arizona leaves code adoption to local jurisdictions, and Pinal County sits on the 2018 codes. Read the current limits in Information Bulletin 014 before you pour a footing, and measure from the low side of the grade when you do.

title: Scottsdale Block Wall, Fence, and Retaining Wall Permits: When You Need One
shortSummary: In Scottsdale you need a permit to build any fence over 3 feet tall, a dry-stack or interlocking block wall over 30 inches, or any retaining wall at all. Walls and fences 3 feet and under skip the permit but still need a free courtesy site plan check. Every retaining wall needs engineered plans.
bodyHtml:
Scottsdale runs three separate height triggers for walls, and one of them has no height at all. A fence needs a permit past 3 feet. A dry-stack or interlocking block wall needs one past 30 inches. A retaining wall needs a permit and a stamped engineer's design at any height, even 18 inches. Everything below those lines stays permit-free but still goes past the city, through a free site plan check that keeps the wall off easements and out of the drainage path.

The three permit triggers

You need a Scottsdale building permit once a wall or fence crosses one of three lines. The city lists the jobs that require a permit:

Constructing any fence taller than 3-feet in height Building dry stack stone or interlocking block walls over 30-inches in height Constructing a retaining wall

So the fence trigger is 3 feet, the dry-stack or interlocking block wall trigger is 30 inches, and a retaining wall needs a permit at any height. The block-wall number sits lower for a reason: units stacked or interlocked without mortar topple more easily than a mortared or engineered wall. Two cases catch people out. Replacing an existing fence counts as new construction under the same rules. Adding height to a fence already over 3 feet needs a permit too.

The walls you can build without a permit

Walls and fences 3 feet and under skip the permit. They do not skip the city. Scottsdale still runs a courtesy site plan check:

In most residential zoning districts, you do not need a permit for walls and fences (including wrought iron fencing), up to 3' in height.

The review is free and quick. It confirms the wall meets your zoning, stays clear of any easement or drainage watercourse, and does not push water onto a neighbor. Your zoning district sets both how tall a wall may be and how close to the property line it may sit, and those setbacks are covered in Scottsdale residential zoning and setbacks. A short decorative wall along a front yard is the classic no-permit case, as long as it clears the site plan check.

Retaining walls and engineering

The retaining wall is the one type with no exemption at any height. It holds back soil, so it carries load and can fail in a way a free-standing garden wall cannot. Scottsdale requires engineered plans for every one of them, stamped by an Arizona-licensed engineer or architect. There is a shortcut on the low end. For a wall 4 feet or less, the city publishes a standard detail, its Minimum Standards for Retaining Walls 4 ft. high or less, and you can build to that instead of paying for a custom design. A retaining wall submittal also needs a full grading and drainage plan showing top-of-wall and finished-grade elevations along the wall.

Scottsdale's fee structure is worth reading before you design. The city bills retaining wall review by the hour plus a charge per linear foot, and it collects the first hour of plan review when you submit. Length drives that fee, not height, so a long low terrace can review more expensively than a shorter, taller wall doing the same job.

A north Scottsdale hillside case

Suppose a homeowner on a sloped north Scottsdale lot wants a 5 foot privacy wall along the back and a low retaining wall to level a side-yard patio. The 5 foot wall clears the 3 foot line, so it takes a permit. The retaining wall takes a permit and an engineer no matter how short it is. At 3 feet it fits the city's standard 4-foot detail, so the engineer builds to that rather than a custom design and the cost stays down. The submittal puts both walls on a grading plan with top-of-wall and finished-grade elevations, shows neither wall sitting on the utility easement, and carries the engineer's stamp on the retaining wall. The privacy wall sits on a footing sized for the soil under it.

Before you set a string line

Measure first, and measure from the low side. A fence at 3 feet or under, or a garden wall at 30 inches or under, stays permit-free and still gets the free courtesy site plan check. An inch over puts you in permit territory. Treat any retaining wall as a permitted, engineered job from day one, and reach for the city's standard 4-foot detail whenever the wall is low enough to qualify. Keep every wall off your easements and out of the drainage path, because that is exactly what the courtesy review looks for. If the wall encloses a pool yard, it gets reviewed with the pool, as covered in the Scottsdale pool and spa barrier permit. Permit and review fees are itemized in the Scottsdale permit and impact fee schedule.

Source

The standard retaining wall detail is the city's Minimum Standards for Retaining Walls 4 ft. high or less. Retaining walls are engineered to the building code Scottsdale adopts, tracked in the ICC code adoptions for Arizona.

Height thresholds and the retaining wall fee formula both get revised. Take your wall lengths and elevations to Scottsdale Planning and Development for the live numbers before you order block.

title: Scottsdale Pool and Spa Permit and Barrier Requirements: What You File and Fence
shortSummary: A pool or spa in Scottsdale needs its own building permit, and the city will not issue it until a permitted home already sits on the lot. You file a scaled site plan and pool engineering. State law requires a five-foot barrier with a self-latching gate around the water before you can fill it.
bodyHtml:
Scottsdale will not issue a pool permit for a lot that has no permitted house on it. That one rule sets the order of operations on a custom build: the residence permit comes first, the pool follows as its own separate application, even when the two are going in the same season. That pool permit covers three things at once, the shell, its electrical, and the safety barrier around the water. The barrier itself comes from state law, and the city checks it twice, once on your site plan and again in the field before the pool holds water.

When Scottsdale requires a pool or spa permit

Every in-ground pool and spa in Scottsdale needs a building permit, and the city ties that permit to a finished, permitted home. You cannot pull a pool permit on a bare lot. The rule is short and firm:

No pool permit will be issued without an existing permitted residence.

You apply through the Scottsdale SPUR portal, the same online system used for the house. If you pull the permit yourself instead of hiring a licensed contractor, you file the owner-builder declaration at submittal. The one pool permit carries the pool structure, the electrical bonding and grounding the water needs, and the barrier that encloses it. Spas are submitted the same way as pools, and whether a spa also needs the safety barrier depends on the state depth rule covered in whether a hot tub or spa needs a pool barrier.

How Scottsdale reviews the barrier

Scottsdale does not treat the fence as a field detail to sort out later. One of the city's pool submittal categories is a Pool/Spa Site Review with Fence, and filing under it means handing in design calculations for the fence and for any retaining walls holding the pool deck. The barrier is drawn, calculated, and reviewed with the shell.

What the barrier has to be comes from state law, A.R.S. 36-1681, which Scottsdale enforces through the pool permit. The statute sets the floor:

The pool shall be entirely enclosed by at least a five foot wall, fence or other barrier as measured on the exterior side of the wall, fence or barrier.

The gate opens away from the pool and latches on its own, with the release at least 54 inches above the ground so a small child cannot reach it. Where a wall of the house forms one side of the enclosure, the law allows a listed motorized safety cover, or self-latching protection on the doors and windows opening to the pool, in place of a fence on that side. The full state rule, including the barrier alternatives, is broken out in Arizona's pool barrier law under A.R.S. 36-1681.

What you submit

The pool submittal is a new site plan drawn to scale plus the pool's engineering. Scottsdale requires a fresh site plan for the pool and will not accept it bolted onto your approved house plans. Allowed scales are 1 inch to 10 feet, 1 inch to 20 feet, or 1/8 inch to 1 foot. The plan has to show the whole lot and call out:

  • The pool and any decking, dimensioned from the house and from every property line, with the setbacks your zoning district requires.
  • Existing water, sewer, and septic lines. The pool cannot sit on top of a sewer tap or a septic system, so those get drawn in. On a septic lot the plan lists the Maricopa County permit number.
  • The pool equipment location, screened at least 12 inches above the highest part of the equipment and kept out of any easement. Equipment cannot sit within 10 feet of an opening into a neighbor's living space.
  • A 5 foot construction buffer to any protected native desert area on the lot.

For the engineering you pick standard or custom. A standard pool cites a pool standard plan number already on file with the city. A custom pool needs its own engineered plan and calculations. Either way the city wants a Pool Engineer's Authorization letter and the design calculations with the submittal.

How it plays out on a real lot

Suppose a standard pool goes in behind a new home on a 9,000 square foot R1-7 lot in south Scottsdale. The builder files the pool as its own SPUR permit, cites the standard plan number, and draws the shell 8 feet off the back of the house so it clears the sewer tap shown on the plan. The equipment pad sits in the side yard, screened 12 inches above the pump and clear of the utility easement. A five-foot view fence with a self-latching gate encloses the yard, and the gate latch is mounted 54 inches up. At inspection the city checks the barrier and the pool's electrical before the pool is filled. Until that barrier passes, the pool cannot legally hold water or be used. The same inspectors who sign off the house handle the pool, following the Scottsdale inspection sequence. One more field rule: a pool cannot be drained or backwashed into a wash, the street, or a natural area, so the plan shows where that water goes.

Sequencing the pool into a custom build

Get the house permitted first. Scottsdale issues no pool permit without an existing permitted residence, so a pool penciled into the same construction schedule as the slab is already out of order. Put the barrier in the pool budget rather than the yard budget, because the pool is unusable until the fence and gate pass. Draw the site plan around your sewer tap, septic, and easements before the designer shapes the pool, since a shell drawn over a utility line comes back as a correction. Take the standard pool plan when your design allows it; it reviews faster and cheaper than a custom engineered pool. On a lot with protected desert, hold the 5 foot buffer, which runs into the Scottsdale environmentally sensitive lands rules. Pool trade fees land on top of your house permit, itemized in the Scottsdale permit and impact fee schedule.

Source

The pool and spa submittal categories and the permitted-residence rule are published by the City of Scottsdale on its Plan Submittal Requirements page. The scaled site-plan items, equipment screening, and drainage notes come from the city's Minimum Requirements for Site Plan Submittal, Single Family Residential Pool Permit. The five-foot barrier and gate rule is state law at A.R.S. 36-1681.

Submittal categories and barrier details get revised between code cycles. Have your pool contractor confirm the current Scottsdale requirements before the site plan goes in.

title: Scottsdale Solar PV Permit: The Small-Scope Review Path for Rooftop Panels
shortSummary: A rooftop solar PV system in Scottsdale needs a building permit, and every application gets reviewed. An array that meets the city's panel placement guidelines qualifies for a fast small-scope review. Ground-mounted systems and layouts that break the guidelines go to full plan review. Wiring follows the 2020 electrical code.
bodyHtml:
Adding solar panels to a Scottsdale roof takes a building permit, but not the full plan review a new house goes through. Scottsdale sorts rooftop solar into two lanes. A standard array that sits low and follows the city's placement rules gets a quick small-scope review. Anything unusual, and any ground-mounted system, gets a full plan review. Either way the panels are checked against the fire, structural, and electrical codes before the permit issues.

How Scottsdale reviews a rooftop solar permit

Scottsdale reviews every solar permit, and the layout of your panels decides how deep that review goes. The city puts it directly:

Solar array systems complying with the "Solar Panel Placement Design Guidelines" will be eligible to receive a small scope review; all other submittals, including ground mounted solar systems, will be required to submit for a full plan review.

A small-scope review is the fast lane. It is the city confirming that a familiar, low-profile array meets the rules. That clears faster than a full engineering review. It is also different from the online minimum permit Scottsdale uses for routine electrical work like a panel upgrade or a rewire, which needs no plan review at all. A solar array is always reviewed. What you control is which lane it lands in. The City of Scottsdale is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), so its building officials run this review and set the placement rules.

The placement rules that earn the fast review

To qualify for the small-scope review, the array has to sit low and leave the roof reachable for firefighters. The clearances come from the International Fire Code the city enforces, at IFC 605.11:

  • Panels stay at least 3 feet below the ridge.
  • Each roof slope keeps two 3 foot wide access pathways running from the eave up to the ridge.
  • On a roof with hips and valleys, panels stay at least 18 inches off a hip or valley when they sit on both sides.

Height off the roof matters too. On a south-facing pitched roof, the top of the panels stays within 8 inches of the roof surface and runs parallel to it. On a north, east, or west facing pitched roof, panels tilt no more than 15 degrees and rise no more than 24 inches above the roof. On a low-slope or flat roof, panels stay within 30 inches of the roof surface. Break any of these, or mount the system on the ground, and the permit moves to full plan review.

What you submit and the code it meets

A rooftop PV submittal is a small package of plans and product data. Scottsdale wants:

  • A site plan and roof plan showing where the array sits, drawn to scale of 1 inch to 20 feet or tighter.
  • A roof framing plan giving the framing type, spacing, and span, plus the mounting locations and details.
  • Electrical one-line and three-line diagrams, with the short-circuit current listed on each string.
  • Cut sheets and listings for the inverters and modules.

The wiring is checked against the 2020 National Electrical Code, the edition Scottsdale enforces. The array goes in under NEC Article 690 and gets the required warning labels. If the array is heavy, meaning dead loads over 50 pounds at the mounting points, the city requires a structural analysis. Two zoning wrinkles can change the path. A home with Historic Property zoning files a pre-application for historic review first. A solar job in a multi-family district needs a homeowner association approval letter with the submittal. The full list of codes Scottsdale enforces, including the 2020 electrical code, is in Scottsdale's adopted building codes.

One tilt angle, two review lanes

Suppose a homeowner in a standard R1-7 neighborhood adds a 20-panel system flat against a south-facing tile roof. The panels sit 5 inches above the tile, stop 3 feet short of the ridge, and leave a 3 foot walkway up each side. The layout follows the placement guidelines, so the permit qualifies for the small-scope review and clears quickly. The installer pulls it through the SPUR portal, or the homeowner files the owner-builder declaration to self-perform. Once the panels are up, a final inspection has to pass before the system energizes and ties to the grid. Now change one thing. Raise those same panels on a 20 degree tilt to chase winter sun and the array breaks both the 15 degree limit and the height limit, so the identical house drops into full plan review instead.

Keeping the permit in the fast lane

Design the array to the placement rules and the review stays short. Mount the panels low, parallel to the roof, and 3 feet below the ridge. Keep the fire access paths clear. Get your installer the roof framing type, spacing, and span early, because the framing plan and a possible structural check are what stall a submittal. Check your zoning before you assume the fast lane, since Historic Property and multi-family lots carry their own extra step. The tilt decision is where most of the money hides: a few degrees of extra winter yield can trade a small-scope review for a full one. Plan for the final inspection too, which the system needs before it energizes, and which slots into the Scottsdale inspection sequence with the rest of your build. Whether solar pencils out on a new build is a separate question, covered in is solar worth it on a new construction home in Arizona.

Source

The small-scope versus full-review rule, the panel placement guidelines, and the submittal list are published by the City of Scottsdale in its Residential Solar Energy Systems submittal guidelines, linked from the city's Plan Submittal Requirements page. Scottsdale's adopted 2020 electrical code is confirmed in the ICC code adoptions for Arizona.

Placement guidelines and the adopted electrical edition both move between code cycles. Check the current version of the submittal guidelines with Scottsdale Planning and Development before your installer draws the roof plan.

  • ICC Code Adoptions for Arizona (2020 NEC)

title: IRC E3607 System Grounding: How Your Home Ties to Earth and Why the Main Bond Matters
shortSummary: IRC Section E3607 grounds your home's electrical system at one point: the main service. There, the main bonding jumper ties the neutral to the metal enclosure, and the grounding electrode conductor runs to earth. This single bond is what makes a breaker trip during a ground fault instead of leaving metal parts live.
bodyHtml:
Grounding sounds like one idea, but the code treats it as two. Grounding ties your electrical system to the earth. Bonding ties all the metal parts together so they sit at the same voltage. Section E3607 of the International Residential Code sets where those two meet: one point, at your main service, and nowhere downstream of it.

The one bond point

Your system is grounded and bonded together at the main service, and only there. Inside the service enclosure, a part called the main bonding jumper connects the neutral wire to the metal box and to the equipment grounding wires. The code is exact about it:

An unspliced main bonding jumper shall be used to connect the equipment grounding conductor and the service-disconnect enclosure to the grounded conductor.

From that point, a grounding electrode conductor runs out to the earth connection. The neutral and the ground share one bond, made once.

Why neutral and ground split after that

Past the main service, the neutral and the ground never touch again. Every subpanel and circuit keeps them on separate bars. A detached casita or a garage subpanel is fed with a four-wire feeder for this reason: two hot wires, a neutral, and a separate ground. If the neutral and ground were re-bonded at a subpanel, normal current would start flowing on the ground wires and on metal parts, which is exactly what the single-point rule prevents.

What the bond actually does for you

The main bond is a safety device, not a formality. For example, a hot wire inside your dryer can rub through its jacket and touch the metal frame. With a solid bond and a ground path, that fault turns into a dead short. The breaker sees a surge of current and trips in a fraction of a second. Without the bond, the dryer frame can sit quietly energized, waiting for someone to touch it and the floor at once. The bond turns a hidden hazard into a tripped breaker.

The Arizona ground is the weak link

The bond is only as good as the earth connection it feeds, and desert soil is a poor conductor. Dry, rocky ground and caliche resist current far more than damp soil does. That is why the electrode side of the system, covered in the grounding electrode system, leans on the concrete-encased electrode cast into your foundation footing. Monsoon lightning gives you a second reason to want a solid path to earth. The grounding conductor is sized from your service, so it scales with your electrical service and panel. Add a whole-house generator or battery and the inspector checks grounding and bonding a second time at the transfer equipment. Section E3607 of the 2021 IRC carries the full text.

  • IRC main bonding jumper (E3607.5) explained

title: IRC E3608 Grounding Electrode System: Ground Rods, the Ufer, and Arizona Desert Soil
shortSummary: IRC Section E3608 lists the electrodes that connect your home to the earth: a metal water pipe, a concrete-encased electrode in the foundation, a ground ring, a driven rod, or a plate. Every one present must be bonded together. In dry Arizona soil, the concrete-encased electrode does most of the work.
bodyHtml:
A ground fault or a lightning surge needs somewhere to go, and that somewhere is the earth. Section E3608 of the International Residential Code defines how your home connects to it. The section lists five kinds of grounding electrodes, and it carries one firm rule: every electrode present at your home has to be bonded together into a single system.

The five electrodes the code accepts

E3608 recognizes five ways to reach earth, and the list opens with the metal water pipe:

A metal underground water pipe in direct contact with the earth for 10 feet (3048 mm) or more.

Here is the full list in plain terms:

  • A metal underground water pipe, touching soil for 10 feet or more. It always needs a backup electrode.
  • A concrete-encased electrode, also called a Ufer. It is 20 feet of half-inch rebar, or 20 feet of 4-gauge copper, cast into a footing with at least 2 inches of concrete around it.
  • A ground ring of at least 20 feet of 2-gauge bare copper, buried 30 inches deep.
  • A driven rod or pipe, at least 8 feet long.
  • A buried metal plate with at least 2 square feet of surface.

Whichever of these exist at your home have to be tied together. On a rural lot served by a well or by hauled water, the first item on that list simply is not there, since no metal water main runs from the street. The list gets shorter, so the electrodes that remain carry the whole job.

Why the Ufer wins in Arizona

The concrete-encased electrode is the workhorse in a desert build, and the reason is history. Herbert Ufer solved this problem for the U.S. Army in 1942, grounding bomb-storage vaults near Tucson and Flagstaff, where the dry ground had no water table and driven rods could not reach a low resistance. Concrete holds moisture and spreads contact across a large surface, so a Ufer often measures a few ohms where a lone rod struggles. The 2021 code requires the concrete-encased electrode when it is present, and every new home with a concrete footing has one available. Your builder ties a length of rebar or copper into the footing before the pour, and it becomes the primary ground.

The lone ground rod problem

A single driven rod is often not enough by itself. The code assumes one rod may not grip the earth well, so it requires a second electrode unless the rod tests at 25 ohms or less. For example, in the dry, rocky soil and caliche common across Maricopa and Pinal County, hitting 25 ohms with one rod is hard. That is why an Arizona service usually pairs the foundation Ufer with a driven rod, spaced at least 6 feet from any other rod, rather than trusting a rod alone.

Where the electrode conductor stops

The electrode system is the earth end of your system grounding. The grounding electrode conductor runs from your service to these electrodes, and the code caps how big it has to get: never larger than 6-gauge copper to a rod, or 4-gauge copper to the concrete-encased electrode. That cap is why a 400-amp service does not need a 400-amp-sized wire out to the ground rod. Everything upstream starts at your electrical service and panel, sized as explained in what size electrical service does a custom home need in Arizona. A pool adds its own earth-bonding rules under pool equipotential bonding. Which code edition your city enforces can shift grounding details, so confirm it in the building code editions by city reference. Section E3608 of the 2021 IRC has the electrode list in full.

title: IRC E3703 Required Branch Circuits: The Kitchen, Laundry, and Bath Circuits Your Home Needs
shortSummary: IRC Section E3703 sets the minimum circuits every new home must have. The kitchen needs at least two 20-amp small-appliance circuits. The laundry area needs its own 20-amp circuit, and the bathrooms need one too. The garage gets a 20-amp circuit, and central heating equipment gets its own dedicated circuit.
bodyHtml:
Your electrician does not get to guess how many circuits your kitchen or laundry room needs. Section E3703 of the International Residential Code sets the floor. It names the branch circuits every new home must have, separate from the general lighting and outlet circuits, so the rooms that pull the most power do not share one overloaded wire.

The circuits the code requires

E3703 names five required circuits on top of your general-purpose wiring:

  • Two or more 20-amp small-appliance circuits for the kitchen, dining room, and pantry.
  • One 20-amp circuit for the laundry area.
  • One 20-amp circuit for the bathrooms.
  • One 20-amp circuit for the garage.
  • One dedicated circuit for central heating equipment.

The code states the kitchen rule plainly:

A minimum of two 20-ampere-rated small-appliance branch circuits shall be provided.

Each of these runs on 20 amps, which uses 12-gauge copper wire. That is a step up from the 15-amp, 14-gauge wire behind most lighting.

Why the kitchen needs two circuits

The two-circuit kitchen rule exists because small appliances draw heavy current. A 20-amp circuit carries about 2,400 watts (20 amps times 120 volts). A single air fryer can pull 1,500 watts, and a toaster oven another 1,200. Run both on one circuit and the breaker trips. For example, splitting the counter outlets across two circuits lets a Scottsdale family run the coffee maker, the toaster, and a griddle at breakfast without going dark. The two circuits share the counter, so side-by-side outlets usually sit on different ones.

Laundry, bathroom, and garage circuits

Three more circuits each guard against a specific overload.

  • The laundry circuit is a 20-amp line that serves only the laundry-area outlets. It keeps a washer and a plug-in gas dryer off a shared circuit.
  • The bathroom circuit is a 20-amp line for the bathroom outlets. One such circuit can feed several bathrooms, or it can serve everything in one bathroom, but it cannot mix with general room wiring. This matters because a hair dryer alone pulls up to 1,800 watts.
  • The garage circuit is a 20-amp, 120-volt line for garage outlets. In an Arizona garage it often feeds a second freezer, which is why the code keeps it off the house lighting. An RV garage needs more than that one circuit anyway, since a 30- or 50-amp RV receptacle is a dedicated run of its own.

Dedicated circuits for the big equipment

Central heating equipment gets its own circuit, and so do most large appliances. The code requires an individual branch circuit for the furnace or air handler. Permanently wired air conditioning and its helpers, like a condensate pump, can share that heating circuit. Beyond E3703, your dishwasher, disposal, microwave, and electric range each land on a circuit sized to the appliance nameplate. For a desert home the biggest dedicated loads are the air conditioning condensers, which drive the whole service size covered in what size electrical service does a custom home need in Arizona.

The rule is the same across Arizona

Required branch circuits do not change from Phoenix to Casa Grande. Every Arizona city adopts these minimums through the IRC, so the two kitchen circuits and the laundry, bath, and garage circuits apply everywhere. One thing does change the count: E3703 writes these requirements per dwelling unit. A detached casita with its own kitchen is a second dwelling unit, so the list starts over out there. What varies by city is the code edition, which can affect related rules like tamper-resistant and GFCI outlets. Confirm your city's edition in the building code editions by city reference. These circuits land on your electrical service and panel, each on its own breaker, and they set the wire size and breaker pairing that comes next. Section E3703 of the 2021 IRC lists them all.

title: IRC E3705 Conductor Sizing and Overcurrent Protection: Matching Wire to Breaker in Arizona Heat
shortSummary: IRC Section E3705 pairs each wire size with a maximum breaker: 14-gauge copper on a 15-amp breaker, 12-gauge on 20 amps, and 10-gauge on 30 amps. The breaker protects the wire from overheating. In hot Arizona attics, the code also makes you lower a wire's rated capacity, which can force a larger size.
bodyHtml:
The breaker in your panel is not there to protect your appliances. It is there to protect the wire in your walls. Section E3705 of the International Residential Code sets the pairing between the two. Each wire gauge gets a maximum breaker size, so the wire can never carry more current than it can shed as heat. Get the pairing wrong and the wire cooks before the breaker ever trips.

Matching wire size to breaker

The heart of E3705 is a simple pairing for the copper wire used in most homes:

  • 14-gauge copper takes a 15-amp breaker.
  • 12-gauge copper takes a 20-amp breaker.
  • 10-gauge copper takes a 30-amp breaker.

The rule runs one direction. A 20-amp breaker needs 12-gauge wire or thicker, never 14-gauge. You can always put heavier wire on a smaller breaker, but never lighter wire on a bigger one. That is why a 20-amp kitchen circuit is wired in 12-gauge, while a 15-amp bedroom lighting circuit can use 14-gauge.

The breaker protects the wire

Overcurrent protection is the reason the pairing is strict. Every circuit gets an overcurrent device, the breaker or fuse, at the point where it connects to the panel. Its job is to open the circuit before the wire heats past its rating. A breaker sized to the wire trips on a short or an overload. A breaker too large for the wire lets the wire overheat inside a closed wall, which is the fire risk the code is built to stop.

Arizona heat lowers a wire's capacity

Here is the part that bites in the desert. A wire's rated capacity assumes a surrounding temperature near 86°F. Above that, the code makes you reduce it. As E3705 puts it, for hotter spaces you:

multiply the allowable ampacities specified in Table E3705.1 by the appropriate correction factor.

A Phoenix attic in July runs 130°F to 150°F, far above 86°F. Around 135°F, for example, the code cuts a 12-gauge wire's rated capacity by nearly a third. A single 12-gauge cable still supports its 20-amp breaker with a little room left. But bundle several cables together through that superheated attic and a second reduction stacks on top of the heat cut. Together they can pull the circuit below 20 amps, so the electrician has to upsize the wire or route it out of the heat.

There is a design answer to this, and it is one you pick long before the electrician shows up. A conditioned attic, sealed with spray foam insulation at the roof deck instead of on the ceiling, sits inside the cooled envelope and runs within a few degrees of the rooms below. The wire in that attic sees something near 86°F instead of 140°F, so the correction factor barely bites and the home runs stay at their table ampacity.

Why this shows up on Arizona plans

Conductor sizing is uniform code, adopted the same way in every Arizona city. The heat correction is national too, but it matters more here than almost anywhere. It is one reason a careful builder keeps long home runs out of the hottest attic zones and sizes them for August, not January. Wire sizing works alongside the required branch circuits that feed your rooms and the service and panel those circuits start from. Planning a heavy load like a car charger? Read how to wire a new Arizona home for EV charging before the walls close. The ampacity tables and correction factors sit in Section E3705 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC E3901 Receptacle Placement: The 6-Foot Rule and Kitchen Outlets
shortSummary: IRC Section E3901 decides where the outlets go in your home. The main rule is that no point along a wall is more than 6 feet from a receptacle, which spaces them about 12 feet apart. Kitchens, bathrooms, hallways, and outdoor areas each get their own required outlets on top of that.
bodyHtml:
Where the outlets land is not up to wherever the electrician feels like drilling. Section E3901 of the International Residential Code sets it. These are rules to know before your walls close up. Sliding a couch across a room to reach a far-off outlet is a daily annoyance you can design out now.

The 6-foot rule

The core rule for living spaces is easy to picture:

no point along the floor line in any wall space is more than 6 feet, measured horizontally, from a receptacle outlet.

In practice that spaces outlets about 12 feet apart. It also means any stretch of wall 2 feet wide or more gets its own outlet, including the short wall beside a doorway. Follow it and a lamp cord reaches a wall from anywhere in the room, with no extension cords stretched across a doorway.

For example, a 16-foot bedroom wall with a single outlet at its midpoint leaves both corners 8 feet away, and the inspector writes it up. Set the outlets 2 feet in from each corner instead and they land 12 feet apart, which puts the worst spot on that wall, the midpoint, exactly 6 feet from each one.

Kitchen counters

Counters get a tighter rule, because that is where small appliances plug in. Along a counter, no point can be more than 24 inches from an outlet. That is close enough for a mixer or a toaster to reach without an extension cord. Those outlets sit on or above the counter, and no more than 20 inches above it. An island or peninsula counter that is big enough needs at least one of its own.

Bathrooms, hallways, and outside

A few spots carry their own rules. Every bathroom needs an outlet within 3 feet of the outside edge of each sink basin. A hallway 10 feet or longer needs at least one. Outside, the code calls for an outlet at the front and back of the house, plus one in the garage and one in the laundry area. Many of these have to be shock-protected as well, which is a separate rule.

Universal, not desert-specific

Receptacle placement is one part of the code that does not change from the desert to the mountains. Arizona cities and counties adopt the national electrical rules through the IRC. So the 6-foot rule and the counter spacing read the same in Scottsdale and in Casa Grande. What shifts by city is the code edition your AHJ enforces, and that mostly moves the shock-protection line. Confirm your edition in the building code editions by city reference.

One local wrinkle is worth knowing. E3901 counts by dwelling unit, not by building. A detached casita is its own dwelling unit, so the 6-foot rule starts over inside it. A 400-square-foot guest house still owes counter outlets and an outlet by the bathroom sink.

Where placement stops and protection starts

Placement is only half the story. The other half is which of these outlets have to be GFCI or AFCI protected, and how they all land back on your electrical service and panel. Planning circuits for solar or home automation? Lay them out in the same pass and you skip a round of rework. See should I prewire a new home for solar and automation. Section E3901 of the 2021 IRC has the placement rules in full.

title: IRC E3902 GFCI and AFCI Protection: Where Your Home Needs Each
shortSummary: IRC Section E3902 requires two kinds of electrical protection in a new home. GFCI outlets guard against shock in wet areas like bathrooms, kitchens, garages, and outdoors. AFCI protection guards against electrical fires on the circuits feeding living areas and bedrooms. Which code edition your Arizona city adopted changes exactly where each one is required.
bodyHtml:
Two small devices in your electrical panel do very different jobs, and the code requires both in a new home. One stops you from being electrocuted. The other stops your wiring from starting a fire. Section E3902 of the International Residential Code sets where each has to go. The exact list depends on which code edition your Arizona city adopted.

GFCI: shock protection for wet places

A GFCI, short for ground-fault circuit-interrupter, watches for power leaking to ground. That is what happens when a hair dryer falls in a full sink, or when you touch a live wire. It cuts power in a fraction of a second, fast enough to keep a shock from turning fatal. The code calls for GFCI protection at outlets wherever water and power meet: bathrooms, kitchen counters, garages, laundry areas, crawl spaces, and every outdoor outlet. That last group matters here. It covers your patio outlets, the pool equipment, and the outlet feeding a misting system.

AFCI: fire protection for living areas

An AFCI, or arc-fault circuit-interrupter, watches for a different danger. It looks for the small, hot arcs thrown off by damaged wiring, a pinched cord, or a loose connection. Those arcs are a leading cause of house fires. The code puts AFCI protection on the branch circuits feeding the living side of the house, meaning the:

outlets installed in kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms.

That reach extends to bedrooms, closets, hallways, and similar rooms. Most of your general-purpose circuits end up AFCI-protected.

Two different jobs, sometimes both

Keep them straight this way. GFCI is about people and shock, in wet spots. AFCI is about wiring and fire, in living spaces. A few rooms owe both at once. For example, a kitchen counter outlet sits in a wet area and rides a circuit the AFCI list already names, so it needs each kind of protection. An electrician covers that with one dual-function breaker at the panel instead of two separate devices. You do not choose between them. You put each where the code puts it. Both types carry a test button, and pressing those buttons is one of the checks an inspector runs at final inspection.

Why the edition matters in Arizona

This section has changed more than most between recent codes. The IRC points to the National Electrical Code, and Arizona AHJs are split. Some still enforce the 2017 edition, others the 2020. The 2020 edition pushed GFCI into more places, including the disconnect at your outdoor air conditioning condenser. Every home here has that condenser. So the edition your city adopted can decide whether that one disconnect needs GFCI. Confirm your edition in the building code editions by city reference.

Where the protection lives

The special breakers that provide GFCI and AFCI protection sit in your service and panel. For the alarms that warn your family when something else goes wrong, see the smoke alarm rules. Planning circuits for solar or home automation? Start with whether to prewire a new home for solar and automation. Section E3902 of the 2021 IRC names every required location.

title: IRC E4204 Pool Equipotential Bonding: The 8 AWG Copper Grid
shortSummary: IRC Section E4204 requires an equipotential bonding grid around every permanent pool and spa. Solid copper wire, no smaller than 8 AWG, ties the pool shell, the deck within 3 feet, metal fittings, pump equipment, and the water itself into one connected network so no dangerous voltage can build between them.
bodyHtml:
A pool mixes water, bare feet, and electricity from lights, pumps, and nearby equipment. If two metal parts near the pool sit at even slightly different electrical potential, a swimmer who touches both can become the path between them and feel a shock. Section E4204 of the International Residential Code stops that by tying everything conductive around the pool into one connected grid, so there is no voltage difference to feel.

What equipotential bonding does

Bonding and grounding sound alike but do different jobs. Grounding gives fault current a path back to the panel. Bonding links metal parts to each other so they all sit at the same voltage. The code calls this an equipotential grid, and its whole purpose is to remove the small voltage gaps, called gradients, that build up in the area around a pool. When every part a swimmer can reach is bonded to every other part, there is no gap to shock across, even if stray voltage is present on the system.

What has to be bonded

The grid is built from real copper, not an afterthought. The code requires the parts to be tied together with:

insulated, covered or bare solid copper conductors not smaller than 8 AWG.

That wire connects the parts the code lists:

  • The pool shell, usually through its steel reinforcing or a copper grid.
  • The perimeter deck surface.
  • The metal parts of the pool structure.
  • The metal shells and brackets behind underwater lights.
  • Metal fittings like ladders and rails.
  • The electrical equipment that runs the water, such as the pump motor.
  • Fixed metal within reach, like fences or a nearby raceway.

The perimeter bonding reaches 3 feet out from the inside pool walls. It is arranged in a grid of about 12 inches by 12 inches, set a few inches below the surface. The water itself is bonded too. A fitting keeps at least 9 square inches of conductive surface in contact with the pool water at all times.

The Arizona angle

Arizona has one of the highest rates of backyard pools in the country, and in the Scottsdale, Fountain Hills, and Paradise Valley custom market a pool is close to standard. That makes E4204 a section your build will almost certainly hit.

Timing is the thing to watch. The bonding grid goes in while the pool shell is still steel and dirt, before the gunite and long before the deck is poured. An inspector checks the copper and its connections at that stage, because once the concrete deck and cool decking cover it, there is no way to see or fix it without demolition. So the pool electrician and the shell crew have to coordinate before the pour.

For instance, a Paradise Valley crew bonds the shell steel and the pump but stops the perimeter grid at the coping. The inspector measures out from the inside wall, finds bare dirt where the 3-foot ring belongs, and fails the bond inspection. Adding the missing copper before the deck pour is a morning of trenching. Finding it after the cool decking is down means breaking concrete to get to it.

Skipping or shortcutting the grid is not a cosmetic miss. It is the difference between a safe pool and a real shock hazard at the water's edge.

Which edition applies to your build

The IRC electrical chapters follow the National Electrical Code, and equipotential bonding has been in the code for years, though the NEC edition your city references shifts the fine points. Arizona AHJs are split across editions, so confirm which one your lot falls under in the building code editions by city reference before the pool is engineered.

The other half of a safe pool

Bonding works next to the pool's other electrical protection. The pump and any pool receptacle need GFCI protection so power cuts fast if current leaks, and the whole pool load is fed and sized from your electrical service and panel. That covers the electrical side. The barrier and fencing rules cover the drowning side, and they run on their own permit track, described in what permits you need to build a pool with a new home. Chapter 42 of the 2021 IRC holds the bonding text.

title: IRC G2411 CSST Bonding: Protecting Gas Lines from Lightning
shortSummary: Section G2411 requires the gas piping in your home to be electrically bonded. Flexible CSST tubing gets an extra rule: it must connect to the home's grounding electrode system through a bonding jumper no smaller than 6 AWG copper, so a nearby lightning strike drains to ground instead of arcing through the thin tubing wall.
bodyHtml:
Corrugated stainless steel tubing, or CSST, is the flexible gas line that installs faster than rigid black iron and shows up in most new Arizona homes. It carries one safety rule that rigid pipe does not, and in a state with violent summer lightning, that rule earns its keep. Section G2411 of the International Residential Code spells it out.

What Section G2411 requires

Section G2411 works in two layers. Every gas piping system, whatever the material, has to be electrically bonded so a fault current has a safe path back to ground. Systems built with CSST then get a second, dedicated bond straight to the home's grounding electrode system.

The bonding jumper shall not be smaller than 6 AWG copper wire or equivalent.

That single copper jumper is the whole safeguard. It ties the gas tubing to the same ground as the electrical service, so the two metal systems sit at the same voltage when a surge hits.

Why bonding CSST stops a fire

The danger here is not the gas catching a spark at the burner. It is lightning. A strike on or near the house dumps a huge voltage onto every metal system inside. If the CSST is not bonded, that energy can jump, or arc, from a nearby metal object to the thin wall of the tubing, burn a pinhole, and ignite the gas inside. Bonding gives the surge an easier route to ground, so it drains away instead of punching through the tubing. That is why the rule reads as a lightning rule, and why Arizona's monsoon storms turn it from paperwork into real protection.

How the bond is actually installed

The details are specific, and an inspector checks them. The jumper is a solid or stranded copper wire, at least 6 AWG, run as short as practical and no longer than 75 feet measured along the wire. It clamps to the gas system downstream of the meter, or downstream of the propane second-stage regulator, on a length of rigid pipe, a steel fitting, a manifold, or a brass CSST fitting. It never clamps to the corrugated tubing itself. The far end connects to the grounding electrode system: a ground electrode, the grounding electrode conductor, or the service enclosure, using a clamp listed for the job. One clamp bonds the entire system, no matter how many runs branch off it.

The black-jacket exception

Newer arc-resistant CSST, sold with a black jacket marked AR, is built to shrug off a strike on its own and does not need the extra bonding jumper (Section G2411.3). The common yellow CSST does need it. If any yellow tubing is in the system, or if a black-jacket system is later modified with a piece of yellow tubing, the whole system gets bonded the standard way. When there is any doubt, a careful builder bonds it.

Propane versus natural gas in Arizona

Both fuels follow the same bonding rule, but the attachment point differs. On natural gas, the jumper connects downstream of the utility meter. On propane, common on rural lots around Rio Verde and other spots outside city gas service, it connects downstream of the tank's second-stage regulator. For example, on a propane-fed home in Rio Verde, the electrician clamps a 6 AWG copper jumper to the steel pipe just past the second-stage regulator and runs it to the ground at the electrical service, a path kept well under the 75-foot limit. The lightning risk is the same for both fuels, so the bond is required either way.

Which code edition your city uses

The CSST bonding language did not change between the 2018 and 2021 IRC. The ICC reaffirmed it without modification for the 2021 edition. What can differ is a local amendment, since a handful of AHJs add their own wrinkles. Check your city's adopted edition, and any amendments, in the building code editions by city reference.

Who has to coordinate on this

One jumper, two trades. The plumber sets the gas piping and the electrician lands the bond, which is exactly why the connection gets missed on a job where nobody owns it. Put it on somebody's scope in writing. The rest of the gas install is covered under fuel gas piping, and the system has to pass the gas pressure test before it goes into service. The ground the tubing bonds to is the same one established for your electrical service. Chapter 24 of the 2021 IRC carries the bonding text.

title: IRC Fuel Gas Piping: Appliance Shutoff Valves and Sediment Traps
shortSummary: The IRC gives every gas appliance in your home its own shutoff valve, set in the same room, within 6 feet, and upstream of the flexible connector. Most appliances also get a sediment trap, a capped stub of pipe that catches rust and scale before the debris can foul the appliance's gas valve.
bodyHtml:
If your Arizona home runs gas to a cooktop, a water heater, a pool heater, or a patio fire feature, the International Residential Code wraps that piping in a handful of safety rules. Two of them land at every appliance connection: a shutoff valve you can actually get to, and a small trap that catches the rust and scale a gas line sheds. Neither is complicated. Both are easy to miss by a few inches.

A shutoff valve at every appliance

Every gas appliance gets its own shutoff valve, and the code is exact about where that valve goes:

The shutoff valve shall be within 6 feet (1829 mm) of the appliance, and shall be installed upstream of the union, connector or quick disconnect device it serves.

It also has to sit in the same room as the appliance, and it has to be provided with access. That last clause is the one people miss. A valve is not accessible if you have to slide a range out of its cabinet or unscrew a closet panel to reach it. The point is control. If one appliance leaks, you or a plumber kills the gas to that unit in seconds, with no hunt for the meter out in the yard.

Sediment traps

Most gas appliances also get a sediment trap, sometimes called a drip leg. It is a short stub of pipe with a cap on the bottom end, and gravity does the rest. Rust, scale, and moisture drop into it instead of reaching the appliance's gas valve, where debris can foul the seat.

Placement is what makes it work. The trap goes downstream of the appliance shutoff valve and as close to the appliance inlet as practical, so it catches whatever the last stretch of pipe sheds. Built the usual way, it is a tee fitting with a capped nipple hanging vertically off the bottom opening. Turn that nipple sideways and it collects nothing.

The exemption list is short and worth knowing. Illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers, decorative vented fireplace appliances, gas fireplaces, and outdoor grills need no trap, and neither does an appliance that ships with one built in (Section G2419.4). Everything else gets one.

For example, say a Gilbert home runs gas to a range, a tankless water heater, a pool heater, and an indoor gas fireplace. That is four shutoff valves, one in the same room as each unit and within 6 feet of it. Only two of the four also get a sediment trap: the water heater and the pool heater. The range and the fireplace both sit on the exemption list.

The other two rules on a gas rough-in

Two more Chapter 24 requirements get checked on the same visit, and each has its own page here. Before gas flows, the installer caps the piping and pressurizes it to prove no joint leaks, and the test pressure, the hold time, and what gas may be used are covered under the G2417 pressure test. Flexible CSST tubing has to be bonded to the home's electrical ground so a monsoon lightning surge drains away instead of arcing a pinhole through the thin tubing wall, and the jumper size and the black-jacket exception are covered under G2411 CSST bonding.

Which edition applies to your build

These fuel gas rules are stable across recent IRC editions. Arizona sets no statewide code. Confirm the edition your city or county adopted in the building code editions by city reference, and ask your AHJ about local gas amendments in the same call.

Where the gas lines go from here

Gas feeds several systems covered elsewhere: the water heater when it is a gas unit, a gas fireplace, and the cooktop. A tightly sealed desert home can starve a gas appliance of the air it needs to burn. That is the makeup air and combustion air question, and it is cheapest to settle before framing. Chapter 24 of the 2021 IRC holds the full fuel gas text.

title: IRC G2417 Gas Pressure Test: Proving a New Gas Line Holds
shortSummary: Section G2417 requires every new gas line to pass a pressure test before it goes into service. The installer caps the piping and pressurizes it to at least 3 psig, or 1.5 times the working pressure, then holds it for 10 minutes minimum while a gauge confirms it does not drop. An inspector witnesses the result.
bodyHtml:
Before any gas flows to a new Arizona home, the pipe has to prove it is tight. The test is simple in concept. Seal the system, pump it up with air, and watch a gauge. If the needle holds steady, there are no leaks. Section G2417 of the International Residential Code sets how that test is run and passed.

What Section G2417 requires

Section G2417 requires new gas piping to be pressure-tested and inspected before it is put into service. The installer pressurizes the sealed system to at least 1.5 times its working pressure, and never less than 3 psig, whatever the design pressure. Then the clock starts.

The test duration shall be not less than 10 minutes.

Ten minutes is the floor. Many inspectors ask for a longer hold on a larger system, and some Arizona cities set their own minimum, so the real hold time is worth confirming before the inspector shows up.

The 10-minute, 3-psi test in practice

Here is how it goes on a typical Valley job. The plumber caps every open end of the new gas piping and connects a test gauge, usually a spring gauge or a manometer. The meter and any appliances are valved off or disconnected, because the test checks the pipe, not the equipment. The system is pumped to 3 psi, or higher if the design or the city calls for it. Everyone waits at least 10 minutes and watches the needle. If it holds, the pipe passes. If it drops, there is a leak, and the code says the bad section is replaced, not patched.

What the test gas can and cannot be

The pressure is applied with air, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, or another inert gas. Oxygen is never allowed, because pure oxygen mixed with any trace of oil or gas is a real explosion risk. Leaks are found with an approved leak detector or with soap bubbles brushed on the joints, never with an open flame.

Where the test lands in your build timeline

The gas test happens at rough-in, in the same window as the framing, electrical, and plumbing inspections, before the walls close up. It is one of the checks that has to pass before the gas utility, such as Southwest Gas across most of the Valley, will set your meter and turn on service. For example, on a Cave Creek custom home the gas rough-in, the CSST bonding, and this pressure test are all confirmed together, so plan for them as one phase. A failed test that stalls that phase can hold up drywall.

Which code edition your city uses

The core test, 3 psi held for 10 minutes, reads the same across the 2018 and 2021 IRC, but the details an inspector enforces can vary by city, from a longer hold to a higher test pressure. Cave Creek, for one, inspects to the 2021 IRC, as its own fuel gas checklist shows. Check your jurisdiction's adopted edition in the building code editions by city reference, and ask the AHJ permit desk about any local test amendments. The rules for Cave Creek specifically are written up on their own page.

What the test proves, and what it does not

A passed test says the pipe is tight. It says nothing about whether the pipe was sized for the appliance load, bonded, or trapped, so it is one check among several. The piping itself is covered under fuel gas piping, and CSST bonding gets confirmed in the same visit. On the water side, plumbing tests and inspection proves the supply and waste lines the same way. Chapter 24 of the 2021 IRC has the testing text.

title: IRC M1403 Heat Pump Equipment: Install Rules for an Arizona Home
shortSummary: Section M1403 governs how a heat pump gets installed. The unit must be listed and set up the way its manufacturer directs, and the outdoor condenser has to sit on a support raised at least 3 inches above the ground so defrost water drains away instead of pooling under the equipment.
bodyHtml:
A heat pump is one box that both heats and cools, and it has quietly become the default system for new Arizona homes. It runs on electricity alone, cools all summer, and flips to heating on cold winter mornings. Section M1403 of the IRC sets the short list of rules for putting one in.

What Section M1403 requires

Section M1403 keeps the requirements tight. Install a listed heat pump the way its maker specifies, and give the outdoor unit a proper base.

Electric heat pumps shall be listed and labeled.

The listing means the equipment was tested to a recognized safety standard, UL 1995 or the harmonized UL/CSA 60335-2-40. The manufacturer's instructions then control the details the code does not spell out, from the wiring and refrigerant charge to the airflow clearances around the unit.

The 3-inch base for defrost water

Section M1305.1.3.1 requires equipment supported from the ground to be level and firmly supported on a concrete slab or other approved material raised at least 3 inches above the adjoining ground, so defrost water can drain freely. During a heat pump's heating cycle, the outdoor coil gets cold enough to grow frost, and the system pauses to melt it off. That meltwater has to go somewhere. A unit sitting flat in the dirt would sit in its own runoff, which invites rust and, in cold snaps, a ring of ice.

Why the base still matters in the desert

In the low desert, hard frost is a winter-morning event rather than an all-day problem, so defrost water is lighter here than in a cold climate. The raised base still earns its place for local reasons. It lifts the condenser above blowing dust and gravel that would clog the coil. It keeps the unit clear of monsoon stormwater and irrigation runoff. And a solid, level base gives the installer something to anchor the unit against wind, which ties into the appliance-anchoring rules of Section M1307. For example, an outdoor unit set straight onto decomposed granite in a Rio Verde yard has nowhere to shed water and sits in the blowing gravel. A precast or composite equipment pad clears the 3-inch minimum, holds the coil above the dust line, and lets monsoon runoff pass underneath.

Sizing and the rest of the system

A heat pump only performs if it is sized to the house, so the load calculation under equipment sizing comes first, using Manual J and Manual S. In cooling mode the unit makes condensate, and that water has to be carried away under condensate disposal, a real concern during a humid monsoon week. The air it moves rides through ducts built to duct construction. Skip the sizing step and an oversized unit will short-cycle, which is one reason a new AC can seem to run constantly.

Which code edition your city uses

The heat pump rules are stable, but the edition your plans get checked against depends on the AHJ. A build in Scottsdale, Phoenix, or Fountain Hills may fall under the 2018 or 2021 IRC, and the energy code that governs the unit's efficiency changes more between editions than M1403 does. Confirm your city's adopted edition in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

For most new custom homes in the Valley, a heat pump is the whole HVAC system, so getting the install base and the sizing right up front pays off every summer. To weigh a heat pump against the alternatives, see what HVAC system is best for an Arizona custom home. The heat pump rules live in Chapter 14 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC M1411 Condensate Disposal: Keeping AC Water Out of an Arizona Ceiling
shortSummary: IRC Section M1411 controls how your air conditioner gets rid of the water it makes. When the air handler sits where an overflow could damage the home, the code requires a backup: a secondary drain, an auxiliary pan, or a float switch that shuts the unit off before the pan overflows. In Arizona that backup is what saves a ceiling.
bodyHtml:
An Arizona air conditioner runs for most of the year, and every hour it runs it pulls water out of the air. That condensate has to go somewhere. When the drain clogs, and in the desert they clog with dust and algae, the water backs up and finds the nearest ceiling. IRC Section M1411 is the part of the code that keeps that water from ruining your home.

Where the water goes

A cooling coil drips condensate into a pan under the air handler. A primary drain line carries it away to an approved point. The code wants that line at least 3/4 inch across, pitched at least 1/8 inch per foot, so the water flows out instead of pooling. That primary drain is the everyday path.

The backup the code requires

The real protection is what happens when that primary drain clogs. Where an overflow would damage building components, the code requires a second line of defense. That covers almost any air handler in an attic, or in a closet above conditioned space. You can meet it three ways: a separate secondary drain line, an auxiliary drain pan under the unit, or a water-level shutoff. The most common choice is a float switch, a small device that:

shut off the equipment served prior to overflow of the pan.

When water rises in the pan, the switch cuts power to the air conditioner before the pan can spill. You end up with a warm house and a service call, not a soaked ceiling.

Why this matters so much in Arizona

In many Arizona homes the air handler lives in the attic, directly over a bedroom or a hallway. Water that backs up there runs through the insulation and the drywall before anyone hears it. The code treats the pan and the switch as required, not optional, wherever an overflow could do damage.

Suppose the air handler sits in the attic above a master bedroom and the primary line silts up in its third summer. Water rises in the auxiliary pan, the float switch cuts power, and the house stops cooling on a 110-degree afternoon. You get a service call instead of a ceiling repair.

If the unit sits in a garage or a mechanical room where a spill drains away harmlessly, the backup may not be required. Where the equipment sits decides the rule.

Which edition applies to your build

These condensate rules are consistent across recent IRC editions, though the exact subsection numbers have shifted between them. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm which edition your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your systems

Condensate control is part of the same mechanical system as your HVAC sizing, and it echoes the drip-pan logic that protects a water heater in a finished space. If you are still choosing a cooling system, start with what HVAC system is best for an Arizona custom home. The full requirements sit in Section M1411 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC M1413 Evaporative Cooling: Installing a Swamp Cooler in Arizona
shortSummary: Section M1413 sets how an evaporative cooler, the swamp cooler common on Arizona roofs, gets installed. The unit has to be listed, set on a level platform you can reach for service, flashed where it meets the wall or roof, and fitted with backflow protection so its water line cannot foul the home's drinking water.
bodyHtml:
An evaporative cooler pulls hot desert air through wet pads and blows the cooled air into the house. It is a proven way to fight dry Arizona heat for a fraction of the power that refrigerated air draws. Section M1413 of the IRC covers how that cooler gets installed, so it runs safely and never damages the roof or the water supply.

What Section M1413 requires

Section M1413 requires an evaporative cooler to be listed for the job and installed the way its maker specifies.

Evaporative cooling equipment shall be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.

On top of that, the code adds a few plain conditions. The unit sits on a level platform you can get to for service (Section M1305.1.3.1). Where it passes through an outside wall or the roof, the opening is flashed to keep water out (Section R703.4). The fresh-air intake is placed away from anything that fouls the air (Section R303.5.1). And the water line that feeds it is protected so cooler water can never flow back toward your drinking water (Section P2902).

Keeping cooler water out of your drinking water

The backflow rule is the one most homeowners miss. A swamp cooler is plumbed to the home's potable water so it can keep the pads wet all day. Without protection, a drop in city water pressure could siphon mineral-heavy, standing cooler water back into the house lines. Section P2902 stops that with a backflow assembly on the cooler's supply, the same safeguard the code puts on irrigation lines and hose bibs.

Setting and reaching the cooler on an Arizona roof

Most Arizona swamp coolers are down-draft units that sit on the roof and drop cool air straight into a central ceiling register. That location is why two of the code rules carry real weight here. The platform has to be level and reachable, because the pads, the float valve, and the pump all need service every spring and a shutdown every fall. The roof opening has to be flashed to R703.4, because a monsoon downpour will find any gap around a rooftop curb. For example, a builder in Cave Creek or Apache Junction sets the cooler on a level, flashed curb with a short service walkway. A technician can then swap pads each spring without stepping on loose tile.

Where the air intake can go

The code also cares where the cooler draws its air. Section R303.5.1 keeps a mechanical air intake at least 10 feet from a plumbing vent, a flue, or another source of fouled air, unless the intake sits at least 3 feet below that source. On a roof already crowded with vents, that spacing often decides where the cooler lands.

How evaporative cooling fits the desert

Evaporative cooling works best exactly where Arizona spends most of the year, hot and dry. Drawing 105-degree air through wet pads can deliver supply air in the 70s or low 80s when the humidity is low. The trade-off arrives with the summer monsoon, roughly July through September, when the added moisture in the air cuts how much a swamp cooler can do. That is why many custom homes here run refrigerated air alongside it or instead of it, usually a heat pump. Which one fits your build is its own decision, weighed in evaporative cooler versus refrigerated AC.

Which code edition your city uses

Arizona has no statewide building code, so the edition in force depends on your AHJ. Most Valley jurisdictions run the 2018 or 2021 IRC, and the evaporative-cooling install rules read almost the same across those two. Match your jurisdiction against the building code editions by city list before you lock in the rooftop layout.

How this connects to the rest of your build

Sizing the cooler to the house is part of the load math your HVAC designer runs under equipment sizing. If you also run refrigerated air, its drainage falls under condensate disposal, and the line feeding the cooler ties into your water supply and pressure. The full evaporative-cooling text sits in Chapter 14 of the 2021 IRC.
