title: IRC M1502 Dryer Exhaust Duct: Length, Metal, and the Clearance Rules
shortSummary: IRC Section M1502 keeps a clothes dryer from starting a lint fire. The exhaust duct has to be 4-inch smooth metal, run no more than 35 feet with deductions for every bend, and vent outdoors through a damper at least 3 feet from any opening and 10 feet from an air conditioning condenser.
bodyHtml:
A clothes dryer pushes hot, lint-heavy air out of the house, and if that air cannot get out cleanly, the lint builds up and the heat has nowhere to go. That is how dryer fires start. IRC Section M1502 is a short set of rules built to prevent exactly that, and a couple of its numbers can decide where your laundry room is even allowed to go.

Smooth metal, four inches, no screws

The exhaust duct has to be rigid or semi-rigid metal, four inches across, with a smooth interior. Flexible foil and plastic are out for the concealed run, because their ridges snag lint. The joints also cannot be held together with sheet-metal screws that poke into the airflow, since those screw tips catch lint and grow a clog from the inside out. Smooth metal lets the lint ride the air all the way out instead of collecting in the run.

The 35-foot limit

Length is the rule that quietly shapes floor plans:

The maximum length of the exhaust duct shall be 35 feet.

Every turn spends part of that budget. You subtract 2.5 feet for each 45-degree bend and 5 feet for each 90-degree bend. So a laundry room set in the middle of a sprawling single-story house, a common Arizona layout, can blow past the limit fast.

Suppose that laundry sits 22 duct-feet from the nearest exterior wall, and reaching it takes three 90-degree bends: one off the dryer, one to turn into the wall cavity, one at the termination. Three bends at 5 feet each adds 15 feet, so the run measures 37 feet against a 35-foot ceiling. You move the vent to a closer wall, design out an elbow, or install a listed booster fan rated for the job.

Where it can vent

The duct has to terminate outdoors, never into an attic or a crawl space, through a backdraft damper that closes when the dryer is off. Two clearances matter, and both are easy to trip in Arizona. The outlet has to sit at least 3 feet from any window, door, or other opening into the house, and at least 10 feet from an air conditioning or heat pump condenser. That second clearance is pure desert logic, since you do not want warm, lint-laden air blowing straight into the condenser that cools your home.

Which edition applies to your build

These dryer exhaust rules are stable across recent IRC editions. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm the edition your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

The dryer duct belongs to the same mechanical system as your general duct construction, and like the AC condensate line, it is a spot where a small install detail now prevents a real problem later. Laundry placement also ties into the overall floor plan and mechanical rooms, so as you shape the layout, see what HVAC system is best for an Arizona custom home. The dryer exhaust rules are in Section M1502 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC M1505 Whole-House Ventilation: Fresh Air for a Tight Arizona Home
shortSummary: A modern Arizona home is built tight to keep the heat out, which also traps stale air in. IRC Section M1505 answers that with mechanical ventilation: a whole-house fan sized to the home's floor area and bedroom count, plus local exhaust fans that pull moisture and odor out of every bathroom and the kitchen.
bodyHtml:
A new Arizona home is sealed up tight, and for good reason. Every crack you close keeps the summer heat out and the cooling in. But a tight house also traps stale, humid, pollutant-heavy air inside. IRC Section M1505 is the code's fix, and it is why your builder installs a ventilation fan you might never have thought to ask for.

Why a tight house needs a fan

Older, leaky houses breathed on their own, through gaps around windows and doors and up into the attic. The energy code closed those gaps, sealed the ducts, and wrapped the house in a tight envelope. Recent editions verify that tightness with a blower door test instead of taking it on faith. Good for the power bill, but the fresh air that used to sneak in no longer does. Mechanical ventilation replaces it on purpose, drawing a measured amount of outdoor air into the home so the air inside does not go stale.

The whole-house rate

The code sets how much air the system has to move:

The whole-house mechanical ventilation system shall provide outdoor air at a continuous rate.

How much depends on the size of the house and how many people are likely to live in it, so the amount comes from a formula: 0.01 times the floor area in square feet, plus 7.5 times the number of bedrooms plus one. For example, a 2,500 square foot four-bedroom home gets 25 cfm from the floor area and 37.5 cfm from the bedroom count, or about 63 cfm of continuous fresh air. A dedicated fan, or your HVAC system pulling in outside air on a timer, delivers it.

Local exhaust for baths and the kitchen

On top of that whole-house air, the wet rooms get their own exhaust fans to push moisture and odor straight outside. A bathroom needs a fan rated for at least 50 cfm if it runs on demand, or 20 cfm if it runs continuously. A kitchen needs 100 cfm on demand, usually through a vented range hood, or 25 cfm continuous. Go bigger and the rule flips: a hood moving more than 400 cfm has to be paired with makeup air, so the exhaust cannot depressurize the house and pull combustion gases back down a flue. In the desert that bathroom fan earns its keep, because it carries out the shower humidity that would otherwise feed mold in a sealed house.

Why it matters in Arizona

Picture a tightly built 2,500 square foot home with its ducts sealed to the energy code. From May into September nobody in the Valley opens a window, so for roughly five months that fan is the only fresh air the house gets. Without it, cooking, showers, and breathing drive humidity and carbon dioxide up with nowhere to go.

Which edition applies to your build

Mechanical ventilation rules have tightened across recent code editions, and the exact rate can differ between the 2018, 2021, and 2024 versions. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm which edition your city or county adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

Ventilation is the other half of the building thermal envelope: you seal the house tight, then ventilate it on purpose. It works alongside your HVAC system, which often carries the fresh-air duct into the return. For the bigger picture on cooling and comfort in the heat, see what HVAC system is best for an Arizona custom home. The ventilation rules are in Section M1505 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC N1101 Energy Code Scope: Arizona's Climate Zone 2B
shortSummary: IRC Section N1101 is the scope of the residential energy code, and it sets the climate zone that drives every insulation and window number in your build. The whole Phoenix metro, plus Casa Grande and Apache Junction, sits in climate zone 2B, the hot-dry zone that tells the code to design for cooling.
bodyHtml:
Every insulation R-value, every window rating, and every duct-sealing target in your build traces back to one input: your climate zone. IRC Section N1101 is the short scope section that sets that zone and points the rest of the energy code at it. Get the zone right and the whole chapter falls into place. It is the piece of the code most tied to where in Arizona you are building.

What N1101 sets up

Chapter 11 of the IRC is the residential energy code, and it carries the same rules as the International Energy Conservation Code (IECC). N1101 is its front door. It states the scope, defines the terms the chapter uses, and assigns your climate zone from a table organized by state and county.

The reason the zone matters so much is that the energy code is really about one thing: the insulated shell that separates your indoor air from the outdoors. The code names that shell the building thermal envelope and defines it as:

The basement walls, exterior walls, floors, ceilings, roofs and any other building element assemblies that enclose conditioned space or provide a boundary between conditioned space and exempt or unconditioned space.

Your climate zone decides how hard that envelope has to work, and everything downstream in conditioned space follows from it.

Arizona's climate zones

Arizona is not one climate, and the code knows it. The state runs from hot desert to mountain snow, so the county table spreads it across four zones. The number is the temperature band and the letter is the moisture. Almost all of it is dry, so the letter is usually B.

The whole Jematell service area sits in climate zone 2B, the hot-dry zone. In Maricopa County that means Phoenix, Scottsdale, Rio Verde, Cave Creek, Fountain Hills, and Carefree. In Pinal County it means Casa Grande and Apache Junction. Pima, Yuma, and La Paz counties are 2B as well. From there the map climbs with elevation. The southeast and northwest counties land in zone 3B. The higher central counties, like Gila and Yavapai, reach 4B. The high country of Coconino, Navajo, and Apache counties, including Flagstaff, sits all the way up in cold-dry zone 5B. For example, Flagstaff sits in 5B and Scottsdale in 2B. Same code chapter, different column: the Flagstaff house is designed around holding heat in, the Scottsdale house around keeping the sun's heat out.

Why zone 2B shapes a Phoenix house

In 2B, the enemy is heat coming in, not heat leaking out, so the code tunes the house for cooling. That is why a Valley home leans on low solar heat gain windows, a well-insulated attic, and tight, sealed ducts, rather than the thick walls a cold climate would ask for. The single most Arizona-specific number is the window solar heat gain coefficient, which the code holds low to keep the sun's heat out. The exact prescriptive values live in the building thermal envelope section, but N1101 is what points your project at the 2B column in the first place.

N1101 also lays out how you prove the house complies. You can meet each prescriptive number one by one, model the whole building's performance in software, or hit an energy rating index target, and every path also has to meet an added-efficiency requirement. Most Valley custom homes take the prescriptive route because it is the simplest to permit.

Which edition applies to your build

The climate zone map and the 2B assignment for the metro are the same in the 2018 and 2021 codes, so this part has been stable. The 2024 edition pushes the prescriptive numbers and equipment harder and adds new efficiency options, but it does not move Phoenix out of 2B. Because Arizona cities adopt the energy code on their own timelines, confirm the edition your jurisdiction enforces in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

N1101 is the setup, and the rest of the chapter is where the work happens. The insulation and window minimums are in the building thermal envelope section, and the HVAC controls and duct sealing targets are in the systems section. For the design side of the same goal, see how to design a custom home to stay cool in the Arizona heat. The scope and climate zone rules sit in Chapter 11 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC N1103 Duct Sealing and Leakage Testing in an Arizona Attic
shortSummary: IRC Section N1103 makes a new home's ducts get sealed and then leak-tested. The postconstruction limit is 4 cubic feet per minute of leakage per 100 square feet of floor area. In Arizona, where ducts run through a scorching attic, meeting that limit is what keeps the cooling you paid for inside the house.
bodyHtml:
In Arizona the ductwork that carries your cool air usually runs through the attic. That attic can hit 140 degrees in July. Every leak either dumps the air you paid to cool into the attic, or pulls superheated attic air back into your returns. IRC Section N1103 makes the builder seal those ducts, then test them to prove it.

Sealing is mandatory

The first requirement is blunt:

Ducts, air handlers and filter boxes shall be sealed.

The air handler itself has to be built to leak no more than 2 percent of its design airflow. Sealing means mastic and solid mechanical connections at every joint. Cloth duct tape does not count. It dries out and lets go in attic heat. Wrapping the ducts to the right R-value is part of the same job, and it keeps attic heat from bleeding into the air inside.

Then the ducts get leak-tested

Sealing is verified, not just assumed. A technician pressurizes the duct system and measures how much air escapes. The code sets the limit by the size of your home. After construction, total leakage has to be 4 cubic feet per minute or less for every 100 square feet of conditioned floor area. Ducts buried deep in attic insulation face an even tighter limit of 1.5 cfm per 100 square feet.

For example, a 2,000 square foot home is allowed no more than 80 cfm of total duct leakage. Come in at 120 and the crew reseals the joints and retests before the house passes. That is why the mastic goes on right the first time, because reopening a sealed attic duct run in July is the job nobody wants.

The rest of N1103

Ducts are the headline, but N1103 also covers the other systems that drive a home's energy use: a programmable thermostat for control, insulation on the hot water lines so you are not heating the attic, and equipment that is correctly sized for the house rather than oversized. Each one trims what a desert home burns to stay comfortable.

Why the number matters in Arizona

Picture that same 2,000 square foot home with its air handler and trunk lines sitting in a 140 degree attic. If the ducts leak badly, the air conditioner runs longer, the back bedrooms never quite cool, and the July bill climbs. Meeting the N1103 limit keeps the cooled air where you want it. A high SEER rating on the equipment only pays off if the ducts feeding it are tight.

Which edition applies to your build

The 2021 IRC energy provisions are stricter than the 2018 in places, and Arizona cities and counties each adopt their own edition, with some still on 2018. Confirm which one governs your build in the building code editions by city reference, because it sets your duct target.

How this connects to the rest of your build

Duct sealing pairs with the building thermal envelope that N1102 controls, and with the HVAC sizing that decides how much air those ducts have to carry. For the bigger picture on cooling a desert home, start with what HVAC system is best for an Arizona custom home. The systems rules live in Section N1103 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC P2708 Shower Requirements: The 900-Square-Inch Rule and Anti-Scald Valves
shortSummary: IRC Section P2708 requires a shower compartment to hold at least 900 square inches of interior space and measure at least 30 inches across, kept clear to 70 inches above the drain. It also requires an anti-scald valve, balanced-pressure or thermostatic, that limits water to 120 degrees Fahrenheit at the head.
bodyHtml:
A custom shower has two rules that matter most. It has to be big enough to actually stand and turn around in, and it has to protect you from a sudden blast of scalding water. Section P2708 of the International Residential Code sets both. If you are planning a large walk-in shower, the kind common in Scottsdale and Cave Creek custom homes, these numbers shape the tile layout before the first stud goes up.

The minimum size

A shower cannot be a cramped box. The code sets a floor on how much room it has to give you:

Shower compartments shall have not less than 900 square inches of interior cross-sectional area.

That 900 square inches is measured inside the finished walls, and the compartment also has to be at least 30 inches across in its smallest direction. Both of those have to hold from the threshold up to at least 70 inches above the drain, so the space does not pinch in at shoulder height. Fixture valves, the showerhead, and grab bars do not count against the room. There is one trade allowed: a narrower 25-inch width is fine if the shower makes up for it with at least 1,300 square inches of area.

For a doorless walk-in, a shape people love in the desert for its open, spa feel, the same minimums apply at the showerhead. Designers often run these showers to 4 feet by 5 feet or larger, well past the floor, which is why the code rarely limits a custom design. It just stops a shower from being shrunk into an unusable corner.

The anti-scald valve

The second rule is a safety device you cannot see. Section P2708.4 requires every shower and tub-shower valve to control temperature on its own, using one of three types: balanced-pressure, thermostatic, or a combination of both. The valve has to be set so it can never send water hotter than 120 degrees Fahrenheit to the head.

Here is why it matters. For example, in an older-style valve, when someone flushes a toilet or starts the dishwasher, cold water gets pulled away and the shower suddenly runs hot. A balanced-pressure valve senses that shift and holds the mix steady. A thermostatic valve watches the actual temperature. In Arizona, this cuts two ways. A gas or heat-pump water heater can deliver very hot water, and in summer the cold line itself can run warm because the pipe sits in hot ground, so a good valve keeps the shower from swinging to a scald. These valves carry a standard stamp, either ASSE 1016 or ASME A112.18.1, which your inspector checks.

Settle the numbers before the tile

Both of these rules land on the plan, not on the punch list. The 900 square inches and the 30-inch width decide the framed opening; the valve type decides what sits inside the wall. Downstream, your shower drains through a fixture trap into the drainage system, and its temperature rides on the same 80 psi supply limit as the rest of the house. Designing a large primary bath? See what a spa-style primary bathroom includes. Which edition your AHJ enforces is listed in the building code editions by city reference. Chapter 27 of the 2021 IRC holds the full fixture rules.

title: IRC Water Heater Installation: Drain Pan, Drain Line, and Seismic Strapping
shortSummary: Where a water heater leak could reach finished space, the residential code sets the tank in a pan at least 1.5 inches deep, drained by a three-quarter-inch line to a safe outlet. Seismic strapping applies only in the higher design categories, which most of Arizona sits below. A garage tank on a slab often needs neither one.
bodyHtml:
A water heater is one of the few appliances in a new home that can fail dangerously. So the code wraps it in a short list of firm rules. Most of Arizona builds to the 2021 International Residential Code, and its Chapter 28 sets how the tank gets drained, secured, and relieved. None of it is complicated. Skip any one piece and you have an easy inspection failure.

The relief valve, in one line

Every storage tank needs a temperature-and-pressure relief valve, and the settings and the discharge piping have a section of their own: see P2804 water heater relief valves for the pressure cap, the temperature trigger, and where that discharge line is allowed to end.

The drip pan and its drain

Where a leak could reach finished space, the tank sits in a pan. Think of a heater in an interior closet, or one on an upper floor. The pan has to be at least 1.5 inches deep. Its drain pipe has to be at least three-quarters of an inch across. That pipe runs to an approved waste receptor, or out to the exterior, and the code is exact about where it ends outside:

terminate not less than 6 inches and not more than 24 inches above the adjacent ground surface.

The logic is simple. If the tank starts to weep, the water shows up somewhere visible and harmless, on the ground outside, instead of inside a wall or a ceiling below.

The trigger is the damage, not the tank. A heater standing on a garage slab usually needs no pan at all, which is why so many Valley garages have a bare tank sitting on the concrete. Put that same heater in an interior closet and the pan, the drain line, and the exterior outlet all come with it.

For example, say the heater sits in an upstairs laundry closet on a Chandler build. It gets a pan at least 1.5 inches deep, a three-quarter-inch drain line dropped down inside the wall, and an outlet on the exterior wall somewhere between 6 and 24 inches above the dirt. Nothing about that setup stops a leak. It just makes sure the first sign of one is a wet patch by the foundation instead of a stained ceiling over the dining room.

Seismic strapping, and why Arizona usually skips it

The IRC also calls for water heaters to be strapped against earthquakes. That rule only bites in the higher seismic design categories: D0, D1, and D2, plus townhouses in category C. Where it applies, the strap wraps the tank at its upper third and its lower third. It has to resist a sideways force of about one-third of the full tank's weight. Most of Arizona sits below that line, in the lower categories. So a detached custom home here is usually not required to strap its heater at all. Plenty of builders strap anyway. The hardware costs a few dollars, and a gas tank that topples and shears its supply line is a real hazard. Confirm your project's seismic design category. That number, not the state line, decides whether strapping is mandatory.

Which edition applies to your build

These water heater rules are stable from one code edition to the next. What shifts between the 2018, 2021, and 2024 codes is the exact section numbers and a few details. Arizona has no statewide code. Each city and county adopts its own, so check which edition your AHJ enforces in the building code editions by city reference before your plumber sets the unit.

When the heater gets signed off

The tank is pressure-tested and approved as part of the home's plumbing tests and inspection, not as a separate visit. Its running cost rides on the same efficiency choices you make for your HVAC system. Weighing a solar or heat pump tank to cut that cost? Start with whether solar is worth it on a new Arizona home. Chapter 28 of the 2021 IRC holds the full set of requirements.

title: IRC P2804 Water Heater Relief Valves: Settings and Discharge Piping
shortSummary: IRC Section P2804 requires every storage water heater to have a temperature-and-pressure relief valve, or a separate pressure valve and temperature valve. The pressure setting cannot exceed 150 psi and the temperature valve opens by 210 degrees. A discharge pipe then carries any release safely down near the floor.
bodyHtml:
A storage water heater holds a lot of energy. If the thermostat sticks on, the tank keeps heating water it cannot use, and pressure inside climbs fast. Section P2804 of the International Residential Code keeps that from ending in a burst tank or a scald. It covers the relief valve itself and, just as much, the pipe that carries a release to a safe spot.

The two ways to relieve the tank

The code lets you protect the tank two ways: a single combination temperature-and-pressure valve, or a separate pressure valve paired with a separate temperature valve. Most new homes use the combination valve, often called a T&P valve, threaded into the top of the tank.

The settings are fixed. The pressure valve has to open at no less than 25 psi above the system pressure and at no more than 150 psi. The temperature valve has to open at no more than 210 degrees, and its sensing tip has to sit in the top 6 inches of the tank, where the water is hottest. Those two triggers cover the two ways a tank turns dangerous: too much pressure, or water hot enough to flash to steam.

Where the discharge pipe has to go

A relief valve that dumps scalding water at head height is its own hazard, so P2804 is strict about the pipe that carries the release away. The pipe drains by gravity to a safe end point and never has a shutoff or check valve in its path, because a closed valve would defeat the whole system. It ends over an air gap so nothing can siphon back:

Discharge through an air gap located in the same room as the water heater.

A few more rules round it out. The pipe is at least as wide as the valve outlet, which on a residential tank means three-quarters of an inch, and it is built from an approved material rated for hot water. It serves that one valve and nothing else. It ends no more than 6 inches above the floor or the drain it empties into, and at least two pipe-widths above that surface, so a release lands low and stays visible instead of spraying a person.

What this looks like on an Arizona build

For example, say your tank sits in the garage of a Gilbert or Surprise home. The plumber runs the T&P discharge line down the wall and ends it about 4 inches off the slab, pointed at the floor, with nothing capping it. If the valve ever lets go, you see water on the garage floor and know something is wrong.

Arizona adds two wrinkles. First, incoming water and garage air both run hot in summer, so the tank already sits closer to its limits. Second, many Valley homes have a pressure-reducing valve at the water service, which turns the plumbing into a closed system. In a closed system, heated water cannot push back toward the street, so pressure spikes land on the relief valve and it starts to weep. The fix is a thermal expansion tank, covered under water supply and pressure. A relief valve that drips is usually telling you that expansion tank is missing or waterlogged, not that the valve is bad.

Which edition applies to your build

The relief valve idea is stable across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 codes, though section numbers and small details shift between them. Arizona sets no statewide code, so each city and county adopts its own edition. Confirm which one your AHJ enforces in the building code editions by city reference before your plumber sets the tank.

The one thing to look at after move-in

A T&P line that stays dry is doing its job. A wet one is a message. Check the end of that pipe once a season for the first year, since a slow drip there is the cheapest early warning your plumbing gives you. P2804 is the detailed relief-valve rule inside the broader water heater installation requirements, which also cover the drain pan and seismic strapping. The valve and its pipe get checked during plumbing tests and inspection. Weighing a heat pump or solar tank to cut the running cost? That choice ties into whether solar is worth it on a new Arizona home. Chapter 28 of the 2021 IRC carries the relief valve text.

title: IRC P2902 Backflow Prevention: Protecting Drinking Water from Cross-Connections
shortSummary: IRC Section P2902 protects your drinking water from backflow, water flowing the wrong way through a pipe. It requires backflow preventers wherever clean water could meet dirty water, such as outdoor hose bibbs, lawn irrigation, and pool fills. In Arizona, where most homes water desert plants, these devices sit on every build.
bodyHtml:
Every home has spots where clean drinking water can meet dirty water. A hose lying in a bucket. A sprinkler line buried in fertilized soil. A pool auto-fill valve. Section P2902 of the International Residential Code exists to keep the dirty side from ever flowing back into the pipes you drink from. In Arizona, where nearly every custom home has in-ground irrigation and many have a pool, this is one of the plumbing rules that shows up on almost every plan.

What the code requires

Section P2902 requires your potable water system to be protected so contamination can never flow back into it. The code states it plainly:

A potable water supply system shall be designed and installed so as to prevent contamination from nonpotable liquids, solids or gases.

The danger is called backflow, water running the wrong way through a pipe. It happens two ways. Backsiphonage is when supply pressure drops, say, a water main breaks down the street, and the drop pulls water backward like a straw. Backpressure is when something downstream, like a pump, pushes at a higher pressure than the city main. Either way, whatever sits on the dirty end can get pulled or shoved into your drinking water.

The devices that stop it

The code lists approved backflow preventers in Table P2902.3, ranked by how much protection they give:

  • Air gap. A physical vertical space between a faucet and the flood rim of a sink or tub. It is the simplest and strongest, because air cannot siphon. The gap has to be at least twice the width of the faucet opening, and never less than one inch.
  • Atmospheric vacuum breaker. A valve that opens to the air and breaks a siphon. Its critical level has to sit at least 6 inches above the highest point of the piping it serves, and no shutoff valve can be placed downstream of it.
  • Pressure vacuum breaker. Like the atmospheric type but rated for constant pressure, so valves can sit downstream. Its critical level mounts at least 12 inches above the highest point of the downstream piping, which on a sloped lot is not always the highest sprinkler head.
  • Reduced pressure principle assembly. The highest level of protection, required where the risk is severe. It stops both backsiphonage and backpressure.

Hose bibbs and irrigation in an Arizona yard

Two everyday features drive most residential backflow work. First, outdoor hose bibbs, the spigots on your exterior walls. Section P2902.4.3 requires each one to have a vacuum breaker, because a hose left sitting in a pool, a bucket of weed killer, or a pet's water dish can siphon back on a pressure drop. Most new sillcocks come with one built in.

Second, lawn and yard irrigation. Section P2902.5.3 requires an atmospheric vacuum breaker, a pressure vacuum breaker, or a reduced pressure assembly on the system. If you inject fertilizer through the irrigation, the code steps you up to a reduced pressure assembly. Imagine a typical Scottsdale build with a zoned drip system watering desert plants. The installer sets a pressure vacuum breaker about a foot above the highest head, so a break in the city main cannot pull fertilizer-laced soil water back toward the kitchen tap. Expect the assembly to be tested when it goes in. The recurring annual test that commercial and multi-family properties owe is a different matter: Arizona's rule at A.A.C. R18-4-215(C) does not apply to single-family residences used solely as residences, unless your water provider identifies a cross-connection problem on the property.

Two more cross-connections a desert lot creates

Rural and reuse-minded builds add sources a city lot never has. A cistern topped off by a truck of hauled water, the normal arrangement on unserved land around Rio Verde, sits squarely on the nonpotable side of the line. Wherever a potable pipe fills or supplements that tank, you have the exact connection Table P2902.3 exists to break. A graywater line is nonpotable by definition too, so it never ties back into a supply pipe anywhere on the property. Name both on the plumbing plan rather than leaving them for the inspector to find.

Where backflow work shows up on your schedule

Backflow devices go in with the water service and the irrigation, not at the end of the job, and the whole system gets checked at your plumbing inspection. They share that service with the 80 psi limit and pressure-reducing valve, and a PRV is itself one of the parts that closes the system. For which code edition your city enforces, see the building code editions by city reference, and for the yard itself, what a pool permit involves. Chapter 29 of the 2021 IRC carries the full requirements.

title: IRC P2903 Water Pressure: The 80 PSI Limit and Thermal Expansion
shortSummary: IRC Section P2903 caps the water pressure inside your home at 80 psi. Where the city main runs higher, and parts of the Phoenix area do, a pressure-reducing valve is required. That valve creates a closed system, so a water heater then needs an expansion tank to absorb the pressure that heating water builds up.
bodyHtml:
Water pressure is one of those things you only notice when it is wrong, either a weak trickle at the tap or a bang in the pipes when a valve shuts. Section P2903 of the International Residential Code sets the ceiling on that pressure and handles a side effect that trips up a lot of builds. It matters in Arizona, where some city water mains push pressure well past what a house should ever see.

The 80 psi ceiling

The code puts a hard cap on the pressure inside your home:

The static water pressure shall be not greater than 80 psi.

Too much pressure wears out valves, hammers fixtures, and shortens the life of a water heater. Where the city main arrives above 80 psi, and several Phoenix-area systems do, the code requires a pressure-reducing valve, a PRV, installed right where the water service enters the house, to bring the pressure down into a safe range.

The catch: thermal expansion

Here is the part people miss. A PRV, or a backflow preventer, or a check valve, turns your plumbing into a closed system. Water can flow in, but it can no longer push back out to the street. Now heat your water heater. Water expands as it warms, and in a closed system that expansion has nowhere to go, so the pressure climbs, sometimes well past 80 psi, and the water heater's relief valve starts to weep. The code's answer is a thermal expansion tank, a small tank that gives the expanding water somewhere to go. Whenever you have a closed system and a storage water heater, that expansion control is required, not optional.

Why it matters in Arizona

For example, take a home on a city main delivering 95 psi. Your plumber sets a PRV at the service entry to bring the house down to around 65 psi. That solves the pressure, but it also closes the system, so the same plan now needs a small expansion tank near the water heater. Skip it and you get a relief valve that drips, a water heater that ages fast, and a warranty callback. The two pieces, the PRV and the expansion tank, belong on the plan together.

Rural lots reach the same place by a different road. A home on a well or a cistern has no city main to knock down, so the 80 psi ceiling rarely comes into play at all. The check valve on that well still closes the system, though, and a closed system with a storage water heater still needs expansion control.

Which edition applies to your build

The 80 psi cap and the expansion rules are stable across recent IRC editions. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm which edition your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

What to check on the plan

Two items, one line each. Look for a PRV at the service entry if the main runs hot, and an expansion tank at the water heater if anything closes the system. Both are cheap at rough-in and annoying later. The water heater's relief valve and drain pan are the safety net when neither one is there, and the whole supply system gets pressure-tested at your plumbing inspection. For the full sequence of what gets checked as the house comes together, see the steps to building a custom home in Arizona. Chapter 29 of the 2021 IRC has the supply and pressure rules.

title: IRC P3005 Drain Slope and Cleanouts: Getting the Waste Line Right Before the Pour
shortSummary: IRC Section P3005 sets how steeply drain pipes must slope and where cleanouts go. A 3-inch or larger house drain needs 1/8 inch of fall per foot, and smaller lines need 1/4 inch. Cleanouts are required every 100 feet, at the sewer junction, and at each turn over 45 degrees.
bodyHtml:
The drain lines under your house have one job: carry waste away using nothing but gravity. Section P3005 of the International Residential Code sets how steeply those pipes have to fall and where the access points, called cleanouts, have to go. On an Arizona slab-on-grade home, most of this pipe is buried under the concrete, so getting it right before the pour is the whole ballgame. You cannot re-slope a drain after the slab is down.

On the post-tension slab foundation common across the Valley, you cannot casually saw your way back in either. That concrete holds steel cables under tension, so opening it means locating and working around them. A drain correction that would be a bad afternoon on a conventional slab becomes a specialty job here.

The right slope

A drain pipe has to fall at a steady, specific angle. Too flat and the water sits and solids settle out. Too steep and the water can race ahead and leave the solids behind. The code sets a minimum fall by pipe size. A pipe 2-1/2 inches or smaller has to drop 1/4 inch per foot, about a 2 percent grade. A pipe 3 inches or larger has to drop at least 1/8 inch per foot, about a 1 percent grade.

A typical house has a 3-inch or 4-inch main building drain, so its floor is 1/8 inch of fall per foot of run. Smaller branch lines, such as the 2-inch pipe from a shower or a laundry, need the steeper 1/4 inch per foot. Many plumbers build the bigger lines closer to 1/4 inch per foot anyway, for margin.

In practice, a 48-foot main drain at 1/8 inch per foot falls 6 inches from end to end. Run that same 48 feet at the steeper 1/4 inch per foot and the fall doubles to 12 inches, so the line leaves the house half a foot lower. On a long, flat Valley lot, that extra 6 inches comes out of the trench depth at the sewer connection.

The code also bars a pipe from shrinking as it goes:

The size of the drainage piping shall not be reduced in the direction of flow.

In plain terms, a 3-inch line can never neck down to a 2-inch line downstream, because that would choke the flow and back it up.

Where cleanouts go

A cleanout is a capped fitting that lets a plumber run a snake into the line to clear a clog. The code does not leave their placement to chance. Section P3005.2 requires a cleanout in a few set spots:

  • At intervals of no more than 100 feet along any horizontal drain.
  • At the junction of the building drain and the building sewer, where the house line meets the line out to the city or to a septic system, either at the junction or within 10 feet upstream.
  • At every change of direction greater than 45 degrees.

Each cleanout has to match the pipe size, up to a 4-inch cap, and it needs clear space in front of it to work a rod in, at least 18 inches for the pipe sizes in a house. On an Arizona custom home with a long, spread-out floor plan, the 100-foot rule and the 45-degree rule usually mean cleanouts are brought up to grade outside, near the kitchen and each bathroom stack, so a future clog is a driveway job and not a wall-opening job.

The review to do before the pour

Walk the underground plumbing with your plumber while it is still open trench and pipe on dirt. Count the cleanouts against the three rules above, and check that no line necks down going downstream. Every fixture feeds this drain through a trap, and the whole system breathes through the vents that terminate through the roof, so both have to be roughed in before anything gets covered. It all gets pressure-tested at your plumbing inspection. For site drainage around the house, see how a Maricopa County drainage clearance works, and for which edition your city enforces, the building code editions by city reference. Chapter 30 of the 2021 IRC holds the full drainage rules.

title: IRC P3009 Graywater Systems: Arizona's Type 1 Reuse Permit
shortSummary: IRC Section P3009 covers graywater soil absorption systems, the reuse of lightly used drain water for underground irrigation. The code hands the technical rules to your state. In Arizona that is the Department of Environmental Quality, whose Type 1 permit lets a home reuse under 400 gallons a day with no application.
bodyHtml:
Reusing household drain water to keep a desert yard alive is one of the smartest moves an Arizona home can make, and the code has a place for it. IRC Section P3009 covers graywater soil absorption systems, which take drain water from a few household fixtures and put it underground to water plants. What surprises most people is how short the section is, and why.

What counts as graywater

Graywater is the lightly used water your home makes from washing, not from toilets or the kitchen. The code defines it as the:

Waste discharged from lavatories, bathtubs, showers, clothes washers and laundry trays.

Water from toilets, kitchen sinks, and dishwashers is not graywater. It carries waste, grease, and food, which makes it blackwater, and it has to go to the sewer or septic system. The dividing line matters because graywater can be reused with light handling, while blackwater cannot. For a plain-language breakdown of the sources, see the graywater glossary entry.

What P3009 actually requires

Here is the part that trips people up. P3009 does not spell out tank sizes, soil tests, or trench depths. It is a short section that points graywater soil absorption systems to the rules of the state authority that regulates them. The model code sets the category and then hands the details to your jurisdiction.

In Arizona, that authority is the Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ). So a builder here does not size a graywater system to a plumbing-code table. They build it to ADEQ's recycled water rules. That is the real content behind this section for a Valley home.

Arizona's Type 1 graywater permit

Most homes fall under ADEQ's Type 1 Recycled Water General Permit for Gray Water, written at A.A.C. R18-9-D701. It covers a private residence reusing less than 400 gallons of graywater a day. The permit is automatic. You file no application and pay no fee, as long as the system meets a set of best-practice conditions. The main ones:

  • Keep the water on your own lot, contained inside the property line.
  • Apply it below the surface or under a cover such as mulch. Drip and flood work; spraying does not.
  • Avoid human contact with the graywater and with the soil it waters.
  • Do not surface-apply graywater to food plants. Trees and shrubs are the exception, as long as the edible part never touches the water, which is what puts citrus and nut trees back on the list.
  • Keep hazardous chemicals out of it, and do not store it, since standing graywater turns septic within about a day.

Above 400 gallons a day there is no Type 2 rung to step onto, because Arizona has no Type 2 general permit for graywater. Anything the Type 1 permit does not cover goes straight to the Type 3 Recycled Water General Permit at A.A.C. R18-9-D702, which reaches up to 3,000 gallons a day. Type 3 is a genuine filing: a Notice of Intent to ADEQ listing your graywater sources and showing the flow calculation, then written authorization back from the department before the system runs. A single-family home rarely gets close to 400 gallons a day, so Type 1 is almost always the path.

Plan it during rough-in

For example, a custom home in Cave Creek can send its laundry and shower drains to a separate graywater line that feeds a drip field under the desert trees, reusing hundreds of gallons a week. The catch is that this only works if the drain lines are split during the plumbing rough-in. Running a second set of stub-outs while the walls are open costs very little. Adding them after drywall means opening finished walls and a slab, which is expensive. If graywater interests you at all, decide before rough-in, which is the cheapest point in the whole build-on-your-lot timeline to build it in. In a climate where water is the scarcest thing on the lot, that reuse stretches a well or a city tap and carries a yard through the summer.

Which edition applies to your build

Graywater provisions have moved and been renumbered across recent codes, and the 2018, 2021, and 2024 editions organize on-site water reuse a little differently. The constant is that the IRC defers the working rules to the state, so in Arizona the ADEQ permit governs no matter which edition your city adopted. Confirm your city's edition in the building code editions by city reference.

Keeping the two water systems apart

A graywater line is part of the same drainage system that gets checked at your plumbing tests and inspection, and it runs alongside the potable water supply and pressure system without ever touching it. If you are still deciding how to plant the yard, weigh it against the options in artificial turf versus desert landscaping. The soil absorption section sits in Chapter 30 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC P3103 Plumbing Vent Terminals: Roof Height and Clearances
shortSummary: IRC Section P3103 sets where your plumbing vents can exit the roof. Every open vent pipe has to rise at least 6 inches above the roof, and its terminal has to sit at least 10 feet from any window, door, or air intake, or 2 feet above it. The rules keep sewer gas out of the house.
bodyHtml:
Those short pipes sticking up through your roof are plumbing vents, and they do two quiet but important jobs. They let your drains breathe so water flows instead of gurgling, and they carry sewer gas up and away from the house. Section P3103 of the International Residential Code sets exactly how high they rise and how far they stay from anything you breathe near.

Six inches above the roof

Every open vent pipe that passes through the roof has to stand up above it:

terminate not less than 6 inches above the roof.

That height keeps roof debris, and in colder climates snow, from capping the pipe and choking the vent. On the flat and low-slope roofs common in Arizona, six inches is easy to hit and easy for an inspector to confirm. If the roof doubles as a deck or a patio, the pipe has to go much higher, up to 7 feet, so nobody is standing right next to an open sewer vent.

Ten feet from anything you breathe

The second rule is about where the gas goes once it leaves the pipe. A vent terminal has to sit at least 10 feet, measured horizontally, from any door, operable window, or mechanical air intake. If it has to be closer than that, it must instead rise at least 2 feet above the top of that opening. The logic is simple. Sewer gas should vent to open sky, not drift back through a window or get pulled into a fresh-air intake. In Arizona that intake clause matters, because homes here pull outside air in for ventilation.

Why it matters for your build

For example, take a two-story Arizona home where the guest bath vents out near a second-floor window. If the vent terminal lands within 10 feet of that window and does not rise 2 feet above it, it fails the rule. The fix, moving or extending the pipe, is far cheaper before the roof is finished than after, which is why vent routing is worth catching on the plans rather than on inspection day.

Moving a vent is not free, either. The stack needs a clear path up between roof trusses, so a pipe that has to travel 8 feet sideways to clear a window usually picks up an offset in the attic, or splits into a second stack. That is a framing conversation as much as a plumbing one, and it costs almost nothing while the trusses are still on paper.

Which edition applies to your build

P3103 is stable across recent IRC editions. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm which edition your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

Where the vents get checked

Vents are part of the drain, waste, and vent system that gets pressure-tested at your plumbing inspection, well before anyone is looking at the roof. They then share that roof with your roof covering, where every pipe penetration has to be flashed watertight, so a vent that gets relocated late costs you a roofing repair on top of a plumbing one. For the full sequence of what gets checked as the house comes together, see the steps to building a custom home in Arizona. Section P3103 of the 2021 IRC carries the terminal rules.

title: IRC P3201 Fixture Traps: The Water Seal That Keeps Sewer Gas Out
shortSummary: IRC Section P3201 governs the traps under every fixture, the U-shaped bends that hold a water seal against sewer gas. Each trap needs a seal 2 to 4 inches deep, and each fixture needs its own. S-traps, bell traps, and drum traps are banned. In dry Arizona air, unused traps evaporate and must be refilled.
bodyHtml:
Every sink, tub, shower, and floor drain in your home has a U-shaped bend in the pipe just below it. That bend, the trap, holds a small plug of water that blocks sewer gas from rising into the room. Section P3201 of the International Residential Code controls how deep that water plug has to be, how each fixture connects to it, and which trap designs are banned. In Arizona's dry air, one rule in this section matters more than the rest: keeping the trap from drying out.

How deep the water seal has to be

The whole system works on a shallow pool of water sitting in the trap. The code fixes how much:

Each fixture trap shall have a liquid seal of not less than 2 inches and not more than 4 inches.

Less than 2 inches and the seal is too thin to hold back gas or gets siphoned away too easily. More than 4 inches and the trap starts catching debris and clogging. Each fixture also has to have its own trap. The code bars putting two traps in a row on one fixture, which would trap air between them and slow the drain to a crawl. And the trap has to sit close to the fixture, no more than 24 inches of vertical drop from the fixture outlet down to the trap.

The traps you cannot use

Section P3201.5 bans several old or unreliable trap designs. The one a homeowner is most likely to run into is the S-trap, the shape that curves down, back up, and then straight down again. An S-trap can siphon its own water out as the fixture drains, breaking the seal. Also prohibited:

  • Bell traps and drum traps, older designs that clog and are hard to clear.
  • Crown-vented traps, where a vent is taken off the top of the trap.
  • Traps with moving parts, which fail over time.

The modern P-trap, the shape under every code-compliant sink, is what replaces all of these. Trap sizes are set by fixture: a lavatory uses a 1-1/4 inch trap, a kitchen sink or tub uses 1-1/2 inch, and a shower or floor drain uses 2 inch.

Why dry Arizona air makes this a real problem

A trap only works while it holds water, and water evaporates. In the low humidity of the Phoenix and Scottsdale area, a trap on a fixture nobody uses can dry out in weeks. Think of a guest-bath shower, a garage floor drain, the bathroom in a detached casita that hosts visitors twice a year, or a second home closed up for the summer. Once it does, sewer gas drifts straight up into the house, and the fix is as simple as running the tap for a moment. For fixtures that sit unused, the code allows a trap seal primer, a small valve that trickles a little water into the trap to top it off, or a barrier-type device that seals the drain when it runs dry. For example, say a Scottsdale owner locks up a second home from May through September. Nothing refills those 2-inch seals for four months, so the family walks back into a house that smells like the sewer main. Thirty seconds at each tap clears it. That is why a dried-out trap is almost always the answer when a rarely used Arizona bathroom starts to smell.

Decide about primers before rough-in

If your plan has a garage floor drain or a bathroom that will sit idle for months, ask your plumber for a trap seal primer on those two while the walls are open. It is a small line item then and a wall repair later. A trap only holds its seal if the drain is vented, which is why traps and the vents that run through the roof get designed together, and both feed the drainage system under the house. Your shower and every other fixture rides on this seal. For which code edition your AHJ enforces, see the building code editions by city reference, and if you are still picking fixtures, what a spa-style primary bathroom includes. Chapter 32 of the 2021 IRC holds the full trap rules.

title: IRC Fireplace and Chimney Rules: Hearths, Clearances, and Chimney Height
seoTitle: Fireplace and Chimney Code: IRC R1001
shortSummary: The IRC's Chapter 10 sets how a fireplace and chimney are built so they do not set the house on fire. A hearth extension protects the floor from embers, a masonry chimney keeps a set clearance from framing and rises well above the roof, and most custom homes use a listed, factory-built unit installed to its own instructions.
bodyHtml:
A fireplace is a controlled fire inside your house, so the code treats it with the caution it deserves. Whether you want a great-room fireplace or one off the patio, the IRC's Chapter 10 sets how it and its chimney get built. It comes down to a few clearances, a chimney that clears the roof, and one factory-built shortcut most custom homes take.

The hearth extension

The floor in front of a fireplace has to be noncombustible, not carpet or wood, out to a set distance, so a popping ember lands on stone or tile instead of your flooring. For a larger opening, one that is 6 square feet or more, the code is specific:

extend not less than 20 inches in front of and not less than 12 inches beyond each side of the fireplace opening.

A smaller fireplace needs a little less, 16 inches in front and 8 inches to each side. Either way, the extension shapes the flooring layout around the hearth, so it belongs on the plan early.

Clearance from combustibles

Heat travels through masonry, so the code keeps a chimney away from the wood framing it passes. A masonry chimney inside the house or within an exterior wall needs a 2-inch air space to any combustible material. One built entirely outside the exterior wall needs 1 inch. That gap is not optional, and it cannot be packed with insulation, because the point is open air, not fill.

A chimney that clears the roof

A chimney has to draft well and keep sparks away from the roof, so it has to rise above it. The rule built into the code, often called 3-2-10, is that a masonry chimney extends at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes through, and at least 2 feet higher than any part of the roof or structure within 10 feet of it. On a low-slope Arizona roof that is usually a modest stack. On a stepped roofline it gets tall fast.

For instance, say the great-room fireplace sits on a wall where the chimney passes through a single-story roof, and the two-story section of the house rises 8 feet away. The 3-2-10 rule then measures off that taller section, so the stack has to finish 2 feet above the upper roof rather than 3 feet above the roof it actually pierces. Sliding the fireplace to a wall clear of the two-story mass can take several feet off the chimney, and off the front elevation.

The factory-built shortcut

Most custom homes today do not lay up a masonry firebox from scratch. They install a factory-built fireplace, a complete listed unit tested to the UL 127 standard, with its own matching chimney and clearances. When you use one, you follow the manufacturer's listing instead of the masonry tables, including its own hearth extension. It is faster, it is lighter, and for a gas fireplace it is almost always the route a builder takes.

Which edition applies to your build

These fireplace and chimney rules are stable across recent IRC editions. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm the edition your city or county adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

A gas fireplace also needs air to burn safely, which is its own problem in a tight house and comes down to makeup-air. The details are in do I need combustion or makeup air for a gas fireplace in a tight Arizona home. If you are planning an outdoor fireplace or fire pit instead, start with do I need a permit for a fire pit or outdoor fireplace in Arizona. And the chimney is one more roof penetration that has to tie into your roof covering and its flashing. The full rules are in Chapter 10 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R309 Garages and Carports: Floors, Slope, and the Carport Line
shortSummary: IRC Section R309 sets the basics for a home's garage and carport. The floor has to be noncombustible and sloped so liquids run to a drain or out the door, a carport has to be open on at least two sides or it counts as a garage, and any garage door opener has to meet the UL 325 safety standard.
bodyHtml:
A garage looks like the simplest part of a house, but the code still keeps a short list of rules for it, and a couple of them catch people off guard. IRC Section R309 covers what the floor is made of, which way it slopes, what actually counts as a carport instead of a garage, and the one safety rule for an automatic door. Here is what applies to a new Arizona home.

The floor: noncombustible and sloped

A garage floor has to be an approved noncombustible material, which in practice means a concrete slab. The parking area also has to pitch in a set direction:

sloped to facilitate the movement of liquids to a drain or toward the main vehicle entry doorway.

That slope carries off dripped fluids, tracked-in monsoon water, and anything you hose down, instead of letting it pool against the back wall and seep toward the house. It is a small detail your slab contractor sets when the garage is poured, and it is easy to get wrong if no one is paying attention.

Carport or garage? The two-sides rule

The code draws a clean line between the two. A carport has to be open on at least two sides. If a structure built for parking is closed in on more than two sides, the code stops calling it a carport. It becomes a garage, and it has to meet every garage rule, including the fire separation from the house. One example makes the line concrete: a two-car carport open at the front and along one end meets the two-sides rule. Wall in that end for a storage bay and only the front stays open, so the structure is a garage on paper. That change is a permit item. It goes through plan review like any other alteration, and the shared wall has to meet the R302 standard. Carports do get one break: asphalt is allowed as the floor at ground level, where a garage needs the noncombustible slab.

The garage door opener

The IRC does not require you to install an automatic opener at all. But if you do, R309 requires it to be listed and labeled to UL 325. That is the standard behind the auto-reverse feature, which stops the door and backs it off when something, or someone, is underneath. That is the rule that keeps a closing door from trapping a child or a pet.

What R309 does not cover

The fire wall between the garage and the living space, the self-closing door into the house, and the ban on a door opening straight into a bedroom are not in R309. Those live in the fire-resistant construction rules of R302. R309 stays focused on the floor, the carport definition, and the opener.

Which edition applies to your build

R309 is stable across recent IRC editions. Because Arizona cities and counties each adopt their own, confirm the edition your AHJ enforces in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

A garage touches several parts of the code at once: the fire separation from the house, the footings under its slab, and its size and intended use, which is where a large or car-collector garage gets planned. The garage and carport rules themselves are in Section R309 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R316 Foam Plastic: Thermal Barriers and Ignition Barriers
shortSummary: IRC Section R316 controls foam plastic insulation, which burns fast and gives off heavy smoke. The code caps its flame spread and smoke rating, and it requires a thermal barrier, usually half-inch gypsum board, between the foam and the living space. Attics and crawl spaces with limited access can use a lighter ignition barrier instead.
bodyHtml:
Foam plastic insulation does a lot of good in an Arizona home, but it has one problem: it burns fast and throws off thick, black smoke. IRC Section R316 is the code's answer. It limits how the foam can burn, and it forces a fire-rated cover between the foam and the rooms you live in. Spray foam and rigid foam board both fall under it.

What R316 requires

R316 works in two layers. First, the foam itself has to pass a burn test. Foam plastic used in a home must have a flame spread index of 75 or less and a smoke-developed index of 450 or less, measured at the thickness you plan to install. Second, the foam has to sit behind a thermal barrier that holds back fire long enough for people to get out. R316.4 puts it this way:

foam plastic shall be separated from the interior of a building by an approved thermal barrier of not less than 1/2 inch gypsum wallboard

Half-inch gypsum board (standard drywall) is the common way to meet it. A 23/32 inch wood structural panel, or any product tested to the NFPA 275 fire standard, also works. The idea is simple: you should not be able to see or touch bare foam from inside a finished room.

The ignition barrier exception for attics and crawl spaces

Attics and crawl spaces get an easier rule. Where the space is entered only to service utilities and access is limited, the foam can be covered by a lighter ignition barrier instead of the full thermal barrier. An ignition barrier is a thinner protective layer, such as 1.5 inch mineral fiber, 0.25 inch wood structural panel, or 0.375 inch particleboard. Many spray foam products also carry an ICC evaluation report that lets them stay exposed in an attic with no cover at all, as long as the installer follows the tested conditions. This exception is why a foamed attic can show bare foam and still pass inspection.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, take a common Arizona high-performance detail: spray foam applied to the underside of the roof deck to make a sealed, conditioned attic. Because that attic has no drywall on the roof slope, the foam is exposed. To pass, the builder either sprays a product listed for exposed use or coats the foam with an ignition barrier. In the garage the rule is tighter. Foam in a garage wall or ceiling has to sit behind 1/2 inch gypsum board, the same thermal barrier the house gets, because a garage is a frequent ignition point. Insulated concrete form (ICF) walls follow R316 too: the foam faces have to be covered with 1/2 inch gypsum board on the inside.

Which edition applies to your build

R316's numbers, the 75 flame spread limit, the 450 smoke limit, and the 1/2 inch thermal barrier, hold steady across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC. Because Arizona has no statewide code and each city adopts its own edition, confirm which one governs your build on the Arizona building code editions by city page.

How this connects to the rest of your build

R316 works alongside the fire-resistant construction rules of R302, where the same gypsum board often forms the garage-to-house fire wall. When foam seals an attic, it changes how you handle roof ventilation and how you finish a habitable attic. If you are weighing a foam-core wall system, see whether ICF homes are worth it in Arizona. The full section is R316 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R318 Subterranean Termite Protection: What an Arizona Home Needs
shortSummary: IRC Section R318 requires new homes in termite-prone areas, which cover Arizona's low desert, to be built with subterranean termite protection. Builders choose from set methods: a soil-applied termiticide, a bait system, pressure-treated or naturally durable wood, physical barriers, or steel framing. In very heavy zones, foam plastic below grade faces added limits.
bodyHtml:
Termites are the number one structural pest in the Phoenix and Tucson metros. The desert subterranean termite works year round in warm soil. Section R318 of the International Residential Code (IRC) makes a builder design that pressure out of a new home. It applies to any home in an area the code flags for termite risk, and all of the Arizona low desert qualifies.

What R318 requires

R318 does not force one product on you. A home in a termite area has to use at least one approved method of protection:

In areas subject to damage from termites ... methods of protection shall be one of the following methods or a combination of these methods.

The code lists six methods. The most common is a soil termiticide, a chemical put in the ground under and around the house. The others are a termite bait system, pressure-treated wood, naturally durable termite-resistant wood, physical barriers such as steel mesh or a treated sand layer, and steel framing. Most Arizona homes use the soil termiticide. A licensed applicator sprays it on the graded pad and the footing trenches, right before the slab is poured. It is the low-cost method, and it covers the whole footprint at once.

Why Arizona sits in the very heavy zone

The code ties the rule to a map. The 2021 IRC uses the Termite Infestation Probability map, Figure R301.2(7). It sorts the country into four bands, from "none to slight" up to "very heavy." Arizona's low desert, including the Valley, falls in the "very heavy" band, the top one. That rating does two things. It makes termite protection mandatory on a new home. It also triggers a second rule for foam plastic.

Under R318.4, you cannot put foam plastic insulation on a foundation below grade in a "very heavy" area. That means no rigid foam (polystyrene or polyiso) on the outside face of a foundation wall, or under a slab, below the soil line. The one exception is a design that adds an approved termite barrier for the foam and the framing. Foam gives termites a hidden path up into the wood, and an inspector cannot see them tunnel through it. Where foam is used above grade, the code wants at least a 6-inch gap between the foam and bare soil. That leaves a strip you can inspect.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, take a custom home in Cave Creek. The termite treatment is a set step in the foundation work. After the pad is graded and the plumbing is set, the applicator sprays the soil termiticide across the pad and into the footing trenches. Then the crew lays the vapor barrier and pours the slab. The treatment is cheap next to the build, often a few hundred dollars, and it carries a renewable warranty. If your energy plan calls for rigid foam at the slab edge, your builder has to detail it so it does not break the foam rule. Usually that means keeping foam off the below-grade face, or adding a termite barrier and a visible inspection gap. That is one more reason the footing and slab-edge details get drawn with care on a desert home.

Edition note and related rules

R318 is stable across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC, though the map's figure number has shifted between editions. Termite protection also works with R317, which calls for treated or naturally durable wood where framing sits close to concrete or soil. Which edition your city enforces is on the Arizona building code editions by city page. For the soil work at the same stage, see do I need a soil test to build a house in Arizona. Read the full section on the ICC site: 2021 IRC R318 on codes.iccsafe.org.

title: IRC R322 Flood-Resistant Construction: Building in an Arizona Flood Zone
shortSummary: If your Arizona lot sits in a mapped flood hazard area, IRC Section R322 controls how you build. The lowest floor must sit at or above the design flood elevation, any enclosure below it needs flood openings and flood-resistant materials, and your utilities have to sit above the flood level.
bodyHtml:
Arizona floods in flashes. A dry wash can run several feet deep with fast water during a monsoon storm. Large parts of the state sit inside FEMA-mapped flood zones. If your lot is one of them, IRC Section R322 changes how you build, and a floodplain approval sits on top of your normal building permit. Here is what R322 actually asks for.

When R322 applies

R322 only kicks in when your lot is in a designated flood hazard area, usually a Special Flood Hazard Area on a FEMA flood insurance rate map. In that case your county floodplain administrator has a say alongside the building department. If you are buying land near a wash or a river, confirm your flood zone before you design. It drives your foundation height, your materials, and your budget. Start with the Maricopa County floodplain use permit question.

How high the lowest floor has to sit

The core rule is height. Your lowest floor has to sit at or above the design flood elevation, the flood level your community adopts for a major storm. Arizona's most common flood areas are shallow-flooding AO zones, where water sheets across the desert a foot or two deep. There the code sets a floor. If the map lists a depth number, you build up to that depth above the highest adjacent grade. If it does not, you go up at least 3 feet. Many Arizona communities then add freeboard on top, a foot or so above the base flood elevation for margin. A Valley builder usually gains that height with a taller stem wall and imported fill rather than piers.

For example, take an AO zone lot with a mapped depth of 2 feet. The lowest floor has to sit 2 feet above the highest adjacent grade, and a 1-foot local freeboard puts the finished floor 3 feet up. On a flat desert lot that is a taller stem wall, imported fill, and a driveway that has to climb the same 3 feet to meet the garage.

The code is careful about what counts as the lowest floor. A garage or storage space below that level does not automatically put you in violation, as long as it stays unfinished, flood-resistant, and:

useable solely for vehicle parking, building access or limited storage.

Openings, materials, and utilities below the line

Any enclosed area below the design flood elevation needs flood openings. The usual case is a parking space under a raised house. The openings let water flow in and out on its own, so a wall of floodwater cannot push the enclosure over. Floors and walls below that line have to be flood-damage-resistant materials, meaning they can get wet and dry out without failing. Electrical gear, HVAC equipment, plumbing, and ductwork also sit at or above the flood level. One storm should not take out the systems that make the house livable.

Which edition and local rules apply

R322 is stable across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC, but your local floodplain ordinance can be stricter than the base code, especially on freeboard. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm both the edition and the flood rules your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference.

How this connects to the rest of your build

Building in a flood zone means R322 plus a separate floodplain approval, and it changes how you plan drainage and foundations. Because a lender is involved, price in flood insurance on your construction loan early. FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program provisions stand behind the elevation and materials rules. The full requirements are in Section R322 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R326 Habitable Attics: Turning Attic Space Into a Real Room
shortSummary: IRC Section R326 sets the rules that turn attic space into legal living space. A habitable attic needs the same minimum floor area and ceiling height as any room, at least half the required floor area at 7 feet, plus its own escape window and a real stairway, not a pull-down ladder.
bodyHtml:
An attic can be storage, or it can be a real room, and the code treats those very differently. IRC Section R326 is the short list of rules that turn attic space into legal, livable space. If you want a bonus room, a loft, or a bedroom tucked under the roof, R326 sets the floor area, the ceiling height, the escape route, and the stair you need.

What makes an attic habitable

A habitable attic is finished space in the attic that people use like any other room, and it has to meet the same basics. The floor area has to hit the minimum room size in Section R304. The ceiling height is measured a special way because the roof slopes. At least half of the required floor area has to have a ceiling of 7 feet or taller, and any part of the room under 5 feet does not count toward the required area at all. So a room can have low knee walls at the edges, as long as the middle stands full height over enough floor.

The one-third rule

R326 also decides whether your attic counts as another full story of the house, which can change other requirements. A habitable attic is treated as its own story above grade plane unless it stays small:

the occupiable floor area is not greater than one-third of the floor area of the story below

Add a fire sprinkler system and that limit rises to one-half. Stay under the line and the attic is livable space without being counted as a separate story. Go over it and the house is treated as having another full story, which can pull in more code.

Egress and access

Because people sleep and sit in a habitable attic, it needs a way out in a fire. Every habitable attic has to have an emergency escape and rescue opening, the same egress window a bedroom needs under R310: a clear opening of 5.7 square feet, at least 24 inches high and 20 inches wide, with the sill no higher than 44 inches off the floor. It also needs real vertical access. A fixed stairway that meets R311.7 is required, not the pull-down ladder that serves a storage attic.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, a two-story Cave Creek home might frame a bonus room over the garage inside the roof. To make it legal living space, the builder gives it a dormer or a raised ridge so 7 feet of height covers at least half the floor, adds an egress window in the dormer, and runs a full stair up to it.

The catch is that it has to be designed in from the start. Standard roof trusses fill the attic with webbing and leave no clear span for a room, so a habitable attic needs attic trusses or stick framing specified before the roof package is ordered. Arizona adds one more problem: heat. An attic room bakes unless it sits inside the cooled envelope, which in practice means a conditioned attic, a roof deck sealed with spray foam and served by real air conditioning rather than a passive vent. That foam has to follow R316, and the sealed roof changes your attic ventilation approach.

Which edition applies to your build

The habitable attic rules, the one-third area limit and the ceiling height method, are stable across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC. Confirm the edition your city enforces on the Arizona building code editions by city page.

How this connects to the rest of your build

R326 leans on several other sections at once: the ceiling height rules of R305, the escape and rescue opening of R310, and the stairway rules of R311.7. A storage attic that never becomes living space instead follows the lighter attic access rule of R807. If you are comparing ways to add square footage, see whether you can build a house with a basement in Arizona. The full section is R326 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R327 Swimming Pools, Spas and Hot Tubs: The ISPSC and Arizona's Stricter Law
shortSummary: IRC Section R327 writes no pool rules of its own. It hands pool design to the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code, whose model barrier is 48 inches. Arizona's own statute overrides that with a taller barrier, so the code layer that still matters here is the climb and gap detail: 4-inch openings, 45-inch rail spacing.
bodyHtml:
A pool is the default backyard feature on an Arizona custom home, and it is also the top drowning risk for young children in the state. IRC Section R327 is one of the shortest sections in the book. It writes no pool rules of its own. It names another code and steps aside. A state statute then overrides the barrier height that code sets, which leaves R327 carrying a narrow set of details: the ones about climbing over and squeezing through.

What R327 actually says

R327 hands the job to a separate model code. That is the whole section:

The design and construction of pools and spas shall comply with the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code.

The ISPSC carries the model barrier rules plus the rest of a pool: deck surfaces, entrapment protection at suction outlets, drains, and where the equipment pad can sit. None of that has an Arizona statute behind it, so it reaches your build only through whatever pool code your city or county actually adopted.

Where the model code stops and Arizona's statute starts

The ISPSC sets a 48 inch minimum barrier. Arizona's own pool law is taller, and it applies statewide whether or not your jurisdiction ever adopted a pool code. Barrier height, gate hardware, latch height, the safety-cover alternative, and which homes are covered at all: on every one of those the statute governs and the model number is beside the point. Those specifics live on the A.R.S. 36-1681 pool barrier page. Build to the statute first, then check what your city adds on top.

The climb and gap rules the code layer carries

Height is half a barrier. The rest is whether a child can get through it or up it.

No opening can pass a 4 inch ball. That single number sets picket spacing, and it is the same sphere rule the code uses for guards elsewhere in the house. A chain-link fence needs a mesh tight enough to stop the same 4 inch object.

Climbing comes down to rail placement. Horizontal rails have to sit at least 45 inches apart, far enough that a child cannot use the lower one as a step to the top. A fence that cannot meet that spacing has an alternative: put the rails on the pool side, out of reach from the yard, with gaps no wider than 1.75 inches. Solid block, the usual Valley choice, sidesteps the question because there is nothing to grab.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, on a new Scottsdale home with a backyard pool, the barrier gets checked at plan review and again before final inspection. Most Valley builders use the perimeter yard wall, at least 5 feet of block, as the main barrier, then add a self-closing gate on any side access. If the design lets a covered patio open straight to the pool, the city may require a separate pool-side fence so the house doors are not the only thing between a toddler and the water. Each jurisdiction runs its own review: see the pool and spa barrier permit for Maricopa County, Scottsdale, Fountain Hills, or Paradise Valley, and fold the barrier into the cost to add a pool.

Which edition and local rules apply

R327's reference to the ISPSC is stable across the 2021 and 2024 IRC, and the 2018 IRC used a similar pool reference. What matters more in Arizona is that the state pool law applies statewide, and your AHJ can add stricter rules on top of it. Confirm your local edition and amendments on the Arizona building code editions by city page.

How this connects to the rest of your build

A pool barrier is a cousin of the guards that R312 requires on raised decks and balconies: both use the 4 inch sphere rule to stop a child from slipping through. Pool wiring and metal parts follow their own safety rule in pool equipotential bonding. The full section is R327 of the 2021 IRC.
