title: IRC R328 Energy Storage Systems: Home Battery Rules
shortSummary: IRC Section R328 governs home battery systems, like a solar backup battery. Each unit is capped at 20 kWh, and the total in an indoor utility space is capped at 40 kWh. Batteries must be listed to UL 9540, kept out of bedrooms, and spaced about 3 feet apart.
bodyHtml:
Home batteries showed up on Arizona roofs and garage walls faster than the building code could keep pace. The 2021 IRC caught up with Section R328, the first version of the residential code to set specific rules for a stationary battery like a Tesla Powerwall or an Enphase system. It controls how big the battery can be, where it can go, and how it has to be tested.

What R328 requires

R328 starts with a listing. A home energy storage system (ESS) has to be listed and labeled to UL 9540, the safety standard for the whole battery unit. From there the code caps the size. A single ESS unit can be no larger than 20 kWh, and the total inside an indoor spot like a utility closet, basement, or storage room is capped at 40 kWh. An attached or detached garage, or a detached accessory structure, doubles that ceiling to 80 kWh. The units also have to sit at least 3 feet apart, unless the maker's UL 9540A fire test shows a shorter distance is safe.

Where a battery can and cannot go

Location is the heart of R328, because a battery fire is hard to put out. The code keeps batteries out of the spaces where people sleep. Here is the core limit:

ESS shall not be installed in sleeping rooms, or closets or spaces opening directly into sleeping rooms

Allowed spots are the ones you would expect: an attached or detached garage, a dedicated utility closet, a basement, a storage or utility room, or outside on an exterior wall or a ground mount. Outdoor units have to keep clearance from doors and windows so a fire cannot vent straight into the house.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, a Fountain Hills home adding rooftop solar often pairs it with two Powerwalls at 13.5 kWh each, mounted on the garage wall. That is two units of 27 kWh total, so it clears the 20 kWh per-unit cap and fits the garage. The pair either keeps the 3 foot spacing or mounts closer, which the Powerwall's UL 9540A fire test allows. Arizona homeowners add batteries for two reasons: backup power when summer heat strains the grid or a monsoon storm drops a line, and savings on time-of-use electric rates. The garage wall is their common home because R328 pushes the battery out of the bedrooms and hallways.

Which edition applies to your build

This is one section where the edition really matters. R328 is new in the 2021 IRC. It did not exist in the 2018 IRC. If your city still enforces the 2018 code, your battery is governed instead by the electrical provisions, the maker's instructions, and the fire standard NFPA 855, which cover much of the same ground. Because Arizona cities adopt different editions, check what your AHJ enforces on the Arizona building code editions by city page before you plan the install.

How this connects to the rest of your build

A storage battery is the back half of a solar project, so R328 works with the rooftop solar rules of R324 and the same city solar permits, such as the Scottsdale solar PV permit or the Maricopa County solar PV permit. Since the garage is the usual location, it also overlaps the garage rules of R309. If an HOA and its CC&Rs are in the picture, see whether an HOA can stop you from putting solar on your house. The full section is R328 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R404 Foundation and Retaining Walls: The Arizona Engineering Line
shortSummary: IRC Section R404 sets how foundation walls and retaining walls are built and reinforced. Foundation walls are sized from tables by wall height and soil pressure. Any retaining wall not braced at the top that holds back more than 48 inches of unbalanced soil has to be engineered, which is common on Arizona hillside and expansive-soil lots.
bodyHtml:
A foundation has two structural parts in the code. R403 covers the footings that spread the load onto the soil. Section R404 of the International Residential Code (IRC) covers the walls that stand on those footings: the foundation walls, including the stem wall under a slab-on-grade house, and any retaining walls that hold back a slope. In Arizona, where lots run from flat desert to steep foothills and the soil often swells, R404 is where a lot of the engineering happens.

What R404 requires

R404 sizes a foundation wall to the load pushing on it. A concrete or masonry foundation wall is selected from the code's tables using three inputs: the height of the wall, the height of unbalanced backfill against it, and the sideways pressure of the soil (written as an equivalent fluid density). Taller walls, deeper backfill, and heavier soil all call for a thicker wall and more steel. An 8-inch nominal wall is the common minimum, with reinforcement placed per the table. A plain concrete wall is allowed only in light-load cases, so most walls need rebar.

Retaining walls get their own rule. A freestanding retaining wall crosses into engineered territory once it holds back real height:

Retaining walls that are not laterally supported at the top and that retain in excess of 48 inches of unbalanced fill ... shall be designed in accordance with accepted engineering practice.

That 48-inch line (measured as unbalanced fill, roughly the bottom of the footing to the top of the retained soil) is the trigger. Above it, the wall has to be designed by an engineer to resist overturning, sliding, soil pressure, and water uplift, and it needs its own permit.

The Arizona angle: expansive soil and slopes

Two local conditions push more Arizona walls into engineering. First, expansive soil. Valley clay swells when it gets water and shrinks when it dries, which raises the sideways pressure on any buried wall and can heave a stem wall that was not designed for it. A soils report sets the design pressure, and on a bad lot the fix is a stiffened, often post-tensioned foundation rather than a plain wall. Second, slopes. Hillside lots in Fountain Hills, Cave Creek, and Paradise Valley routinely need site walls taller than 48 inches, so those walls get stamped drawings and a separate review.

A real example

For example, on a build in the Fountain Hills foothills, a lot with a 5-foot grade change needs a retaining wall. Because 5 feet is over the 48-inch line and the wall is not braced at the top, an engineer designs it: footing size, wall thickness, rebar, and often weep holes or a drain behind it to relieve water pressure. The house itself may sit on a short grade beam and stem wall sized to the soils report. None of that is optional once the numbers cross the code's thresholds.

Edition note and related rules

The R404 wall tables and the 48-inch retaining-wall trigger carry across the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC. Local amendments and the soils report drive the actual design, so confirm the edition your city enforces on the Arizona building code editions by city page. R404 works directly with the footings of R403 and the slab of R506. For how a swelling lot changes the design, see foundation design for expansive soil in Arizona. The section text is on the ICC site: 2021 IRC R404 on codes.iccsafe.org.

title: IRC R507 Deck Requirements: Ledger Attachment and Lateral Load in Arizona
shortSummary: IRC Section R507 governs how an exterior deck is built and, most of all, how it attaches to the house. The ledger has to be bolted rather than nailed, a separate lateral-load connection ties the deck back to the floor framing, footings carry the loads to the ground, and guards are required more than 30 inches above grade.
bodyHtml:
Deck collapses almost always trace back to one thing: how the deck was attached to the house. IRC Section R507 exists to prevent that. It sets how an exterior deck connects to the home, how it sits on the ground, and how it keeps people from falling off the edge. In Arizona this matters most on hillside lots and second-story balconies, where a deck can sit well off the ground.

The ledger connection, and why nails are banned

A deck attached to the house hangs from a ledger board fastened to the home's floor framing. The code requires 1/2-inch lag screws or through-bolts, driven into at least 1.5 inches of solid wood and staggered along the board. Nails are not allowed. They work loose and pull out under load. The fasteners also have to reach all the way through:

the tip of the lag screw shall fully extend beyond the inside face of the band joist.

Flashing over the ledger is part of the same rule. Water that rots the ledger destroys the connection holding the deck up.

The lateral load connection

Bolting the ledger down is not enough by itself. The code also requires a separate lateral load connection. That is a hold-down device tying the deck framing back into the house floor, so horizontal force cannot peel the deck off the wall. Think of a crowd shifting their weight at the same moment. This is the piece that was missing in the collapses that pushed the code to add it. In practice it is a pair of tension hold-downs run through the deck joists and anchored into the house framing.

Footings and guards

The deck's posts land on concrete footings sized to carry the load down to firm soil. The same design-load rules apply to them as to the rest of the house, set out in design criteria. And wherever the deck's walking surface sits more than 30 inches above the grade below, the code requires a guard along the open sides.

Say a hillside lot drops 4 feet across the deck footprint. The uphill corner ends up 14 inches above grade and the downhill corner 62 inches. The 30-inch line then falls partway along each side, so the guard requirement picks up there and carries around the low end, even though the same deck sits under the line at its uphill corner.

Decks versus patios in Arizona

R507 is about structural, usually raised wood decks and balconies. A ground-level concrete patio poured on grade is not a deck under R507, so it needs no ledger or lateral connection. Most Arizona homes have covered patios at grade. Hillside and two-story designs often add a true raised deck for the view, and that is where R507 applies in full.

Which edition applies to your build

R507 has grown more detailed across recent editions. The 2021 IRC carries prescriptive tables for ledgers, joists, beams, and connections. Because Arizona cities and counties each adopt their own, confirm the edition your AHJ enforces in the building code editions by city reference before your framer sets the ledger.

How this connects to the rest of your build

A deck ties several code sections together: the footings that carry it, the guards that protect its edges, and the wall it hangs on. If what you want is a covered outdoor space rather than an raised deck, start with the ramada and shade structure permit question. The full deck provisions are in Section R507 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R609 Exterior Windows and Doors: Wind Rating and Flashing in Arizona
shortSummary: IRC Section R609 makes every exterior window and glass door strong enough for the local wind. Each unit carries a design pressure rating and an AAMA label proving it was tested, and it must be installed and flashed to the maker's instructions. In Arizona that is what holds up to monsoon wind, dust, and rain.
bodyHtml:
A window is a hole in your wall, and in a monsoon that hole has to hold back wind-driven rain, blowing dust, and gusts that can top a hundred miles an hour. IRC Section R609 is the rule that makes sure the windows and glass doors in a new home are actually built and installed to take it.

The design pressure rating

Every exterior window and glass door has to resist the wind load for your specific site. The code ties that load to the design wind speed and the exposure of your location, and it shows up on the unit as a design pressure, or DP, rating. A window rated for a higher pressure holds back a stronger gust before it leaks or fails. In open Arizona desert the exposure is unforgiving and the design wind speed is real, so the DP rating is not a spec to gloss over, especially on the tall or wide glass that custom homes love.

For instance, take a 16-foot multi-slide door on the windward wall of an exposed ridge lot. Big panels and open exposure both push the required design pressure up, so a stock unit that passes on a sheltered infill lot may not clear the rating here. Catch that at plan review and it is a spec change. Catch it after the opening is framed and it is a much more expensive one.

The label that proves it

You do not have to take the maker's word for the rating. The code requires exterior windows and sliding doors to be tested by an independent lab and to carry a label. That label lists the manufacturer, the performance rating, and the inspection agency, all tied to the AAMA/WDMA/CSA 101 standard that governs window and door performance. When your plans are reviewed, that label is how the city confirms the glass actually meets the wind load for the site.

Installation is half the code

A strong window installed wrong still leaks. So R609 leans hard on the manufacturer. Windows have to be:

installed and flashed in accordance with the manufacturer's written installation instructions.

The flashing is the part that fails most in Arizona, where a hard monsoon rain drives water straight at the head and sill of every opening. Done right, the flashing laps into the water-resistive barrier and sheds that water back out of the wall. Done wrong, it funnels the water into the framing, where it can rot studs and feed mold for years before anyone notices.

What R609 does not cover

R609 treats the window as a structural and weather unit. It does not decide where you need tempered safety glazing, which is R308, or how large a bedroom egress window must be, which is R310, or the heat performance of the glass, which the energy code sets through U-factor and SHGC limits. Those separate rules all apply to the same window.

Which edition applies to your build

Watch the section number here. Older codes carried these rules as R613, and the 2015 IRC renumbered them to R609, where they have stayed since. The substance did not change. Arizona sets no statewide code, so confirm which edition your AHJ adopted in the building code editions by city reference, and read the section number that matches it.

How this connects to the rest of your build

Windows sit where several codes meet: the safety glazing rules that force tempered glass in risky spots, the egress sizing in every bedroom, and the energy code's efficiency ratings. For the wall those windows sit in and how it handles the desert, start with whether stucco homes are good for Arizona. The window performance rules are in Section R609 of the 2021 IRC.

title: IRC R903 Roof Weather Protection: Flashing, Coping, and Monsoon Drainage
shortSummary: IRC Section R903 keeps a roof watertight through flashing, coping, and drainage. Flashing goes wherever the roof meets a wall or penetration, a cricket is required behind any chimney wider than 30 inches, and a low-slope roof that traps water needs a secondary overflow drain or scupper. On Arizona parapet roofs, these details carry the monsoon.
bodyHtml:
A roof has two different jobs in the code. R905 sets which covering goes on which slope. Section R903 of the International Residential Code (IRC) handles the parts that actually stop water at the weak points: the flashing, the coping on a parapet, and the drainage. On a flat-roofed desert home taking a monsoon downpour, R903 is doing most of the work.

What R903 requires

Flashing is metal or membrane installed at every joint where water could sneak in: where the roof meets a wall, where the slope changes, and around every penetration like a vent, skylight, or chimney. Metal flashing has to resist corrosion and be at least 0.019 inch thick, with No. 26 galvanized sheet as the benchmark.

Chimneys get a specific rule. On the uphill side, water runs down the roof and piles against the chimney unless you divert it:

A cricket or saddle shall be installed on the ridge side of any chimney or penetration more than 30 inches wide.

A cricket is a small ridged structure that splits the water around the obstruction. A parapet wall needs a coping across the top, a weatherproof cap at least as wide as the wall, so water does not soak down into it. For drainage, a roof that cannot shed water over its edges needs roof drains at the low points. Where a blocked drain would pond water behind a parapet, R903 requires a backup. That secondary overflow drain or scupper sits with its inlet 2 inches above the roof low point, so if the primary drain clogs, water escapes before it loads the structure. Overflow scuppers are sized larger, with an opening at least 4 inches tall.

What it means for an Arizona custom home

For example, a contemporary home in north Scottsdale with a flat roof and parapet walls lives or dies on R903 details. There is no slope to carry water off the edge, so the roof drains to interior drains or through-wall scuppers, and the code wants a second path in case the first clogs during a hard monsoon cell. The parapet tops get coping, and every parapet-to-roof corner gets flashing tied into the water-resistive barrier on the wall. One Arizona break: the code's ice-barrier rule, which protects cold-climate eaves from ice dams, does not apply here, because the low desert does not freeze that way. Heat, not cold, is what ages these details, so the flashing metal and sealant choices matter.

Edition note and related rules

R903's flashing, cricket, coping, and drainage rules hold steady from the 2018 through the 2024 IRC. Which edition your city enforces is on the Arizona building code editions by city page. R903 works with the covering rules of R905, the framing under R802, and, when you reroof later, the prep rules of R908. For how the wall sheds water below the roofline, see exterior wall covering under R703. The section text is on the ICC site: 2021 IRC R903 on codes.iccsafe.org.

title: IRC R908 Reroofing: When an Arizona Roof Must Strip to the Deck
shortSummary: IRC Section R908 controls reroofing. You can lay a new covering over an old one only if the deck is sound, but the code forces a full tear-off when the roof is water-damaged, already carries two layers, or is tile, slate, or wood shake. In Arizona, that means most tile reroofs strip to the deck.
bodyHtml:
Most of chapter 9 is about a new roof. Section R908 of the International Residential Code (IRC) is about the next roof. It sets what you are allowed to do when the covering wears out and it is time to reroof. The core question is whether you can lay new material over the old, or have to strip the roof down to the deck first.

What R908 requires

Before anything goes back on, R908.2 asks whether the structure can carry the new roof. A covering heavier than the original triggers a load check. Then R908.3 draws the line between a recover (new covering over old) and a full replacement. A recover is the cheaper option, but the code bans it in several cases:

A roof recover shall not be permitted where the existing roof has two or more applications of any type of roof covering.

You also tear off down to the deck when the existing deck is water-soaked or deteriorated. Same when the current roof is wood shake, slate, clay or concrete tile, or asbestos-cement. In plain terms: you get at most two layers of asphalt shingles before the next reroof has to be a tear-off. You generally cannot leave old tile or shake in place under a new roof. There are narrow exceptions, such as metal panels or tile laid over an existing wood-shake roof, but do not plan around them.

What it means for an Arizona tile roof

For example, most custom homes across the Valley wear concrete or clay tile. R908 means a tile reroof is almost always a strip to the deck. That is not wasted work here. On an Arizona tile roof the tile is a rain and sun screen, and the underlayment beneath it is the actual waterproof layer. Heat and ultraviolet cook that underlayment from below and above, so it often fails decades before the tile does. A typical Valley reroof lifts and stacks the existing tile, tears off the old underlayment, installs a new high-temperature membrane, and relays the same tile. While the deck is open, the crew redoes the flashing and checks the attic ventilation, because those are far easier to fix with the tile off. It is also the natural moment to step up to a cool roof tile or coating, since the tile is already off and stacked. A reroof needs its own permit in every Valley jurisdiction.

Edition note and related rules

The recover-versus-replacement rules and the two-layer limit in R908 read the same in the 2018, 2021, and 2024 IRC. Confirm the edition your city enforces on the Arizona building code editions by city page. Reroofing pulls in the covering rules of R905, the flashing of R903, and the framing capacity set by R802. The truss or rafter design fixes how much weight the roof can carry. The section text is on the ICC site: 2021 IRC R908 on codes.iccsafe.org.

title: Surprise Adopted Building Codes: The 2024 I-Codes That Apply to Your Build
seoTitle: Surprise, AZ Building Codes: The 2024 Editions
shortSummary: Surprise builds to the 2024 International Residential, Building, Energy, Plumbing, Mechanical, Fuel Gas, Fire, and Existing Building codes plus the 2023 National Electrical Code, with local amendments. The City adopted them December 2, 2025, by Ordinance 2025-14, effective January 1, 2026.
bodyHtml:
A new house in Surprise is checked against a set of national model codes that the City Council voted to adopt, then edited with local amendments. The edition matters, because a detail drawn to the 2018 codes and one drawn to the 2024 codes can call for different framing, wiring, or energy work. This page lists the codes Surprise enforces today, when they took effect, and how the city handled the switch from the older edition.

Which codes Surprise enforces

Surprise adopted the 2024 family of International Codes (often called I-codes) plus the 2023 electrical code, by Ordinance 2025-14. Here is the list the city publishes, effective January 1, 2026:

  • 2024 International Residential Code (IRC): one- and two-family homes and townhouses. This is the main code for a custom house.
  • 2024 International Building Code (IBC): larger and commercial buildings.
  • 2024 International Energy Conservation Code (IECC): insulation, air sealing, duct tightness, and lighting efficiency.
  • 2024 International Plumbing Code (IPC): water supply, drains, and fixtures.
  • 2024 International Mechanical Code (IMC): heating, cooling, and ventilation.
  • 2024 International Fuel Gas Code (IFGC): gas piping and gas appliances.
  • 2024 International Fire Code (IFC) and 2024 International Existing Building Code (IEBC).
  • 2023 National Electrical Code (NEC): all wiring and electrical work.
  • 2017 ICC A117.1: the accessibility standard.

The IRC is the one a single-family builder works in day to day. The City of Surprise is the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) inside city limits, so its Building Safety Division reviews the plans and inspects the work.

What the city says

The city's code page states when and how the new codes were adopted:

On December 2, 2025, the City of Surprise adopted the nationally recognized building and fire safety standards developed by the International Code Council (ICC).

Each model code carries Surprise amendments, collected in one document titled Local Amendments to the 2024 International Codes and the 2023 National Electrical Code, dated January 1, 2026. The rule you build to is the published 2024 edition as changed by that document. A few residential amendments show how local the edits get:

  • Design criteria. The amended IRC Table R301.2 sets a 0 ground snow load, a 105 mph design wind speed (Exposure B unless the building official says otherwise), Seismic Design Category B, a 0 inch frost line, and moderate to heavy termite risk. Flood hazards follow Maricopa County flood control requirements.
  • Small structures. A one-story detached accessory structure of 200 square feet or less, and a fence of 6 feet or less, need no building permit. The 2024 model code allows a 7 foot fence; Surprise lowered it to 6.
  • Energy testing. Third-party testing by RESNET certified raters is accepted for the air barrier checklist, the air leakage test, and the duct tightness test.
  • Permit life. A permit expires if work does not start within 180 days of issue or if 180 days pass between inspections, and every permit expires 24 months after issue unless the work has passed final inspection.

When this comes into play

The switch date is what decides which edition your plans follow. The city's implementation notice says the 2024 codes apply to applications submitted on or after January 1, 2026, while permits already submitted, in review, or under construction were not affected. For a custom home the rule is direct:

Custom Home Plans submitted on or after January 1, 2026, will need to comply with the 2024 Codes.

Production builders were given more room. Standard plans approved under the 2018 I-codes stay valid until January 1, 2027, and a subdivision is not treated as a whole, so two houses in the same neighborhood can be built under different editions depending on when each application went in.

Here is a concrete example. Suppose you bought a set of plans that a designer drew for a Surprise lot in 2024, and you submit them in spring 2026. Because the application is new, the plan reviewer checks the house against the 2024 IRC, the 2024 energy code as amended, and the 2023 NEC. Sheets copied from the 2018 edition can come back with corrections before a permit issues.

What this means for you

Give your designer, engineer, and trades one clear instruction: build to Surprise's 2024 I-codes and the 2023 NEC, with the January 1, 2026 local amendments applied. That prevents the most common plan review correction, a sheet drawn to the wrong edition. When you compare bids, ask each contractor to confirm the price covers current-code work, including the third-party energy tests.

This entry is the anchor for the Surprise building-codes module. See Surprise Residential Building Permit Requirements for how these codes are checked in plan review, and Surprise Residential Zoning and Setbacks for where the house can sit on the lot. For how Surprise compares with other cities, see Arizona building code editions by city .

Source

The adopted codes, the ordinance number, and the effective date are published by the City of Surprise: Currently Adopted Building Codes on surpriseaz.gov . The amendments are in the city's Local Amendments document , and the transition rules are in its 2024 Building Code Implementation Process .

This page is general information, not a code interpretation. Editions and amendments change, so confirm the current adopted code with the City of Surprise Community Development Department before you rely on a specific edition.

title: Surprise Residential Building Permit Requirements: What You File, Review Times and Fees
seoTitle: Surprise, AZ Residential Building Permit: What to File
shortSummary: A new home in Surprise needs a city building permit. You apply online, then upload a complete plan set, soils report, structural calculations, and Manual J, S, and D to ProjectDox. A custom home's first review takes 15 working days, and administrative and plan review fees are due at submittal.
bodyHtml:
You cannot pour a footing or frame a wall on a new Surprise home until the city issues a building permit. The permit is the city's sign-off that your plans meet the adopted codes, the zoning on your lot, and the other city rules. This page walks the real steps: where you apply, what goes in the package, how review works, and what the city charges.

What a residential permit requires

Surprise takes building permit applications online through its Permits and Applications Portal. Once the city accepts the submission, it sends a link to ProjectDox, where you upload the plans and work through review with city staff. The city's handout for a single-family home starts with a plain rule:

Applications must be completed entirely at time of submittal.

For a new house, that package includes:

  • A completed permit and plan review application with the scope of work, address, and Assessor's parcel number, plus a contractor and contact form.
  • An AutoCAD file for addressing and, when required, a sealed boundary survey showing the lot layout, setbacks, rights of way, and access easements.
  • One PDF plan set at 24 by 36 inches with a cover sheet, a site plan with dimensions from the house to every property line, and floor, foundation, roof, elevation, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical plans.
  • Manual J, S, and D calculations for the cooling equipment and ducts, and energy compliance with Chapter 11 of the 2024 IRC.
  • A soils report and structural calculations for gravity, lateral, and special loads.

Some parts go to other reviewers. A grading and drainage plan is reviewed separately by the city's engineering staff, with its own fee. A lot in a floodplain needs a floodplain use permit through the Flood Control District of Maricopa County. And a fire sprinkler system is required when the lot lacks an adequate water supply, which the handout defines as no fire hydrant within 400 feet of the house or too little water flow for the size of the building.

How review and fees work

The city's published standard review times, counted in city working days, give a residential custom home 15 days for the first review, 8 days for each later review, and 2 days for permit issuance. If the reviewer finds corrections, you revise the sheets and resubmit, and each round adds to the calendar.

Fees come at two points. The handout says:

Administrative processing and plan review fees are required at time of submittal and are non-refundable.

The Citywide Fee Schedule (Resolution 2026-16, effective May 19, 2026) builds the building permit fee from the project's valuation:

  • Building permit fee: $100 per permit, plus $6 for each $1,000 of valuation up to $999,999.99, plus $5 for each $1,000 above the first $1,000,000.
  • Plan review fee: 65% of the permit fee.
  • Administrative processing fee: 0.50% of the valuation for the first million, and 0.052% of any valuation beyond it.
  • Re-inspection: $100 per hour with a $200 minimum. A permit extension is $115 the first time.

Here is a concrete example. Suppose the city values your custom home at $500,000. The permit fee is $100 plus 500 times $6, or $3,100. Plan review is 65% of that, $2,015. The administrative processing fee is 0.50% of $500,000, or $2,500. That comes to $7,615 before any grading review, development impact fees, or utility charges. The city can give a fee quote through its permit portal, and the fee schedule changes when the council adopts a new one, so check the current version before you budget.

When this comes into play

  • Build-on-your-lot. Your designer assembles the full package, including the soils report and Manual J, before you apply, because an incomplete package is not accepted.
  • Rural lots. A lot with a private well, a septic system, or no nearby hydrant has more to show on the site plan, such as the well and septic locations and the water source, and may need a sprinkler design.
  • Owner-builder. If you pull the permit yourself instead of using a licensed contractor, you rely on Arizona's owner-builder exemption under A.R.S. 32-1121, which covers a home you intend to occupy yourself, not one built for sale or rent. Selling or renting within one year after completion is treated as evidence the home was built for sale.

What this means for you

Treat the permit as a real budget line and a real schedule step. The administrative and plan review fees are due when you apply and are not refunded, so submit a complete, current-code package the first time. Draw the site plan setbacks from your lot's actual zoning, check early for floodplain and hydrant distance, and line up the grading and drainage review alongside the building review. When we build in Surprise, we handle the permit and schedule the inspections.

This entry sits between the codes and the lot rules in the Surprise module. The codes your plans are checked against are in Surprise Adopted Building Codes , and the yards your site plan must show are in Surprise Residential Zoning and Setbacks . For how valuation-based fees compare across cities, see building permit fees by valuation or square foot .

Source

The application steps are on the city's Permits and Applications page , and the package is listed in its Single Family Resident Application Requirements . Review times come from the city's Standard Review Times , and fees from the Citywide Fee Schedule .

This page is general information, not a substitute for the city's current checklist. Submittal items, fees, and review times change, so confirm the live requirements with the City of Surprise Community Development Department before you file.

title: Surprise Residential Zoning and Setbacks: Where Your New Home Can Sit on the Lot
seoTitle: Surprise, AZ Residential Setbacks by Zoning District
shortSummary: Surprise sorts R-1 single-family lots into six categories by size, from 4,950 square feet to an acre or more. A Category B lot needs a 12 foot front, 20 foot rear, and 5 and 10 foot side yards; a one-acre Category F or RR lot needs 30 foot front and rear and 20 foot sides.
bodyHtml:
Before you draw a floor plan in Surprise, find your zoning district, because the district sets how far the house must sit from each property line. That open distance is called a setback. Surprise's zoning lives in its Land Development Ordinance (LDO), which took effect in January 2021 and replaced the older Unified Development Code. Its single-family rules sort lots into the Rural Residential (RR) district and the Residential Low Density (R-1) district, where the yards grow as the lots get bigger.

What the districts require

The R-1 district does not use one set of numbers. Its Table 106-2c sorts lots into six categories by lot area, each with its own yards and coverage limit:

  • Category A: 4,950 to 7,999 sq ft, 45 ft min width, front 12 ft (25 ft max), rear 15 ft, sides 5 and 8 ft, street side 15 ft.
  • Category B: 8,000 to 11,999 sq ft, 60 ft min width, front 12 ft (25 ft max), rear 20 ft, sides 5 and 10 ft, street side 15 ft, lot coverage 45%.
  • Category C: 12,000 to 17,999 sq ft, 80 ft min width, front 15 ft (30 ft max), rear 20 ft, sides 10 ft, street side 15 ft, coverage 40%.
  • Category D: 18,000 to 27,999 sq ft, 90 ft min width, front 20 ft (35 ft max), rear 25 ft, sides 10 and 15 ft, street side 15 ft, coverage 30%.
  • Category E: 28,000 to 43,559 sq ft, 100 ft min width, front 20 ft, rear 30 ft, sides 20 ft, street side 20 ft, coverage 30%.
  • Category F: 43,560 sq ft (one acre) or more, 130 ft min width, front 30 ft, rear 30 ft, sides 20 ft, street side 20 ft, coverage 25%.

Every R-1 category has a 35 foot height limit. In both R-1 and RR, a garage face must sit at least 20 feet from the opposing property line. A Category B lot with an RV garage may cover up to 55% of the lot.

The RR district, Table 106-2a, is for one-acre homesites in a rural setting. It needs a 43,560 sq ft lot at least 130 feet wide, 30 foot front and rear setbacks, 20 foot side and street side setbacks, a 40 foot height limit, and 25% lot coverage. The ordinance describes its purpose this way:

The rural residential (RR) zoning district provides areas for single-family homes on large lots in a rural setting and acts as an equivalent zoning for properties zoned RU-43 within the county prior to annexation by the city.

When setbacks come into play

  • Build-on-your-lot. Your designer subtracts the setbacks from the lot to find the buildable area. On a 130 by 340 foot Category F lot, you lose 30 feet off the front, 30 off the rear, and 20 off each side, leaving a pad about 90 feet wide and 280 feet deep. Coverage caps the house at 25% of the lot.
  • Corner lots. The street side yard replaces the interior side on the second frontage, so a Category B corner lot gives up 15 feet there instead of 5 or 10.
  • Planned Area Developments. Many Surprise neighborhoods were approved as Planned Area Developments, Marley Park and Prasada among them, and the city publishes each PAD document. If your lot is in one, read that PAD alongside the LDO tables.
  • Rural areas. The city is writing a new, optional Desert Rural (DR) district for existing one-acre rural neighborhoods. The draft keeps the RR yards. The city expects the process to wrap up by the end of 2026, so check whether it has been adopted before you design.

The site plan in your permit package must show the distance from each building corner to the property lines, so the city checks each setback before the permit issues.

What this means for you

Confirm your exact district, lot category, and any PAD before you buy or design. A Category B lot and a Category F lot in the same R-1 district are very different: the front yard goes from 12 feet to 30, the sides from 5 and 10 feet to 20, and coverage drops from 45% to 25%. Watch lot coverage alongside the setbacks, since on a big lot it can limit the house size more than the yards do.

This entry pairs with the rest of the Surprise module. The codes your plans are checked against are in Surprise Adopted Building Codes , and the filing steps are in Surprise Residential Building Permit Requirements . For corner lot rules in general, see corner lot and double frontage setbacks .

Source

The city explains the LDO and links the full ordinance on its Development Ordinances and Design Standards page ; the ordinance itself is on Municode . The R-1 and RR tables above are read from the current LDO text the city reproduced in its proposed Desert Rural code edits . The draft DR district is described on the city's Desert Rural Zoning District page , and PAD documents are on its Planned Area Developments page .

This page is general information, not a zoning determination. Setbacks change with PADs, plats, and amendments, so confirm your lot's district and standards with the City of Surprise Planning and Zoning Division before you design.
